items.title: Thirty years of plant farnesylation research: Few substrates, many gaps, and a clear path forward.
items.abstract: Protein farnesylation - the covalent attachment of a 15-carbon farnesyl isoprenoid to a C-terminal CaaX motif by protein farnesyltransferase (PFT, FTase) - is one of the most functionally important post-translational modifications in eukaryotic biology. In mammals, the biomedical significance of farnesylation is well established. The FTase inhibitor (FTI) lonafarnib treats Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome. FTase remains an oncology target, and chemical proteomic strategies have mapped more than 100 farnesylated substrates at single-protein resolution. In plants, genetic evidence establishes that FTase governs abscisic acid (ABA) signalling, brassinosteroid (BR) homeostasis, cytokinin (CK) partitioning, meristem development, thermotolerance, innate immunity, nitrogen sensing, and drought resilience across Arabidopsis thaliana, barley (Hordeum vulgare), canola (Brassica napus), wheat (Triticum aestivum), soybean (Glycine max), and rice (Oryza sativa). Yet fewer than fifteen substrates have been biochemically confirmed in any plant species after nearly three decades of research, and no crop species has been subjected to prenylome-scale chemical proteomics. This review synthesizes the plant and animal farnesylation literature and argues that this disconnect is methodological rather than biological. We trace the arc from FTase enzymology through the emerging catalogue of confirmed plant substrates, exemplified by the HSP40 co-chaperones J2/J3, the cytokinin-biosynthetic enzyme AtIPT3, and plasmodesmal HIPPs, to crop engineering outcomes. We propose a spatial-switch model to organize the confirmed substrate data into a unifying mechanistic framework, while acknowledging that this model awaits systematic experimental testing. Finally, we outline the chemical biology tools - alkyne-isoprenoid probes, quantitative prenylomics profiling - that must be adapted for plant systems to close the gap between substrate prediction and biochemical validation. Farnesylation exemplifies how a conserved eukaryotic modification can be harnessed for crop improvement once the underlying substrate biology is sufficiently understood.
items.authors: Daszkowska-Golec A, Sundaresan AP, Distefano MD.

items.title: Cell geometry and nuclear organization are associated with founder-cell competence for lateral root initiation in the Arabidopsis root.
items.abstract: Lateral root initiation in Arabidopsis thaliana occurs in xylem pole pericycle (Px) cells, yet the structural features associated with founder-cell competence in differentiated root tissues remain insufficiently defined. Here, we combined spatial cell biology approaches, including three-dimensional analysis of cell geometry, nuclear morphometry, EdU labeling, and auxin-induction experiments, to determine whether Px cells exhibit a structural prepattern before visible organogenesis. Px cells were already distinguishable in the root apical meristem (RAM) by their shorter length along the longitudinal root axis and larger volume relative to the remaining non-xylem-pole pericycle cells (Pr), and this geometrical distinction persisted into the differentiation zone. In the same zone, Px nuclei were less elongated and more spherical than Pr nuclei, indicating a characteristic nuclear organization. In the absence of exogenous auxin, DNA replication activity was confined mainly to inner tissues, particularly the pericycle, vasculature, and developing lateral root primordia. Upon auxin treatment, PIN1 accumulation and EdU incorporation appeared in discrete domains rather than uniformly along the root axis, indicating localized auxin responsiveness and localized cell-cycle re-entry. Continuous auxin treatment for 36h induced formative divisions in the Px domain of the early differentiation zone, where lateral root initiation occurs. Early primordia further displayed internal geometric zonation and pronounced deformation of the overlying endodermis, indicating that internal organization and tissue accommodation arise early during primordium development. Together, these observations support a model in which Px-associated cell geometry and nuclear organization represent structural correlates of founder-cell competence, while emphasizing that functional tests in signaling mutants are required to determine causality.

items.title: Conserved molecular compatibility for MIZ1 function in cytokinin signaling in land plants
items.abstract: Plant roots adjust their growth direction toward water through hydrotropism, a process that in Arabidopsis thaliana requires the endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-associated protein MIZU-KUSSEI1 (MIZ1). Nonetheless, MIZ1 orthologues occur throughout land plants, including lineages lacking true roots, raising questions about the ancestral function of this protein family. Here, we investigated the evolutionary conservation and functional diversification of MIZ1-like proteins across land plants. MIZ1 orthologues from evolutionarily distant land plants failed to restore hydrotropism or cytokinin sensitivity in the Arabidopsis miz1 mutant, despite conserved protein structure and ER localization. In the liverwort Marchantia polymorpha , loss of MpMIZ1a led to altered cytokinin sensitivity and cytokinin-mediated development in both the sporophyte and gametophyte. These phenotypes and gene expression analyses imply a conserved role of MIZ1 in cytokinin-related processes. Despite this functional similarity, protein– protein docking and bimolecular fluorescence complementation revealed species-specific interactions between MIZ1 proteins and their cognate cytokinin histidine kinase receptors in Arabidopsis and Marchantia. Together, our findings indicate that MIZ1 proteins represent ancient land plant regulators of cytokinin-dependent development whose molecular compatibility and developmental outputs have diverged during evolution. We propose that the role of MIZ1 in root hydrotropism represents a derived recruitment of this ancestral module into root-specific environmental response pathways.

items.title: An infection assay recapitulating Xanthomonas translucens pv. translucens natural entry into barley hydathodes
items.abstract: Pathogenic bacteria navigate biological host landscapes to enter and establish infection. How Xanthomonas phytopathogenic bacteria enter specific plant tissues is believed to directly determine the systemic vs. local outcome of infection. Non-vascular Xanthomonas infect leaf mesophyll locally from stomatal pores, while vascular ones enter through hydathode water pores on the leaf margin before invading the xylem for systemic movement. The pathovar Xanthomonas translucens pv. translucens (Xtt) is associated with barley infection, causing both bacterial leaf streak and bacterial blight symptoms by colonizing both the mesophyll spaces through stomatal guard cells and the plant vasculature, respectively. How Xtt reaches the vasculature in barley leaves is yet to be established. In this study, we determined the anatomy of barley hydathodes. A protocol allowing efficient hydathode infection by Xtt was established and caused bacterial blight symptoms, closely mimicking the natural infection process. This study establishes Xtt as one of the few demonstrated hydathode pathogens.
items.authors: Jauneau, A., Cerutti, A., Butchacas, J., Auriac, M.-C., Routaboul, J.-M., Bragard, C., Jacobs, J., NOEL, L. D.

items.title: Concentration-Dependent Regulation of Growth and Development by Calliterpenone through Hormonal Crosstalk in Arabidopsis thaliana.
items.abstract: Plant growth and development are governed by intricate hormonal networks that integrate environmental and endogenous signals. Plant growth regulators can be natural or synthetic chemical compounds that mimic hormonal regulation to alter plant growth and development. Here, we identify Calliterpenone (CT), a tetracyclic diterpenoid isolated from Callicarpa macrophylla, as a novel regulator of growth-defense balance in Arabidopsis thaliana. Phenotypic analyses revealed a clear concentration-dependent response, where low CT levels promoted seed germination, primary root elongation, vegetative growth, and early flowering, whereas higher concentrations inhibited root growth and shifted developmental outcomes. Cellular studies showed that CT regulates root elongation by modulating cell expansion, as evidenced by differential expression of expansin genes. CT also enhanced root hair density, indicating increased auxin responsiveness. Physiological measurements showed that CT improves photosynthetic efficiency, as evidenced by increased chlorophyll content, PSII efficiency, and gas-exchange parameters. Transcriptome profiling uncovered extensive reprogramming of genes involved in photosynthesis, metabolism, hormone signalling, and stress responses. Notably, CT modulated key flowering regulators through circadian and gibberellin (GA)-dependent pathways, enabling floral transition even under altered regulatory conditions. Hormonal analyses revealed that CT promotes GA accumulation at low concentrations, while higher levels induce auxin redistribution and jasmonic acid (JA) accumulation. Gene expression data further showed suppression of auxin biosynthesis but enhanced auxin transport and signalling, alongside a dynamic regulation of JA biosynthesis and turnover. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that CT orchestrates growth and defence by integrating GA-, auxin-, and JA-mediated pathways. This study highlights the potential of CT as a promising regulator for enhancing crop productivity and stress resilience in sustainable agriculture.

items.title: Constitutive elevation of cAMP in Arabidopsis thaliana enhances plant growth, development, and productivity.
items.abstract: Cyclic adenosine 3',5'-monophosphate (cyclic AMP; cAMP) has emerged as a bona fide signalling molecule in plants. Although its regulatory roles in diverse cellular processes are increasingly recognised, the transient nature of cAMP signalling has limited our understanding of its systemic functions at the whole-plant level. In this study, we engineered Arabidopsis thaliana plants to constitutively express adenylate cyclase (AC) activity, thereby enabling sustained elevation of endogenous cAMP levels. The AC transgenic lines exhibited a 1.3- to 1.8-fold increase in endogenous cAMP content relative to wild-type plants. Elevated cAMP promoted accelerated growth and developmental progression, enhanced photosynthetic performance, increased cellular metabolic activity, and improved productivity, as evidenced by 13-14% greater plant height, 12-17% higher 1000-seed weight, and 36-41% greater seed yield per plant. However, these growth advantages were accompanied by increased susceptibility to salinity stress, pathogen infection, and exogenous ethylene treatment compared with wild-type plants. Collectively, our findings establish cAMP as a central regulator of plant physiology that coordinates growth, development, metabolism, and stress responsiveness. While sustained elevation of endogenous cAMP enhances plant growth and productivity, it also increases sensitivity to environmental stimuli, highlighting the importance of precise spatiotemporal regulation of cAMP signalling in maintaining optimal plant performance.
items.authors: Li B, Guo Y, Xu S, Xu R.

items.title: Cytokinin regulates the gravitropic setpoint angle of seminal roots in barley and wheat
items.abstract: Plant root growth angle determines the spatial distribution of roots in soil and thereby influences access to water and nutrients when these resources are heterogeneously distributed. In barley, multiple seminal roots emerge at distinct gravitropic setpoint angles (GSAs) and they reliably re-establish their characteristic growth angles following reorientation, indicating robust intrinsic control. However, the molecular basis underlying GSA variation among roots within a single root system remains unknown. Here, we combined individual root type-specific transcriptomics with laser-capture microdissection to profile gravity-responsive zones (root cap, meristem, and elongation zone). We identified two CYTOKININ OXIDASE/DEHYDROGENASE ( CKX ) genes whose expression in the root cap was associated with root-specific GSA. Functional analysis showed that ckx mutants, which show higher cytokinin levels, exhibit significantly steeper seminal root GSAs, implicating cytokinin catabolism in root angle regulation. Consistent with this, exogenous cytokinin treatment induced a dose-dependent steepening in root angle in barley. Analyses of gravitropic curvature after gravistimulation further showed that ckx mutants exhibit altered gravitropic responses, indicating that CKX -mediated regulation of the root angle depends on gravity-responsive pathways. Notably, GSA-associated CKX expression patterns and cytokinin-dependent root angle responses were also observed in wheat, suggesting a conservation of this mechanism across cereals. Together, these findings identify cytokinin as a key regulator of root specific setpoint angles within a root system architecture, with potential implications for optimizing crop resource acquisition and yield.

items.title: The Arabidopsis outward K+ channel GORK mediates flg22-induced K+ efflux and stomatal closure
items.abstract: Transient K+ efflux occurs rapidly following pathogen-associated molecular pattern (PAMP) perception by pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) as part of pattern-triggered immunity (PTI). However, the molecular identities of the K+ channels responsible for PTI-associated K+ efflux and the mechanisms linking immune signaling to K+ channel regulation remain largely unknown. Here, we show that the channel GUARD CELL OUTWARD RECTIFYING K+ (GORK) is required for K+ efflux and stomatal closure induced by flg22, a model PAMP derived from bacterial flagellin. BOTRYTIS-INDUCED KINASE 1 (BIK1), a receptor-like cytoplasmic kinase associated with immune receptor complexes that functions as a central regulator of PTI, interacts with GORK and phosphorylates the channel on the conserved T199 residue in vitro. Electrophysiological analyses indicate that BIK1 inhibits GORK activity in a kinase-dependent manner and that T199 plays an essential role for GORK function. Together, this study identifies GORK as the key K+ channel executing rapid PTI-associated K+ efflux and associated stomatal closure, thus shedding light on the mechanisms of early immune signaling.
items.authors: Wang, L., Yue, L., Toth, R., Choi, S., Zhang, S., Maierhofer, T., Snoeck, S., Kim, G., Bender, K. W., Lee, Y., Geiger, D., DeFalco, T. A., Hedrich, R., Zipfel, C.

items.title: Cross-species transcriptomics uncovers shared responses to water deficiency in plants.
items.abstract: Deepening our knowledge of conserved molecular mechanisms governing stress responses in plants is fundamental for identifying new core genes and processes involved in tolerance to adverse environmental conditions. For this purpose, we developed a bioinformatic pipeline to retrieve and integrate stress-related RNA-seq transcriptomic data from species of interest and identify core species-specific and cross-species conserved genes and processes involved in stress responses. We utilized this approach to investigate the molecular mechanisms underpinning drought response in Arabidopsis thaliana, Triticum aestivum, and Solanum lycopersicum. We found that hormone signaling, reactive oxygen species catabolism, cell wall organization, photosynthesis, and defense mechanisms were dysregulated in response to drought in at least two species. Among the identified cross-species conserved differentially expressed genes, PUB19, EDL3, RAB18, and AAP6 confirmed to play a key role in drought response. Coexpression networks identified central genes underpinning drought-response, such as HB-7 in leaves and P5CS1 in roots. Leveraging PlantConnectome, several drought-responsive genes not classified as such in Gene Ontology were also detected, including EULS3, PUB19, BFT, DAA1, involved in carbohydrate recognition, ubiquitination, abscisic acid signaling, and membrane integrity maintenance, highlighting the need for further investigation. In conclusion, the developed approach proved effective in identifying core drought-responsive genes and processes and has the potential to be applied to other plant species and types of stress.
items.authors: Punzi F, Zuluaga DL, Tan QW, Mutwil M, Sonnante G, Curci PL.

items.title: Temporal dynamics of photosynthetic inhibition, antioxidant defense, and transcriptomic reprogramming in 'Crimson Seedless' grapevine under saline-alkali stress.
items.abstract: Soil salinization alkalization is among the most critical abiotic stressors affecting crop productivity yet the molecular physiological mechanisms governing grapevine (Vitis vinifera L.) responses to combined saline-alkali stress remain poorly understood. This study investigated the temporal dynamics of 'Crimson Seedless' grapevine plants propagated from cuttings. Integrated morphological transcriptomic physiological data were collected over a 15-day period of progressive saline-alkali stress. The results showed that saline-alkali stress affected photosynthesis in two phases. During the initial days of stress stomatal closure reduced CO2 uptake as evidenced by parallel drops in Pn Gs Ci. In the later stages non-stomatal limitations dominated. Pn decreased by 88% by day 15 while Ci rose despite low Gs. In addition stress triggered ROS accumulation membrane damage osmotic dehydration. Transcriptomic analysis revealed 3,795 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) at 7 days 4,084 at 15 days. Further analysis revealed that stress upregulated MAPK signaling hormone transduction flavonoid biosynthesis while downregulating photosynthesis-related ribosomal genes. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) identified VvWRKY47 as a candidate transcription factor. Quantitative real-time PCR (qRT PCR) validation confirmed that VvWRKY47 expression was induced under saline-alkali conditions. Subcellular localization assays showed the nuclear localization of VvWRKY47 phenotypic analysis of transgenic Arabidopsis plants overexpressing VvWRKY47 revealed enhanced growth performance under salt stress compared to empty vector controls.

items.title: COI1 phosphorylation status drives redox state-mediated thermotolerance in plants
items.abstract: Abstract High temperature increasingly threatens crop growth and yield under climate change. Plants rely on phytohormone signalling to adapt to heat stress, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. One of the plant hormone receptors, the jasmonate receptor CORONATINE-INSENSITIVE 1 (COI1), plays an essential role in conferring plant thermotolerance. However, to date, the molecular mechanisms by which COI1 mediates plant high temperature tolerance remain enigmatic. Here, we characterise moderately high temperature-regulated differential phosphorylation of TaCOI1-1D, one of the wheat COI1 homeologous proteins. We show that TaCOI1-1D is a functional component of the Skp1–Cullin–F-box COI1 (SCF COI1 ) complex and that its heat-regulated phosphosite, Ser16, is conserved with Thr16 in Arabidopsis COI1. Mutating this site enhances the COI1– ARABIDOPSIS SKP1 HOMOLOGUE 1 (ASK1) interaction in both wheat and Arabidopsis. We further demonstrate that Arabidopsis COI1 interacts with the nucleocytosolic monothiol glutaredoxin glutaredoxin S17 (GRXS17). The enhanced COI1–ASK1 binding stabilizes COI1 and promotes the release of GRXS17, allowing the formation of GRXS17 oligomers, a possibly essential state for AtGRXS17’s function in regulating H 2 O 2 scavenging and enhancing thermotolerance in Arabidopsis. Our findings reveal a mechanism in which a moderately high temperature-induced modification of the JA receptor simultaneously stabilizes the receptor and orchestrates redox-dependent thermotolerance.
items.authors: De Smet I, Zhu T, Williams C, Durand AN, Martins L, de Lima CFF, Lysebeth IV, De Cotte BV, Xin M, Pauwels L, Riondet C, Reichheld J, Goossens A.

items.title: Waterlogging and hypoxia in plant abiotic stress.
items.abstract: Waterlogging is a major abiotic stress affecting 12-27% of global cultivated land and causing average yield losses of 20-33% in cereals and legumes. This poses a serious threat to food security in flood-prone regions. Soil saturation reduces gas diffusion nearly 10,000-fold compared to air. This rapidly induces hypoxia or anoxia in the root zone within hours to days. This oxygen limitation forces a metabolic shift from efficient aerobic respiration (approximately 36 ATP per glucose) to anaerobic fermentation (approximately 2 ATP per glucose). This shift results in severe energy deficits, cytoplasmic acidosis, and accumulation of toxic metabolites such as ethanol, acetaldehyde, and organic acids. Plants exhibit diverse adaptive responses to flooding stress, including morphological modifications such as aerenchyma formation, adventitious root development, hypertrophied lenticels, and shoot elongation in deepwater rice. These modifications facilitate internal oxygen transport and gas exchange. At the biochemical level, fermentative enzymes including alcohol dehydrogenase and pyruvate decarboxylase are upregulated, while antioxidant defense systems mitigate oxidative damage during reoxygenation. Hormonal crosstalk among ethylene, abscisic acid, auxin, and gibberellins regulates the balance between escape and quiescence strategies. At the molecular level, oxygen sensing is primarily mediated by the N-degron pathway through Group VII Ethylene Response Factors (ERF-VIIs). Plant cysteine oxidases regulate oxygen-dependent degradation under normoxia, while hypoxia stabilizes ERF-VIIs to activate anaerobic gene expression. Nitric oxide further modulates ERF-VII proteolysis and stability. The Sub1A locus in rice exemplifies genetic adaptation, conferring 14-18 days of submergence tolerance and significant yield advantages in flood-prone environments. Despite these advances, major crops such as wheat, maize, and soybean remain highly susceptible, underscoring the need for translating mechanistic insights into field-level solutions. Integrating CRISPR/Cas-based gene editing, genomic selection, multi-omics approaches, and improved agronomic practices offers promising avenues for developing flood-resilient crop varieties under changing climatic conditions.
items.authors: Kumar A, Kumar M, Kumar N, Saxena K, Parveen R, Singh D, Singh SP, Satyendra, Sultana R, Sinha S.

items.title: NRT1.1 as central signaling hub orchestrating plant growth and stress trade-offs.
items.abstract: Plants must continuously balance nitrogen-dependent growth with adaptation to environmental stresses. The nitrate transporter AtNRT1.1 in Arabidopsis thaliana and its rice ortholog OsNRT1.1B have been reported to integrate nitrogen- and stress-related signals in their respective species. This review synthesizes how NRT1.1 orthologs coordinate nitrate and stress signaling. Experimentally characterized NRT1.1 forms a homodimer, and phosphorylation of a key threonine residue (Thr101) acts as a molecular switch, toggling between high- and low-affinity nitrate transport modes. OsNRT1.1B also functions as a high-affinity ABA receptor in rice. NRT1.1 orthologs may integrate nitrate and ABA signals via allosteric regulation and ligand competition. Signaling triggers cellular responses via calcium signatures and kinase cascades, driving transcriptional reprogramming through NLP transcription factors, including AtNLP2/7 in Arabidopsis and OsNLP3/4 in rice. These responses include root architecture remodeling, rhizosphere homeostasis, nitrogen-phosphorus coordination, and shoot-root developmental synchronization. This review also discusses the evolution of the NRT1.1 signaling, highlighting experimentally supported core functions and lineage-specific innovations. The nitrate transport/signaling module discussed here is supported primarily by studies of AtNRT1.1 in Arabidopsis, whereas the ABA-receptor module is supported mainly by studies of OsNRT1.1B in rice. However, whether mechanisms established in Arabidopsis are conserved and agronomically relevant in other crop species remains to be fully established. Although nitrate- and ABA-related NRT1.1 functions have both been investigated in rice, direct experimental evidence that the two proposed modules operate coordinately within a single species remains limited. Accordingly, this model should be viewed as a comparative and hypothesis-generating framework rather than a universally validated mechanism. Understanding this network may provide a basis for identifying targets to improve nutrient use efficiency, stress resilience, and yield stability, pending validation in target crops.
items.authors: Liu R, Wang S, Wang Y, Song J.

items.title: RUBY expression alters development and metabolism in Arabidopsis.
items.abstract: Genetically encoded reporters are indispensable tools for monitoring gene expression, transformation efficiency, and diverse cellular processes in plants. The betalain-based RUBY reporter has recently emerged as a convenient visual marker requiring no substrates or specialized equipment, and it has been widely used for a variety of applications. However, the developmental and metabolic consequences of its expression remain unexplored. Here, we show that independent transgenic lines of Arabidopsis thaliana expressing RUBY exhibit profound alterations in growth and reproductive development. RUBY-expressing plants were significantly smaller, produced fewer leaves, flowered later, and frequently developed malformed siliques with reduced seed yield. In addition, root architecture was severely impaired, with a marked reduction in the number of lateral roots. This phenotype was not rescued by indole-3-acetic acid (IAA). Targeted metabolomic profiling revealed widespread alterations in amino acid and hormone pools, including reduced indole-3-acetic acid and gibberellin, alongside accumulation of auxin precursors. Disruption of RUBY expression by suppressing the third enzyme (glucosyltransferase) restored the RUBY-associated phenotypes to wild-type. Together, our findings show that RUBY expression in Arabidopsis thaliana is not metabolically neutral; rather, it perturbs both development and metabolism by disrupting hormone and amino acid homeostasis. These results highlight reporter-associated trade-offs and underscore the necessity of regulated expression systems, such as inducible or tissue-specific expression, to expand the utility of RUBY in plant research and biotechnology.
items.authors: Cheema A, Prasad KVSK, Huq E, Reddy ASN.

items.title: Mechanisms underlying the defective development of xyloglucan-deficient root hairs in Arabidopsis thaliana
items.abstract: Hemicellulosic xyloglucan is abundant in the primary cell walls of eudicots and non-gramineous monocots and contributes to their mechanical integrity. Its deficiency results in morphologically abnormal root hairs in Arabidopsis mutants lacking either two XYLOGLUCAN XYLOSYLTRANSFERASE (xxt1 xxt2) or five CELLULOSE SYNTHASE-LIKE C (cslc-∆5) genes, but the cellular and biomechanical mechanisms underlying these abnormalities have remained unexplored. We combined multiple imaging modalities and quantitative modeling to unmask these mechanisms, first observing that xyloglucan-deficient mutants produced fewer and shorter root hairs that grew slower than wild type. Xyloglucan-deficient trichoblasts showed root hair initiation defects, helping to explain the sparseness of root hairs in these mutants. The mutant root hairs also had lower turgor pressure, thicker walls, and wider cross-sections, that explain lack of anisotropic growth, but cellulose organization appeared normal in xyloglucan-deficient root hairs. Brillouin microscopy suggested that xyloglucan-deficient root hairs were softer than wild-type root hairs. Finite element modeling of mutant root hairs predicted lower surface stress and growth rates, which were directly proportional to turgor pressure and inversely proportional to wall thickness. Stress patterns on models hint at potential mechanisms of bulging in xyloglucan-deficient root hairs. We propose that though cellulose orientation specifies the axis of cell expansion, it cannot enforce it without xyloglucan that interlinks microfibrils into a load-bearing network, identifying matrix-cellulose interaction as a distinct and necessary determinant of anisotropic plant cell growth.
items.authors: Zambare, V., McDermond, G., Alonso Baez, L., Yi, H., Hamann, T., Anderson, C. T.

items.title: The lignin deposition responses of different poplar root systems to salt stress.
items.abstract: Salt stress significantly constrains plant growth and development, with the root system serving as the primary organ for sensing and responding to salinity. Poplar (Populus spp.), a widely cultivated tree species, plays a pivotal role in urban greening, windbreak and sand fixation, and various economic sectors. Six poplars as experimental materials to analyze lignin deposition in the root system and variations in the casparian strip under salt stress. Lignin enrichment and changes in the casparian strip are as follows: P. alba × P. glandulosa '84K' showed the most pronounced changes, followed by P. cathayana and P. tremula × P. alba, then P. deltoids × P. euramericana 'Nanlin895', Populus × euramaricana 'Bofeng 3 hao' and P. simonii. Transcriptome sequencing revealed the molecular mechanisms in the 84K poplar and P. simonii with the greatest and smallest lignin increase, respectively. The results reveal that 84K poplar and P. simonii mainly regulate the accumulation of lignin through phenylalanine metabolism, starch and sucrose metabolism, as well as the MAPK signaling pathway under salt stress. This study provides critical theoretical support for elucidating the molecular response mechanisms of root lignin and the casparian strip under salt stress.
items.authors: Meng JH, Zuo WT, Rao L, Liao KP, Liu HC, Wang LQ, Sun TT.

items.title: Environmental, developmental, and genetic factors differentially affect rapid ethylene growth response kinetics in dark-grown Arabidopsis thaliana hypocotyls.
items.abstract: Studies on dark-grown wild-type Arabidopsis thaliana seedlings have demonstrated that the hypocotyls respond to the application and removal of the hormone ethylene with stereotypical growth kinetics. This includes a rapid decrease in growth rate when ethylene is applied that stabilizes at a low growth rate approximately 75 min after the addition of saturating levels of ethylene. Hypocotyl growth rate recovers to pre-treatment levels approximately 80 minutes after removal of ethylene. The growth of plants is influenced by environmental conditions that can vary between laboratories as well as genetic backgrounds and developmental factors. To address the importance of these variables on ethylene responses, experiments were conducted to determine the effects of composition of growth medium, seed size, seedling age, and accession on ethylene growth response kinetics. These variables led to only minor alterations in growth inhibition kinetics when ethylene was added with the largest effect being an acceleration in growth inhibition when nutrients were excluded from the medium. By contrast, growth recovery kinetics upon ethylene removal showed more plasticity. Sucrose accelerated growth recovery, whereas other environmental variables delayed recovery compared to controls. Other variables that are often overlooked, such as seed size and seedling age, also affected growth recovery where older seedlings recovered more slowly and plants from larger seeds recovered faster than plants from smaller seeds. Accessions from more northern latitudes tended to recover faster than those from more southern latitudes. Our data indicate that these factors need to be carefully controlled for optimal reproducibility of responses to ensure accurate interpretation of data and make sure important traits are not masked.
items.authors: Bakshi A, Patel V, Ward A, Ferdous M, Binder BM.

items.title: Light-defined cold acclimation reprograms organ-specific metabolic and transcriptional landscapes for salt stress responses in maize.
items.abstract: Key messageCold acclimation of young maize plants induced a light-dependent, organ-specific reprogramming at the metabolomic and gene expression levels, which significantly altered responses to salinity. It has been shown that light plays a decisive role in cold acclimation in plants. The core objective of the present work was to elucidate how light conditions during cold acclimation affect subsequent salt stress responses by co-regulating various processes among organs maize (Zea mays L.). Plants were cold-acclimated under sufficient light or shade and subsequently exposed to severe cold or salinity. Organ-specific analyses of leaves, stems, and roots combined chlorophyll fluorescence measurements with targeted and untargeted metabolomics, hormone and polyamine profiling, and stress-related gene expression were studied. Cold acclimation under sufficient light established organ-specific metabolic and transcriptional reprogramming that substantially altered subsequent salt stress responses. Light-acclimated plants showed coordinated, pathway-level metabolic adjustments across organs and distinct regulation of key stress-responsive genes, particularly in leaves and roots. Analyses indicated systemic, rather than isolated, metabolic rearrangements. These findings demonstrate that cold acclimation, depending on light intensity, establishes an organ-coordinated acclimated state that modulates subsequent salinity responses, highlighting the importance of environmental history and inter-organ regulation in stress adaptation. This study is the first to systematically reveal the organ-specific and systemic regulatory network underlying the light-temperature-salt interaction in maize.
items.authors: Benczúr K, Gholizadeh F, Pál M, Janda T, Hamow KÁ, Dernovics M, Nagy K, Majláth I, Darko E, Wu J, Van Le N, Szalai G.

items.title: Natural sweet potato transgene Ib-rolB/C enhances abiotic and biotic stress tolerance through redox and defense regulation.
items.abstract: Main conclusionNatural sweet potato transgene Ib-rolB/C enhances abiotic and biotic stress tolerance through coordinated regulation of ROS signaling, antioxidant defense, immune activation, and secondary metabolism. Horizontal gene transfer from Agrobacterium has contributed to plant genome evolution, yet the physiological roles of naturally integrated T-DNA genes remain poorly understood. Cultivated sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas) contains two cellular T-DNA regions, including the IbT-DNA2 locus harboring the naturally acquired gene Ib-rolB/C. Here, we investigated the stress-responsive expression and functional significance of Ib-rolB/C using transgenic Arabidopsis thaliana. The gene was strongly induced by cold, heat, and salinity. Moreover, Ib-rolB/C-expressing plants exhibited enhanced tolerance to abiotic stresses during germination, as well as increased resistance to Pseudomonas syringae and Botrytis cinerea. These phenotypes were associated with moderate ROS accumulation, enhanced antioxidant capacity, elevated GSH/GSSG ratios, reduced lipid peroxidation, and elevated basal expression of stress- and defense-related genes. In addition, Ib-rolB/C expression induced substantial metabolic reprogramming characterized by increased accumulation of flavonol glycosides and camalexin together with reduced glucosinolate levels. Our findings demonstrate that Ib-rolB/C functions as a multifunctional regulator integrating redox signaling, stress adaptation, immune responses, and secondary metabolism, highlighting the evolutionary significance of naturally acquired T-DNA genes in plants.
items.authors: Yugay Y, Rusapetova T, Gorpenchenko T, Vasyutkina E, Degtyareva V, Grigorchuk V, Kudinova O, Bulgakov V, Shkryl Y.

items.title: Tvp38/DedA Family Protein mediates biogenesis of chloroplast peripheral reticulum and envelope-to-thylakoid contacts in Arabidopsis
items.abstract: Chloroplasts of land plants are dynamic organelles essential for photosynthesis, metabolism, and plant adaptation to changing environmental conditions. Within chloroplasts, the inner envelope and thylakoid membranes are spatially separated but functionally interconnected. The inner envelope harbors enzymes involved in lipid synthesis for internal membranes and controls the exchange of metabolites and proteins, whereas the thylakoid membranes accommodate the machinery of the photosynthetic electron transport chain responsible for converting light energy into chemical energy. Therefore, efficient communication between these membrane systems is essential for maintaining chloroplast homeostasis and sustaining photosynthetic activity. In this study we have characterized the role of Tvp38/DedA Family Protein (TVPFP) in mediating inner envelope-to-thylakoid communication in Arabidopsis thaliana. Despite exhibiting wild-type-like growth and similar accumulation of the major thylakoid-anchored photosynthetic complexes, tvpfp mutants displayed reduced photosynthetic activity and increased abundance of photorespiration- and pigment-related proteins. Our results revealed that TVPFP localizes to the chloroplast envelope and undergoes post-translational modification when localized to the thylakoids. The unmodified form of TVPFP is enriched in high-molecular-weight complexes, suggesting that TVPFP oligomers are partially dissolved upon thylakoid relocation. Transmission electron microscopy data showed reduced abundance of vesicles as well as chloroplast peripheral reticulum (CPR) structures connecting the envelope and thylakoids in tvpfp mutants. Together, our results demonstrate that TVPFP fine-tunes photosynthesis by regulating vesicle abundance and biogenesis of CPR structures. Our findings shed light on the importance of envelope-to-thylakoid communication and the role of CPR structures in land plants.
items.authors: Voelkel-Lambertz, M., Bykowski, M., Roediger, A., Kumari, K., Grefen, C., Bock, R., Baginsky, S., Kowalewska, L., Sandoval-Ibanez, O.

items.title: N-glycosylation code diversifies paralogous chitinases to balance plant immunity and growth.
items.abstract: Balancing immunity and growth is a fundamental challenge for plants. Surprisingly, fungal cell-wall chitin elicits robust immune responses without causing growth inhibition, yet constitutive intracellular chitin signalling severely impairs growth. How plants resolve this paradox remains unclear. Here we identify two chitin-inducible, paralogous apoplastic chitinases in Arabidopsis thaliana, MIC1 and MIC2, both possessing direct antifungal activity through chitin hydrolysis. MIC2 generates immunogenic chitin oligomers that activate chitin-triggered immunity, whereas MIC1 ultimately degrades chitin into non-immunogenic dimers and monomers, thereby dampening growth-inhibitory signalling. This functional divergence is dictated by Asn137 glycosylation in MIC1. Removing this N-glycan converts MIC1 into a MIC2-like enzyme. MIC1-like chitinases are widespread in plants, and Oryza sativa Osmic1 mutants exhibit enhanced fungal resistance without growth defects. Our work defines an N-glycosylation code that governs the functional specialization of paralogous chitinases and provides a conserved molecular target for breeding crops with improved fungal resistance and uncompromised growth.
items.authors: Li C, Lin XX, Tian L, Sun W, Liu J, Liu Q, Du Y, Jiang X, Liang Z, Deng YZ, Au SWN, Wan JB, Li JF.

items.title: Catalase import into peroxisomes in Arabidopsis
items.abstract: Summary In eukaryotes, catalases are peroxisomal antioxidant enzymes that maintain cellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) homeostasis. Plant catalases lack canonical peroxisomal targeting signals (PTS), and the mechanism underlying their PEX5-dependent peroxisomal import remains poorly understood. Here, we expressed CAT2 with N- and C-terminal GFP fusions in an Arabidopsis cat2 mutant background and found that only GFP-CAT2 completely restored wild-type function despite comparable catalase activity for both CAT2-GFP and GFP-CAT2. Only GFP-CAT2 localized to peroxisomes, indicating that altered subcellular localization prevented CAT2-GFP functional complementation. Expression of CAT2-GFP in wild-type Arabidopsis and Nicotiana benthamiana revealed in vivo interaction with endogenous catalases leading to co-import into peroxisomes. Localization of YFP fused to various CAT2 C-terminal sections identified the CAT2 C-terminal five amino acids as a functional PTS1-like sequence. These findings define a minimal C-terminal targeting motif for plant catalases that is sufficient for their peroxisomal import.
items.authors: Hu, Z., Tremulot, L., Stolze, S. C., Nakagami, H., Hothorn, M., Ulm, R.

items.title: SRF6, a heat-inducible receptor-like kinase, regulates thermotolerance in Arabidopsis thaliana.
items.abstract: Key messageSRF6 is a heat-inducible, non-RD receptor-like kinase that contributes to thermotolerance in Arabidopsis by modulating heat-, ER stress-, ABA-, and ROS-responsive pathways. Receptor-like kinases (RLKs) are central regulators of plant growth, development, and stress perception, yet their roles in heat stress (HS) responses remain largely unclear. Here, we identify STRUBBELIG-RECEPTOR-FAMILY 6 (SRF6) as a heat-inducible, plasma membrane-localized, non-arginine-aspartate (non-RD) RLK that contributes to thermotolerance in Arabidopsis thaliana. HS significantly induces SRF6 expression, and this induction is attenuated in hsfA1a/b/d/e quadruple knockout and hsfA7b mutants, suggesting that HSFA1s and HSFA7b influence its heat-induced expression. Although SRF6 lacks detectable kinase activity, its sustained expression after heat priming is consistent with a heat-memory-associated response. Functionally, the srf6-1 mutant exhibits impaired thermotolerance, whereas SRF6 overexpression in srf6-1 restores heat tolerance. Targeted gene expression analyses revealed that loss of SRF6 alters the expression of heat-, ER stress-, ABA-, and ROS-responsive genes, including HSP22/70/90/101, CaM3, bZIP28/60, BiP2, AREB1/2, RD29A/B, APX1/2, CAT1, and RBOHD, accompanied by enhanced ER stress and altered heat-memory-associated responses under HS. Together, these findings suggest that SRF6 contributes to cellular stress homeostasis and thermotolerance during HS and provide evidence for a role of the LRR-V/SRF family in plant HS responses.
items.authors: Chang HY, Lai CC, Huang JC, Huang YC, Wu HC, Jinn TL.

items.title: Early humic acid-induced eustress triggers biostimulant responses in Arabidopsis thaliana: RBOHC-derived H2O2 drives growth promotion while RBOHD enables nutritional reprogramming.
items.abstract: Root-applied humic acids (HAs) promote plant development, yet the early signaling mechanisms underlying their biostimulant action remain incompletely understood. Here, we show that treatment of Arabidopsis thaliana roots with a sedimentary humic acid (SHA) triggers a transient eustress-like response, characterized by early inhibition of shoot and root growth and increased H2O2 accumulation in root hairs and apical roots. This initial oxidative phase was followed by enhanced shoot and root growth, supporting the view that SHA acts as an adaptive plant modulator through a controlled stress-related signal. Pharmacological H2O2 scavenging and genetic analysis of NADPH oxidase mutants revealed that SHA-induced growth promotion depends on RBOHC/RHD2-mediated H2O2 production in roots. In rhd2 plants, SHA failed to induce the characteristic H2O2 increase and did not promote shoot or root growth. By contrast, rbohd plants retained SHA-induced growth stimulation but showed impaired activation of nutrient transporter and plasma membrane H+-ATPase genes, limited improvement in shoot nutrient use efficiency, and partial root architectural remodeling. These results indicate that RBOHC-derived H2O2 is required for the growth-promoting response, whereas RBOHD cooperates with RBOHC to engage broader nutritional and developmental programs. SHA also induced extensive hormonal reprogramming in roots and shoots; however, disruption of individual ABA, auxin, jasmonate, or cytokinin signaling components did not abolish growth promotion, suggesting partially redundant hormonal regulation downstream of ROS. Overall, our findings identify an RBOHC-H2O2 module as a primary entry point for SHA-mediated biostimulant action and support a model in which root-localized oxidative eustress coordinates hormonal, developmental, and nutritional reprogramming in Arabidopsis.
items.authors: Rubio Á, Olaetxea M, Erro J, Fuentes M, Zamarreño AM, García-Mina JM.

items.title: Defying salinity, drought, and pH extremes: A multifunctional rhizobacterium, Burkholderia gladioli ST3M-39a, matches fertilizer efficacy in wheat via phosphate solubilization.
items.abstract: Global phosphorus scarcity and the environmental impacts of chemical fertilizers necessitate sustainable microbial alternatives for agriculture. We characterized Burkholderia gladioli ST3M-39a, a maize rhizosphere isolate, as a multifunctional plant growth-promoting rhizobacterium with exceptional climate resilience. The strain achieved rapid phosphate solubilization (177.96 ± 5.26 µg/mL within 24 h; molybdenum-antimony assay), zinc solubilization, and ammonia production, EPS production, produced stress-alleviating enzymes (cellulase and protease), and biosurfactant production. Crucially, it maintained robust growth and phosphate-mobilizing capacity under extreme abiotic stresses: pH 4.5-8.5, 7.5% NaCl salinity, and drought-mimicking low water activity (aw 0.950, 32% sorbitol). The strain was non-hemolytic and non-pathogenic to plants. In wheat trials, ST3M-39a inoculation significantly increased the growth parameters (p < 0.05 vs. those of the uninoculated controls), resulting in 85-92% of the biomass stimulation observed with diammonium phosphate (DAP) fertilizer. This multifunctional stress tolerance, coupled with its near-fertilizer efficacy, positioned ST3M-39a as a transformative bioinoculant for degraded soils. Field validation of its agricultural deployment and ecological impact is now pivotal.
items.authors: Silwal S, Shrestha A, Pokharel S, Khanal BC, Acharya R, Pandey GR.

items.title: PalKCH1 and PalKCH2 are required for tension wood formation and gelatinous layer deposition in Populus.
items.abstract: Tension wood (TW) is a graviresponsive xylem tissue exclusive to angiosperm trees that counteracts gravitational stress. Its hallmark is a gelatinous layer (G-layer) in fiber secondary walls, rich in cellulose and low in lignin. Although kinesins mediate microtubule-microfilament crosstalk, their role in G-layer biogenesis during gravistimulation is unclear in woody angiosperms. We studied two kinesin paralogs, PalKCH1 and PalKCH2, in Populus alba var. pyramidalis during TW development. Both belong to the Group I KCH clade, possessing a kinesin motor domain and a calponin-homology (CH) domain. Multi-omic profiling showed preferential expression in xylem fibers and strong gravistimulation-induced transcription. CRISPR/Cas9 single and double knockout mutants showed normal xylem under upright growth, but responded to gravitational stress with reduced stem bending, narrower TW regions, and fewer G-layer fibers; double mutants were more affected, suggesting dosage dependence. Chemical assays showed that mutants retained the cellulose-rich, lignin-poor TW signature, but the changes were attenuated compared to wild-type. Transcriptomic analysis of double mutants revealed suppression of genes involved in microtubule dynamics, vesicular trafficking, cell wall remodeling, reduced PalWOX4A expression, and repressed cell cycle pathways. Thus, PalKCH1 and PalKCH2 are required for TW formation, likely via cytoskeletal signaling, and represent high-value targets for improving wood quality in Populus.
items.authors: Li J, Qu K, Wang R, Zhang J, Zhou N.

items.title: Genotype-dependent phosphorus acquisition responses of two soybean genotypes under combined low phosphorus and salt stress: evidence from root traits, exudates and rhizosphere microbiome.
items.abstract: Soil salinization and phosphorus (P) deficiency often co-occur in coastal saline-alkali soils, severely limiting crop productivity. Although root exudates are known to mediate rhizosphere microbiome assembly, the coordinated associations among root exudates, rhizosphere microbes, and P acquisition under combined salinity stress and phosphate deficiency remain unclear. In this study, we used two salt-tolerant soybean genotypes differing in P efficiency (A74, P-efficient; A6, P-inefficient) as materials. In a controlled pot experiment, four treatments were established: control (CK), low P (LP), salt (S), and combined stress (LPS). By integrating root phenotypes, P acquisition traits, root exudate metabolomics, and rhizosphere metagenomics, the genotype-dependent rhizosphere responses were investigated. Results showed that, compared to A6, A74 maintained a more extensive root-soil interface and superior P nutritional status under LP and LPS, exhibiting more robust P acquisition responses. Metabolomics and metagenomics identified 16 candidate metabolites and 12 candidate microbial taxa, respectively. Effect-size and correlation analyses prioritized naringenin and Sinorhizobium as candidate components associated with genotype-dependent P acquisition responses. KO annotation identified Sinorhizobium-associated genes with potential roles in phosphonate and phosphinate metabolism and benzoate degradation (e.g., phnJ, pcaC, and mhpD). In summary, these results support a genotype-dependent rhizosphere response pattern involving naringenin and Sinorhizobium, in which coordinated changes in root traits, exudate profiles, and microbial functional potential were associated with the stronger P acquisition response of A74 under combined stress. These findings identify candidate relationships for future functional validation under saline conditions.
items.authors: Zhou X, Cui G, Dong H, Wen S, Li Y, Han M, Wang G.

items.title: Systematic Analysis of the DOF Gene Family in Flowering Chinese Cabbage (Brassica campestris) and the Role of BcDOF56 in Abiotic Stress Adaptation
items.abstract: DNA-binding with One Finger (DOF) transcription factors play crucial roles in modulating plant growth, development, and environmental stress responses. However, the DOF family in flowering Chinese cabbage (Brassica campestris) remains poorly characterized. Here, 67 BcDOF genes were identified in B. campestris, distributed nonuniformly across ten chromosomes and classified into nine subfamilies. Structural analyses revealed that all BcDOF proteins harbor a conserved zinc-finger DOF (zf-DOF) domain, with members within individual subfamilies generally sharing similar motif architectures and exon-intron structures. Evolutionary analyses indicated that whole-genome triplication and segmental duplication were the major drivers of BcDOF family expansion, while purifying selection contributed to the evolutionary conservation of duplicated gene pairs. Promoter analysis revealed abundant cis-acting elements related to hormone signaling and abiotic stress responses. Quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) further demonstrated that many BcDOF genes responded to heat and drought stresses. Among them, BcDOF56 was markedly induced by both heat and drought and localized to the nucleus. Heterologous overexpression of BcDOF56 in Arabidopsis significantly improved heat and drought tolerance, as indicated by reduced malondialdehyde (MDA) accumulation and elevated superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity relative to wild-type (WT) plants. Collectively, these findings advance our understanding of the evolutionary and functional divergence of the BcDOF family and highlight BcDOF56 as a potential target for improving abiotic stress tolerance in B. campestris.
items.authors: Liu J, Liu J, Chen C, Wang Y, Wang B, Feng H, Song S, Zhu Y.

items.title: TaPSP1 negatively regulates osmotic stress response in wheat.
items.abstract: Wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) is a cornerstone of global food security, yet its production is severely threatened by osmotic stress, such as drought-induced water deficit. Identifying and characterizing key genes involved in stress response is crucial for understanding adaptation mechanisms and developing tolerant varieties. In this study, we characterized TaPSP1, a protein containing a peroxiredoxin-like conserved domain, and uncovered its negative regulatory role in the response to osmotic stress. Bioinformatics analysis revealed that TaPSP1 is a hydrophilic, non-secretory protein that is likely localized to the plasma membrane, possessing multiple phosphorylation sites and conserved oxidoreductase domains. Its promoter contains diverse cis-acting elements associated with hormone signaling and environmental responses. Phylogenetic analysis indicated that TaPSP1 is evolutionarily conserved among Poaceae species. Expression profiling showed that TaPSP1 transcript levels gradually decreased under PEG-induced osmotic stress. Functional analysis in transgenic Arabidopsis overexpressing TaPSP1 revealed enhanced sensitivity to osmotic stress, as evidenced by reduced biomass accumulation, lower survival rates, decreased relative water content and proline accumulation, and elevated malondialdehyde levels. Importantly, we further generated TaPSP1-overexpressing transgenic wheat lines, which consistently exhibited an osmotic stress-sensitive phenotype, corroborating the findings from Arabidopsis. Conversely, TaPSP1-RNAi knockdown wheat lines exhibited significantly enhanced osmotic stress tolerance, with increased survival rates, higher proline accumulation, and reduced malondialdehyde content under PEG treatment, providing direct loss-of-function evidence for its negative regulatory role. Transcriptomic analysis further demonstrated that TaPSP1 overexpression broadly reprograms stress-responsive gene expression, suppressing typical defense pathways. Collectively, this study establishes TaPSP1 as a negative regulator of osmotic stress tolerance in wheat, providing a theoretical foundation for improving stress resistance in wheat breeding programs by targeting this negative regulator.
items.authors: Wang K, Zhao D, Zhang T, Jin M, Wang C, Wang J, Qi Y, Wang Z, Zheng Y, Yuan F, Yang J, Zhang X, Zhao L, Zhang H.
items.journal: Plant science : an international journal of experimental plant biology

items.title: The root knot nematode effector MiEFF186 interacts with a splicing factor to reshape plant transcriptome
items.abstract: The root-knot nematode Meloidogyne incognita secretes specific effectors to manipulate root cells and induce their redifferentiation into multinucleate feeding giant cells, which are essential for its development. A dedicated screen identified the M. incognita MiEFF186a effector as a regulator of alternative splicing, a crucial mechanism of transcriptional gene regulation whereby a single gene can produce multiple mature mRNA variants, in plants. EFF186 is expressed in the esophageal glands of nematode juveniles, and in planta , it localizes to the nucleus and accumulates in the nucleolus. A yeast two-hybrid approach identified the nucleolar G-patch protein GDP1/CIS2 as a MiEFF186a target in tomato and Arabidopsis . Transcriptomic analyses of Arabidopsis roots ectopically expressing MiEFF186a or impaired in GDP1/CIS2 function revealed changes in both gene expression and alternative splicing, with partially overlapping responses. Finally, alteration of GDP1/CIS2 expression by virus-induced gene silencing in Solanaceae or in Arabidopsis gdp1 mutants affects susceptibility to M. incognita . Together, these results identify GDP1/CIS2 as a host target of MiEFF186a and support a role for these proteins in the modulation of host RNA metabolism during nematode parasitism.
items.authors: Ranty-Roby, S., Mulet, K., Soule, S., Camborde, L., Huang, K., Lei, P., Philippon, J., Caravel, C., Foubert, P., de Luca, M. B., Huard-Chauveau, C., Jaubert, S., Crespi, M., Zhao, J., Bazin, J., Favery, B., Quentin, M.

items.title: A Blast Fungus Effector Targets a Tubby-like F-box Protein to Suppress Plant Immunity
items.abstract: The blast fungus Magnaporthe oryzae is one of the most destructive pathogens of rice, secreting effector proteins that reprogram host cells to enable infection. Identifying plant targets of these fungal effectors is central to understanding how blast disease is established, but the targets and mechanisms of most effectors remain unknown. Here, we show that a Zinc finger (ZiF)-family effector, Tie1, targets the rice Tubby-like protein (TLP) family, which are membrane-associated plant immunity regulators whose exact functions have not been defined. Tie1 binds a range of rice TLPs and specifically engages with the Tubby-like domain of OsTLP7. Co-expression in planta with Tie1 re-localises this domain from the plasma membrane to the cytoplasm and nucleus, a shift also observed by disrupting the OsTLP7 phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2)-binding site in the absence of the effector. By combining AlphaFold3 structural predictions with allelic variation, we define a putative Tie1/OsTLP7 interface distal to the PIP2-binding site. Furthermore, Tie1 induces transcriptional activation activity of the OsTLP7 Tubby-like domain, and Tie1 overexpression in stable Arabidopsis lines leads to upregulation of genes that repress jasmonic acid (JA) signalling. Taken together, our results indicate that Tie1 inhibits PIP2 binding by OsTLP7 to drive its re-localisation to the nucleus and thereby modulating transcription to suppress JA-mediated plant immunity.
items.authors: Saado, I., Bennett, J. W., Huang, L., Chia, K.-S., Talbot, N. J., Banfield, M. J.

items.title: Melatonin Coordinates Root Cell-Wall Zinc Remobilization and Shoot Transport via Nitric Oxide Signaling Under Zinc Deficiency in Rice.
items.abstract: Although zinc (Zn) deficiency severely inhibits rice growth, it remains unclear how melatonin (MT) promotes adaptation under conditions of insufficient Zn supply. To address this issue, rice seedlings were treated with MT, the NO donor sodium nitroprusside (SNP), or the NO scavenger c-PTIO, alone or in combination, under Zn-deficient conditions. Zn starvation rapidly promoted endogenous MT accumulation in rice roots, together with a 90.2%-179.5% rise in the transcript levels of MT biosynthetic genes. Exposure to Zn deprivation reduced root/shoot length and root/shoot biomass, by 46.2%/31.3% and 27.5%/39.6%, respectively. Among the tested concentrations, 10 μM MT produced the strongest protective effect, increasing root length, shoot height, root biomass, and shoot biomass by 59.9%, 34.2%, 21.7%, and 51.8%, respectively, relative to plants that were merely deficient in Zn. In Zn-deficient plants, MT raised Zn concentration in root and shoot both by 16.2% and xylem sap Zn concentration by 15.6%. MT also increased root cell-wall Zn content, pectin abundance, and pectin-associated Zn by 20.0%, 39.3%, and 31.9%, respectively. At the expression level, MT moderated the induction of OsZIP4, OsZIP5, OsZIP8, OsZIP9, OsZIP10, and OsHMA3 by Zn deficiency and further repressed OsZIP1, implying feedback regulation of the Zn-homeostasis network instead of direct activation of Zn-transporter transcription. Root NO content rose by 29.8% after MT treatment, and SNP elicited increases in root and shoot Zn concentrations comparable to those associated with MT. Overall, the data suggest that an NO-associated response contributes to MT-mediated Zn-deficiency tolerance by restoring Zn homeostasis, promoting apoplastic Zn remobilization and root-to-shoot transport, and limiting oxidative damage.
items.authors: Huang J, Lu QC, Huang W, Wang HY, Wang DB, Shen RF, Zheng L, Zhu XF.

items.title: A calcium-independent CDPK positively regulates drought resistance in maize by modulating the ABA signaling pathway.
items.abstract: Calcium-dependent protein kinases (CDPKs/CPKs) play crucial roles in plant responses to drought stress. In this study, we reveal that ZmCPK1, an atypical CDPK whose kinase activity is calcium-independent, acts as a positive regulator of drought resistance in maize. ZmCPK1 is a constitutively active kinase interacting with and phosphorylates multiple components of the abscisic acid (ABA) signaling pathway, including ZmSLAC1, ZmSnRK2.10, and ZmPP2C11. In the absence of ABA, ZmCPK1 may phosphorylate ZmSnRK2.10 and the N-terminus of ZmSLAC1. ZmPP2C11 reverses this phosphorylation by directly dephosphorylating the N-terminus of ZmSLAC1 rather than suppressing ZmCPK1 kinase activity. ABA treatment and dehydration enhance ZmCPK1-mediated phosphorylation of the N-terminus of ZmSLAC1 at the conserved serine 54 (S54) without affecting ZmCPK1 autophosphorylation, consistent with reduced dephosphorylation resulting from the inhibition of ZmPP2C11 by ABA-bound pyrabactin resistance 1-like (PYL) proteins. Notably, ZmCPK1 phosphorylates ZmPP2C11 at S277, a modification that potentially inhibits its phosphatase activity, and phosphorylates multiple sites on ZmSnRK2.10 to activate it. Thus, ZmCPK1 acts as a constitutive kinase; under optimal growth conditions, it interacts with ZmPP2C11, which dephosphorylates the targets phosphorylated by ZmCPK1. Under drought stress, ZmPP2C11 is inhibited, and phosphorylated downstream targets are activated to promote stomatal closure, thereby positively regulating drought resistance in maize.
items.authors: Fang T, Han Y, Chen Y, Hu X, Zhong Z, Wang T, Wang Y, Qi J, Yang S, Gong Z.
items.journal: Journal of genetics and genomics = Yi chuan xue bao

items.title: Asymptomatic colonization by Botrytis cinerea reveals polarized plant-fungus interfaces before widespread disease
items.abstract: Botrytis cinerea is a necrotrophic pathogen whose destructive growth is typically studied under conditions that rapidly generate visible disease. Yet symptomless associations are well documented, the fungal and host processes operating before widespread tissue collapse remain poorly resolved. We developped an intact Arabidopsis thaliana seedling pathosystem that extends the interval between infection establishment and widespread visible disease. Fungal colonization was quantified using qPCR and a constitutively bioluminescent reporter strain, together with longitudinal plant phenotyping, hormone profiling and multiscale fluorescence microscopy. Substantial fungal colonization occurred while seedlings remained largely green and continued to grow, whereas robust whole seedling accumulation of salicylic and jasmonic acids occurred later. During this interval, B. cinerea displayed diverse tissue-associated infection morphologies. At individual contact sites, fungal walls showed heterogeneous exposure of chitin-associated epitopes, while host cells exhibited focal plasma-membrane polarization toward fungal contact sites, together with cortical actin reorganization. These results show that the interval preceding widespread visible disease is an active and spatially heterogeneous interaction state, in which substantial fungal development and highly organized local host responses are already established. Intact seedlings therefore provide a powerful system for resolving plant-pathogen interactions that are largely obscured in rapid disease assays.
items.authors: Ines, T., Perrine, F., Adrien, P., Bastien, M., Amelie, d. V., BRUEL, C., CHOQUER, M., Nathalie, P., Caroline, B., Gillet, F.-X.

items.title: Melatonin-mediated cross-stress protection in tomato under individual and combined salinity and drought stress.
items.abstract: Tomato production is increasingly threatened by the co-occurrence of salinity and drought, but the protective mechanisms of melatonin under their combination are not fully understood. This study investigated whether foliar-applied melatonin could mitigate the individual and combined effects of salinity and drought in tomato (Solanum lycopersicum). Plants were exposed to 0 or 100 mM NaCl and maintained at 90 or 60% field capacity. Melatonin (100 μM) was sprayed three times at five-day intervals, beginning one day before stress application, and plants were sampled after three weeks. Salinity and drought separately reduced growth, leaf water status, photosynthetic pigments, photosystem II (PSII) efficiency, gas exchange, and K status, while their combination generally caused the greatest inhibition. Combined stress also produced the greatest Na/K imbalance and the highest accumulation of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), methylglyoxal, and malondialdehyde (MDA). Melatonin improved growth and photosynthetic performance under all stress conditions; under combined stress, it increased total dry weight, relative water content, and K by approximately 37%, 18.6%, and 50.2%, respectively, and reduced Na and MDA by 39.8% and 39.9%, respectively, relative to untreated stressed plants. These improvements were associated with higher antioxidant and glyoxalase activities, recovery of ascorbate/dehydroascorbate and reduced/oxidized glutathione redox balance, and coordinated changes in anthocyanin biosynthesis, phenolic metabolism, proline, glycine betaine, free amino acids, and soluble sugars. The protective response was especially evident under combined stress, whereas melatonin had little effect under normal conditions. Overall, melatonin provided stress-dependent protection by linking ion homeostasis, ROS and methylglyoxal detoxification, redox recycling, and osmotic and secondary metabolism. These findings support foliar melatonin as a promising approach for improving tomato tolerance to co-occurring salinity and drought.
items.authors: Huang H, Zhang H, Zeng Q, Wu J.

items.title: P2K1 P2K2 Coordinate Early, Structure-Specific Mechanical Adaptations to Osmotic and Cell Wall Stress in Arabidopsis Roots
items.abstract: The cell wall and plasma membrane (PM) form the interface between a plant cell and its environment yet how their mechanical properties change in response to stress is poorly understood. Here we investigate how the mechanical properties of the cell wall, plasma membrane, and vacuole change in vivo in Arabidopsis thaliana roots in response to hyperosmotic stress and cell wall damage (CWD) using a solvatochromic dye, molecular rotors, and Brillouin microscopy. We observe initially dynamic changes in mechanical properties of the PM that are sensitive to both hyperosmotic stress and CWD, while the cell wall changes are limited and the vacuole adapts only after several hours. In the p2k1 p2k2 double mutant, lacking receptors for extracellular ATP perception, sorbitol-induced effects on PM mechanostasis and early isoxaben-induced increases in PM order are lost. Our results indicate that P2K1 and P2K2 are required to modulate adaptive changes in mechanical properties of the PM induced by hyperosmotic stress and CWD.
items.authors: Amanda, D., Badias, O., Alonso Baez, L., Besten, M., Sprakel, J., Hamann, T.

items.title: Phenotypic Discrimination of Routinely Identified Haploid and Diploid Sweet Corn Seedlings Using Multivariate Classification
items.abstract: Abstract Early discrimination of haploid seedlings is an important step in doubled haploid (DH) breeding because haploid seedlings are typically identified among a much larger population of predominantly diploid progeny. Phenotypic traits expressed during early seedling development have been proposed as useful indicators of haploidy, but their combined discriminatory value across sweet corn breeding materials remains insufficiently characterized. This study evaluated the potential of integrated seedling phenotyping to discriminate seedlings routinely classified as haploid or diploid in sweet corn. Seedlings derived from controlled donor × inducer crosses were characterized for shoot growth, leaf development, root architecture, chlorophyll content, and stomatal traits. Principal component analysis (PCA), pearson correlation analysis, random forest, and linear discriminant analysis (LDA) were used to characterize multivariate phenotypic patterns, identify informative traits, and evaluate classification relative to the routine haploid/diploid classification. Haploid-classified seedlings generally exhibited lower plant height, shorter and narrower leaves, reduced root development, and smaller guard cells, whereas stomatal number showed the opposite pattern. Multivariate analysis indicated that shoot growth, root development, and stomatal characteristics contributed jointly to separation between the two routinely classified groups. Random forest identified leaf length, plant height, stomatal number, and leaf width among the more informative traits, while LDA provided multivariate discrimination between the two groups. These findings indicate that early seedling phenotypes contain information that can support preliminary discrimination of routinely identified haploid and diploid seedlings.
items.authors: Laurenze R, Chang PPC, Azrai M.

items.title: Catabolism of 4-aminobutyrate (GABA) and proteinogenic amino acids sustains the tricarboxylic acid cycle in Arabidopsis thaliana (L.) Heynh. plants under salinity stress.
items.abstract: Glutamate decarboxylases1,2,4 (GAD1,2,4) are calcium/calmodulin-activated enzymes that produce 4-aminobutyrate (GABA) and eventually lead to succinate (GABA shunt), which can theoretically be incorporated into the tricarboxylic acid cycle (TCAC) during abiotic stress. We tested the hypothesis that the GABA shunt is involved in the adaptive response of the TCAC to salinity stress. Quantitative analyses of amino and organic acids, as well as GAD1,2,4 expression, in shoots and roots of soil-grown, late-vegetative-stage Arabidopsis wild-type plants and GAD1,2,4 single, double and triple loss-of function mutants provided a general understanding of the metabolic response to salinity. Salinity induced similar metabolic changes in shoots and roots, though the magnitude of the response was greater in shoots. Several mechanisms could be responsible for the non-cyclic nature of the TCAC with salinity, but inhibition of 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase probably resulted in the diversion of 2-oxoglutarate from the TCAC to the GABA shunt, though activation of this pathway was insufficient to sustain the succinate level observed in the absence of salinity, especially in roots. Both transcriptional and post-transcriptional regulation of GAD could have contributed to activation of the GABA shunt. Inhibition of GAD-mediated GABA production by genetic means was associated with changes in levels of free proteinogenic amino acids, as well as elevated succinate, regardless of salinity stress. Overall, GABA and proteinogenic amino acids serve an important role in ensuring flexible generation of respiratory substrate for TCAC operation and energy production.
items.authors: Flaherty EJ, Hoover GJ, Shelp BJ.

items.title: Red and blue light antagonistically regulate tomato root system architecture by the auxin-mediated SlARF18-SlDRO1 module.
items.abstract: Root system architecture (RSA) is critical for water and nutrients uptake and is affected by light. However, the precise mechanisms by which light quality regulates RSA remain obscure. Here, we showed that red light (R) caused shorter primary root, larger lateral root angle and lower expression of DEEPER ROOTING 1 (SlDRO1), while blue light (B) led to the opposite trend compared to white light. Integrative analyses of hormone quantification, gene expression, GUS staining and auxin transport inhibitor 1-N-naphthylphthalamic acid (NPA) application revealed that the antagonistic effects of R and B on RSA depended on long distance transport of leaf-synthesized auxin from shoot to root. Transcriptome analysis identified a novel auxin response factor (ARF) transcription factor, SlARF18, whose expression paralleled light quality-induced changes in auxin content. Subcellular localization and transcriptional activation assays showed that SlARF18 protein was a nucleus-localized transcriptional repressor. The functions of SlARF18 and SlDRO1 in RSA were verified by virus-induced gene silencing. Yeast one-hybrid, dual-luciferase reporter assays and electrophoretic mobility shift assays revealed that SlARF18 inhibited SlDRO1 transcription by binding to its promoter. Collectively, our results demonstrate that R and B antagonistically regulate tomato RSA by the auxin-mediated SlARF18-SlDRO1 module, providing a novel mechanism for light quality-regulated RSA.
items.authors: Duan J, Yu M, Li M, Ding Y, Wang J, Lin Y, Wang Y, Zhang T, Dong X, Dong H, Piao F, Guo Z.

items.title: Rol-Transformed Kalanchoë Shows Altered Root Allocation and Photosynthetic Responses to Nitrogen Deficiency.
items.abstract: Ri/rol transformation by Rhizobium rhizogenes is well known to alter plant architecture, including shoot compactness, branching and root development. However, its significance for plant responses to nitrogen limitation remains unclear. Here, we investigated developmental, physiological and hormonal responses of an interspecific Kalanchoë laciniata × K. blossfeldiana hybrid to nitrogen deficiency using complementary pot and hydroponic experiments. Nitrogen deficiency strongly reduced leaf area and total biomass in both wild-type (WT) and rol-transformed (Rol) plants. Nevertheless, rol transformation consistently produced a more compact, highly branched phenotype, with increased leaf number, greater side-shoot formation, higher specific leaf area, lower leaf dry matter content, and, in hydroponics, a striking increase in root mass allocation. Rol plants also maintained higher chlorophyll and carotenoid concentrations than WT and showed altered carbon partitioning, with lower soluble sugars but a higher relative proportion of sucrose. Under nitrogen deficiency, Rol plants maintained positive net photosynthesis and higher electron transport, whereas WT plants showed near-complete suppression of CO2 assimilation despite high intercellular CO2 concentration, pointing to strong non-stomatal limitation. Rol plants were characterized by lower ABA and PA concentrations, reduced auxin pools and enhanced leaf cytokinin status. Under low N, greater root allocation in Rol plants was not accompanied by reduced overall growth when root expansion was unrestricted, suggesting compensation through higher specific leaf area and maintenance of photosynthetic function. The strong shift towards root investment highlights a potential role of rol transformation in applications where belowground biomass and root development are especially relevant.
items.authors: Esposito A, Saccardo G, El Khoury YV, Vidal NP, Vrobel O, Tarkowski P, Paponov M, Goreal J, Nielsen KL, Paponov IA.

items.title: Redox regulation of plant hormone signaling transduction.
items.abstract: Plants need to precisely coordinate growth and development with stress responses under constantly changing environmental conditions, and the interaction between redox signaling and plant hormone signaling is an important regulatory mechanism underlying this balance. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are not only oxidative metabolic products generated under stress conditions, but also important second messengers that modulate protein functions through oxidative post-translational modifications (oxi-PTMs). Recent studies have shown that ROS can directly regulate plant hormone signaling transduction through oxi-PTMs. By altering the activity, stability, subcellular localization, or protein interactions of hormone receptors, protein kinases, phosphatases, transcription factors, or hormone metabolic enzymes through redox modifications, ROS regulate the biosynthesis and signaling outputs of multiple hormones, including auxin, abscisic acid (ABA), brassinosteroids (BR), jasmonic acid (JA), salicylic acid (SA), ethylene (ET), and cytokinin (CK). In turn, plant hormones can reshape ROS homeostasis by regulating ROS-producing or -scavenging systems, thereby forming complex bidirectional feedback networks. ROS can also act as common signaling nodes among different hormone pathways to integrate plant growth and development with stress responses. This review summarizes the molecular mechanisms by which redox signals regulate plant hormone signaling transduction, with particular emphasis on the roles of protein redox modifications in hormone perception, signal transmission, and multi-hormone interactions, and discusses the potential of exploiting key redox-sensitive sites for precise crop improvement, with the aim of providing a new theoretical basis for understanding plant environmental adaptation and breeding stress-resistant, high-yielding crops.
items.authors: Jing PW, Li SQ, Chen BH, Wu JX, Li L, Liao CY, Yang H, Lu KK, Song RF, Liu WC.

items.title: Diverse signaling proteins recruit RCC1-Like Domain proteins to the plasma membrane through a common structural framework.
items.abstract: Plants translate diverse environmental cues into spatially regulated growth responses through intracellular signaling mechanisms that remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify the BREVIS RADIX (BRX) domain of RCC1-LIKE DOMAIN (RLD) proteins as a versatile interaction module that recognizes multiple signaling proteins in Arabidopsis. We identified members of the PHYTOCHROME KINASE SUBSTRATE (PKS) and BIG GRAIN (BG) families as novel RLD interactors families, in addition to the previously characterized LAZY1-LIKE (LZY) proteins and BREAKING OF ASYMMETRY IN THE STOMATAL LINEAGE (BASL). Structural, biochemical, and cell-based analyses demonstrate that these diverse partners, despite having divergent interaction sequences, bind a common surface on the RLD BRX domain to recruit RLD to the plasma membrane. This interaction relies on a shared β-strand-based recognition mode, in which distinct peptide conformations accommodate binding to the same BRX-domain surface. Furthermore, we show that RLD2 and RLD3 contribute to hypocotyl phototropism, and that disrupting the conserved PKS interaction motif abolishes PKS4 function in this response. Together, our findings identify the RLD BRX domain as a molecular platform for diverse protein interactions and establish a PKS-RLD module that operates in phototropism. Furthermore, these findings strongly suggest that RLD recruitment to the plasma membrane via PKS underlies phototropic signal transduction.
items.authors: Nishimura, T., Hirano, Y., Vazquez, A. L., Trevisan, M., Sabol, P., Dong, J., Hakoshima, T., Fankhauser, C., Morita, M. T.

items.title: Unravelling the Multifunctional Roles of Plant LIM Proteins in Growth, Development, and Stress Responses.
items.abstract: LIM (Lin-11, Isl-1, and Mec-3 domain) proteins are evolutionarily conserved proteins that regulate diverse cellular processes in plants, including actin cytoskeleton organization, organ size determination, protein stability, and transcription-associated regulation. Therefore, these proteins have emerged as important regulators of plant growth, development, and responses to biotic and abiotic stresses. Numerous genome-wide studies, functional analyses, and mechanistic investigations in diverse plant species have considerably expanded our understanding of this gene family. However, these advances remain dispersed across the literature, present in peace-meal and have not been critically synthesized.
