items.abstract: Plants integrate multiple environmental cues to decide the timing of seed germination. Light promotes germination primarily through photoreceptor phytochrome B (phyB), which eliminates the action of transcription factor PHYTOCHROME-INTERACTING FACTOR 1 (PIF1). Conversely, abiotic stresses typically elevate cytosolic Ca2+ and inhibit germination. However, the coordination of light and calcium signaling during germination under stress conditions remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that salt and osmotic stresses rapidly increase cytosolic Ca2+ in imbibed seeds, and that the calcium sensor CALMODULIN-LIKE 20 (CML20) is crucial for germination tolerance to these stresses. CML20 directly interacts with PIF1 in a Ca2+-dependent manner, suppressing PIF1 self-association, oligomerization, and DNA-binding capacity. Moreover, phyB interacts with CML20 and PIF1 independently, promoting the assembly of the CML20-PIF1 complex and further reducing PIF1's transcriptional activity. Genetic analyses reveal that PIF1 functions downstream of CML20, and that CML20 and phyB operate within the same pathway. Together, our findings define a phyB-CML20-PIF1 module, providing a rapid, reversible, and non-proteolytic mechanism to optimize seed germination under stress conditions.
items.authors: Kang J, Li J, Liu X, Zhao S, Zhong S, Shi H.

items.title: ZJP-2, a novel wild jujube polysaccharide, enhances longevity, cognitive function, and mitigates oxidative stress via mitochondrial regulation in Caenorhabditis elegans.
items.abstract: Oxidative stress, caused by an imbalance between reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and antioxidant defenses, drives aging and age related functional decline. Natural polysaccharides from medicinal plants are promising interventions against oxidative stress related disorders. This study examined the protective effects of a novel polysaccharide (ZJP-2) isolated from wild jujube (Ziziphus jujuba Mill. var. spinosa) against stress induced physiological deterioration in Caenorhabditis elegans. Using lipopolysaccharide exposure, heat shock, and oxidative stress models, we assessed ZJP-2 effects on lifespan, health span, antioxidant capacity, and stress response pathways. ZJP-2 (0.25-1 mg/mL) showed no toxicity and did not inhibit Escherichia coli OP50 growth. Treatment significantly improved locomotor activity, pharyngeal pumping, and reproductive capacity. The optimal dose increased average lifespan by 42.03% and reduced intestinal lipofuscin accumulation by 52.89%. Under heat stress (37 °C), ZJP-2 enhanced thermotolerance and improved survival under oxidative stress. Intracellular ROS levels decreased in a dose dependent manner, accompanied by reductions in malondialdehyde and increases in superoxide dismutase, catalase, and glutathione activities. Gene expression analysis revealed modulation of antioxidant and mitochondrial-associated genes, along with p38 MAPK-associated genes. ZJP-2 also promoted activation of the longevity associated transcription factor daf-16. These findings demonstrate that ZJP-2 enhances stress resistance, reduces oxidative damage, and promotes a healthy lifespan, highlighting its potential as a natural bioactive compound to mitigate stress related aging.
items.authors: Shakir MZ, Ullah I, Usmani MW, Ning J, Liu J, Zhou X, Zhao Y, Du Q, Chen H, Ali M, Wang N, Liu X.

items.title: Optimization of extraction conditions for total flavonoids from Clerodendrum cyrtophyllum Turcz. and its antibacterial activity and mechanism against Staphylococcus aureus.
items.abstract: IntroductionClerodendrum cyrtophyllum Turcz., a traditional Chinese medicinal plant, exhibits broad bioactivity. Nevertheless, the flavonoid constituents conferring anti-Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) activity and their mechanistic basis remain to be elucidated.MethodsTotal flavonoid extraction from Clerodendrum cyrtophyllum Turcz. (TFC) was first evaluated by single-factor experiments to screen key variables and subsequently optimized by a Box-Behnken design (BBD) within response surface methodology (RSM). followed by purification with D101 macroporous resin. Liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) characterized the chemical profile. Antibacterial activity against S. aureus was assessed via inhibition zones, minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC), and growth curves. Mechanisms were explored by evaluating cell surface hydrophobicity (CSH), extracellular alkaline phosphatase (AKP), leakage of nucleic acids/proteins, membrane potential, ATP levels, reactive oxygen species (ROS) content, and morphological alterations.ResultsThe optimal extraction conditions for TFC were determined as 70% ethanol as the solvent, an extraction time of 102 min, a temperature of 64 °C, and a solid-liquid ratio of 1:25 (g: mL), resulting in a yield of 6.48% ± 0.58. After purification, the purity of TFC was increased to 76%, and preliminary analysis identified 85 flavonoid constituents. TFC exhibited inhibition zone diameters of 13 ± 0.45 mm, 16 ± 0.38 mm, and 20 ± 0.45 mm at concentrations of 50, 100, and 150 mg/mL, respectively, with MIC and MBC values of 0.781 mg/mL and 1.562 mg/mL. Notably, TFC effectively inhibited the growth of S. aureus within 24 h. Mechanistic investigations revealed that TFC treatment increased S. aureus CSH and decreased the membrane potential, leading to the leakage of intracellular nucleic acids and proteins, indicating damage to S. aureus cells, which was further confirmed by SEM. Furthermore, TFC induced significant intracellular ATP depletion, decreased intracellular nucleic acids and protein contents, and triggered excessive ROS production.ConclusionThis study optimized the extraction conditions of TFC and successfully obtained TFC rich in multiple flavonoid constituents. TFC exerts potent inhibitory effects on S. aureus by disrupting the integrity of cell walls and membranes, depleting intracellular energy reserves, decreasing the contents of intracellular nucleic acids and proteins, and inducing intracellular oxidative stress.
items.authors: Hu Y, Luo W, Tan C, Pei G.

items.title: Salinity-adapted and core microbiota along the soil salinity gradients encircling the Tarim Basin.
items.abstract: BackgroundSoil salinization affects nearly one-tenth of global drylands and imposes strong environmental filters on microbial communities. The Tarim Basin in Xinjiang, China, is one of the world's largest inland basins and an extreme saline-arid ecosystem, yet a basin-scale understanding of its microbiota remains lacking. In this study, we collected 132 soil samples along a salinity gradient spanning more than 3,000 km encircling the Tarim Basin. By combining amplicon sequencing with measurements of soil physicochemical properties, we aimed to unravel the salinity-adapted microbiota and core microbial taxa characteristic of this extreme environment.ResultsOur results showed that bacterial communities, rather than fungal communities, were strongly shaped by soil salinity. Extremely saline soils exhibited reduced bacterial diversity and were enriched in halophilic and halotolerant taxa, including Natronomonas, Salinimicrobium, Stenotrophomonas, Salinibacter, Halorussus, and Halomicrobium. In contrast, taxa such as Arthrobacter, Rubrobacter, Rubellimicrobium, and Fusarium declined with increasing salinity. Soil cation concentrations (Na+, K+, Ca2+, Mg2+), major anions (Cl-, SO42-), and electrical conductivity all increased significantly along the salinity gradient. Despite this strong environmental filtering, we identified a set of potential core microbiota consistently present across all soils, dominated by Halomonas, Salinimicrobium, Natronomonas, Rubrobacter, and members of the Palleronia-Pseudomaribius group. Their persistent occurrence across the basin suggests that these taxa play key roles in sustaining ecosystem functions within the extreme saline-arid environments of the Tarim Basin.ConclusionsOur basin-scale analysis reveals that soil salinity significantly contributes to microbial community assembly in the Tarim Basin, selecting for specialized halophilic and halotolerant taxa while reducing overall bacterial diversity. The discovery of core microbiota with known salt-adaptation mechanisms highlights the presence of a stable microbial backbone across heterogeneous saline landscapes. These findings provide new ecological insights into how extreme salinity shapes microbiome structure and identify candidate microbial groups potentially contributing to ecosystem stability and plant stress resilience in arid saline environments.
items.authors: Liu X, Jia Q, Tang Q, Ding Y, Zhang Z, Gu M, Huang W, Wang N, Zhang L, Zhu J.

items.title: The PvAURK-PvGRFs regulatory module controls salt tolerance in common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris L.).
items.abstract: The common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris L.) is an important edible legume. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying its salt tolerance remain unclear. Here, we used a panel of 494 diverse common bean accessions and identified Aurora Kinase (AURK) as a key gene associated with salt tolerance using a genome-wide association study (GWAS). Functional validation demonstrated that PvAURK interacts with growth regulatory factors (GRF2 and GRF5) both in vivo and in vitro. All three genes positively regulate salt tolerance in common bean. Transcriptomic analysis showed that PvAURK modulates the salt stress response by regulating the reactive oxygen species (ROS) scavenging system via PvGRF transcription factors, with medium-chain-fatty-acid-[acyl-carrier-protein] ligase (MC-ACPL) and PTHR31388:SF157-PEROXIDASE (SF157-PRx) identified as downstream target genes of PvGRFs. Haplotype analysis showed that Hap2 of PvAURK is associated with enhanced salt tolerance. Key single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) within these haplotypes strengthen the interactions between PvAURK and PvGRFs proteins. PvAURK Hap2 is the predominant salt-tolerant haplotype in natural common bean populations. This study elucidates the role of the PvAURK-PvGRF regulatory module in mediating salt tolerance in common bean. The developed KASP markers are efficient tools for marker-assisted breeding to improve salt tolerance.
items.authors: Yu S, Yu T, Wang L, Sun X, Lyu M, Hu Z, Chang Y, Wang S, Wu S, Ge W, Shen X, Zhang Q, Zhang H, Chen R, Wu J, Jiang Q.

items.title: A cytoskeleton-associated Plasmodium protein critical for organelle segregation.
items.abstract: The malaria parasite, Plasmodium falciparum, replicates asexually within red blood cells by schizogony, a mode of division in which organelles divide multiple times before a final coordinated cytokinesis event, called segmentation, partitions them into dozens of merozoites. The Plasmodium cytoskeleton functions critically during this process, facilitating one-per-cell organelle segregation. Here, we identify and characterize a cytoskeleton-associated protein, PfOGRE (organelle retention, PF3D7_1435600), required for segregation of the mitochondrion and apicoplast, a non-photosynthetic plastid. Immunofluorescence paired with ultrastructure expansion microscopy demonstrates that PfOGRE localizes alongside subpellicular microtubules in nascent merozoites, adjacent to the segregating apicoplast. Conditional knockout of PfOGRE produces organelle-less merozoites with abnormal subpellicular microtubules, impairing asexual replication. Immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry identify several candidate interactors, including PfMyoF. Conditional knockdown of PfMyoF produces similar organelle segregation defects. Together, these results establish PfOGRE as a critical mediator of organelle segregation and define a non-structural role for Plasmodium subpellicular microtubules during this process.
items.authors: Navarro FM, Wagner E, Kraemer S, Gurung P, Dvorin JD.

items.title: Zerumbone alleviates TRESK- and TRPV1-mediated ion currents and reduces excitability of human iPSC-derived nociceptor-like neurons.
items.abstract: Secondary plant metabolites are widely used in traditional and naturopathic medicine to treat pain, infection, and inflammation. The sesquiterpenoid zerumbone, derived from the edible ginger Zingiber zerumbet, has been shown to exert analgesic, antioxidant, antitumoral, and antimicrobial effects in preclinical models, acting through multiple receptor systems including cannabinoid (CB) receptors, peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors, N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors, and the serotonergic system. Zerumbone also modulates inflammatory and nitric oxide-cGMP-K+ATP signaling pathways implicated in antiallodynic responses, yet its direct impact on nociceptor-associated ion channels like the Transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1) and the Twik-related spinal cord potassium channel (TRESK) in human cellular systems remains poorly characterized. In the present study, the antinociceptive properties of zerumbone were investigated in human HEK293-based and induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived nociceptor models. Here, the zerumbone treatment reduced cell viability and proliferation in a concentration-dependent manner without altering TRPV1 or TRESK protein expression. Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings revealed that zerumbone reversibly inhibited TRESK-mediated outward potassium currents upon direct application, whereas bath-applied zerumbone increased outward currents, suggesting context-dependent modulation. In TRPV1-expressing HEK293 cells, SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells, and human iPSC-derived nociceptors, zerumbone reduced TRPV1-mediated ion currents and capsaicin-evoked calcium signals, indicating a direct or competitive inhibitory effect on TRPV1 activity. In iPSC-derived nociceptors, zerumbone decreased action potential firing at moderate depolarizing currents, shifted the resting membrane potential, and increased rheobase, consistent with reduced nociceptor excitability, while no significant changes in TRESK-mediated currents were detected. These data suggest that zerumbone attenuates human iPSC-derived nociceptor-like neuron excitability largely via TRPV1 inhibition, with a more complex, concentration- and application-method-dependent modulation of TRESK. The findings provide a mechanistic basis for the antiallodynic effects of zerumbone observed in rodent models and highlight the need for further studies in human-derived systems to clarify the precise channel-level interactions and their relevance to inflammatory and neuropathic pain.
items.authors: Hoerdler N, Grell A, Chatterjee S, Wischmeyer E, Nossek BA, Dräger O.

items.title: Root responses to mechanical heterogeneity are shaped by pore geometry and root-soil biomechanics
items.abstract: Mechanical limitations to root growth occur when pressure exerted by turgor within root cells is counteracted by excessive resistance of the surrounding soil as well as by that of the cell walls. In a natural soil, however, heterogeneity allows roots to find paths of least resistance, though the governing principles behind this process have yet to be identified. Here, we combined artificial substrates, high-throughput live imaging, advanced image analysis, and mechanical modelling to uncover the principles governing the ability of a root to penetrate or deflect from zones of high mechanical impedance within a heterogeneous substrate. Our findings show that root responses to substrate heterogeneity can be accurately predicted from the pore-matrix geometry when both the mechanical properties of the substrate and those of the roots are known. Consequently, a crucial step toward understanding the physical limitations to root growth may lie in a detailed characterisation of soil mechanical properties.
items.authors: Yao, J., de las Heras Martinez, G., Patko, D., Bico, J., Kolb, E., Dupuy, L. X.

items.title: Comparative chromosome-scale genomics of the ayahuasca liana Banisteriopsis caapi reveals paleopolyploid ancestry and recent tandem-gene expansions as candidate signatures of ethnovariety differentiation
items.abstract: Background: Banisteriopsis caapi is the Amazonian liana that provides the {beta}-carboline-rich vine component of ayahuasca, a traditional Amazonian psychoactive preparation used in Indigenous and ceremonial contexts. The species encompasses culturally recognized ethnovarieties, some differing in stem architecture. Despite its cultural, ecological, and pharmacological importance, B. caapi remains largely unexplored at the genomic level. Here, we generated chromosome-scale genome assemblies for the caupuri and tucunaca ethnovarieties and used them to investigate genome evolution, structural variation, repeat composition, and candidate genomic features associated with ethnovariety-level differentiation. Results: Caupuri and tucunaca assemblies span 1.16 and 1.13 Gb, respectively, each organized into ten high-quality chromosome-scale pseudomolecules. Both genomes retain signatures of two ancient post-gamma duplication components, with related signals also detected in Malpighia emarginata, suggesting that at least part of this paleopolyploid history may predate the divergence of these Malpighiaceae lineages. Against this conserved chromosomal framework, the sampled caupuri and tucunaca genomes differ in structural variation, repeat composition, and gene-family profiles. Transposable element-associated insertions and deletions dominate the structural-variant landscape, while both genomes are highly repetitive, with approximately 78% of their assemblies composed of repetitive DNA largely shaped by LTR retrotransposons, including Gypsy/Retand and Copia/Ale, Copia/Tork, and Copia/Ivana lineages, together with non-autonomous large retrotransposon derivatives (LARDs). Most genes belong to shared orthogroups, indicating a largely conserved gene repertoire. However, candidate ethnovariety-biased differences emerge from the combined remodeling of gene families, LARD and LTR-associated genomic neighborhoods, and comparatively recent local expansions of tandem-duplicated gene arrays encoding signaling receptors, transporters, hormone-associated genes, cell wall and secondary wall functions, and meristem or organ-development pathways. Conclusions: These results indicate that the sampled caupuri and tucunaca genomes differ mainly through localized remodeling of shared genomic modules, including comparatively recent repeat turnover and local tandem-gene expansions. These assemblies provide the first large-scale nuclear genomic resource for B. caapi and a foundation for investigating paleopolyploid evolution in Malpighiaceae and candidate mechanisms of ethnovariety diversification.

items.title: Receptor-like kinase RLK15 binds a fungal RNase effector to enhance autophosphorylation and activate host defense
items.abstract: Fungal pathogens secrete diverse effectors to suppress host immunity, yet the plant receptors that perceive these virulence factors often remain elusive. Here, we identify Ss1624, a secreted RNase from the sugarcane smut pathogen Sporisorium scitamineum, and show that it is recognized by the plasma-membrane-localized CrRLK1L-family receptor kinase RLK15. This recognition triggers canonical immune outputs, including reactive oxygen species burst, callose deposition, defense gene activation, and induces hypersensitive cell death. Mechanistically, Ss1624 physically interacts with the receptor-like kinase RLK15, which is required for Ss1624-triggered cell death. Functional assays indicate that this interaction enhances RLK15 autophosphorylation in a kinase activity-dependent manner, suggesting that Ss1624 can act as an elicitor. Transcript profiling further reveals coordinated expression patterns of Ss1624 and RLK15 during infection, and perturbation of Ss1624 expression alters RLK15 transcript levels and pathogenic outcomes. Extending these findings to rice, the ortholog OsRLK15 contributes positively to resistance to bacterial and fungal diseases without yield penalty in rice. Our results support a model in which a secreted RNase effector is directly sensed by a receptor kinase to initiate broad-spectrum immune responses, providing insights into host-pathogen interactions and identifying RLK15 as a candidate for crop improvement.
items.authors: Li, L., Lian, Y., Zhang, L., Jia, H., Gai, Y., Smagghe, G., Tang, S., Yang, M., Cai, E., Deng, Y., Jiang, Z., Zhang, L., Zhou, X., Chang, C.

items.title: A miniaturized Arabidopsis thaliana - Botrytis cinerea seedling pathosystem and the GreenDayz workflow for longitudinal image-based phenotyping
items.abstract: Plant-pathogen interactions are strongly influenced by host developmental stage, yet many Arabidopsis thaliana-Botrytis cinerea assays remain centred on mature rosette leaves and rely on inoculum loads that may exceed those involved in a primary infection. We established a miniaturized in vitro A. thaliana-B. cinerea seedling pathosystem initiated with a very low conidial dose (nominally ~25 conidia per plate) compatible with both destructive molecular sampling and repeated, non-destructive RGB imaging. The pathosystem was coupled to a low-cost smartphone photo station and to GreenDayZ Phenotyping, a guided image-analysis application with an intuitive graphical interface that standardizes longitudinal RGB image processing and extracts quantitative colour-based phenotypes. Together, the pathosystem and GreenDayZ Phenotyping provide an accessible and reproducible framework for longitudinal phenotyping of low-inoculum seedling infections, in which image-derived trajectories can be aligned with independent molecular readouts.
items.authors: Tguafaiti, I., BRUEL, C., CHOQUER, M., Bournaud, C., Poussereau, N., Gillet, F.-X.

items.title: LMBD2 interacts with components of the ECH/YIP complex and contributes to post-Golgi trafficking in Arabidopsis
items.abstract: Abstract The plant cell wall, composed primarily of polysaccharides, is essential for normal plant growth and development. Many of these polysaccharides are synthesized within and subsequently secreted via the endomembrane system. Mutations in genes including MURUS3 (MUR3), YPT/RAB GTPase-interacting protein 4 homologs (YIP4a/YIP4b), and ECHIDNA (ECH) result in dwarf plants, which is believed to be a consequence of impaired cell wall polysaccharide secretion. Here, we identify a LMBR1 (Limb Development Membrane Protein 1)-like membrane protein (LMBD2) and find that loss of LMBD2 suppresses the secretion and growth defects in the mur3, yip4a/yip4b, and ech mutants. LMBD2 localizes to the trans-Golgi apparatus and trans-Golgi network (TGN)/early endosome (EE), where it interacts with YIP4b and orchestrates TGN/EE-mediated trafficking. Furthermore, LMBD2 can competitively attenuate the interaction of YIP4b and ECH. Our findings establish LMBD2 as a component of endomembrane trafficking homeostasis in plant cells and offer new insights into endomembrane dynamics and their influence on plant development.
items.authors: Wang M, Xu Z, Hoffmann N, Guo S, Dou X, Wang B, Su Y, Qu Y, Song X, O’Neill M, Bjørk PK, Persson S, Xu Y, Wang C, Wang D, Kong Y, McFarlane HE, Zhou G

items.title: Conserved DEAD-box RNA helicases regulate RNA silencing and plant immunity and are targeted by a powdery mildew effector
items.abstract: Abstract RNA silencing is a conserved defense mechanism that protects plants against viruses, bacteria, fungi, and oomycetes. Although diverse pathogens have evolved effectors that suppress host RNA silencing, whether powdery mildew fungi exploit this strategy and the underlying molecular mechanisms remain unknown. Here, we identify CSEP0004, a secreted effector from the barley powdery mildew fungus Blumeria hordei, as an RNA silencing suppressor that promotes fungal virulence. CSEP0004 physically interacts with the evolutionarily conserved DEAD-box RNA helicases Hordeum vulgare RNA helicase 37 (HvRH37) and HvRH52. Genetic analyses demonstrate that HvRH37 and HvRH52 positively regulate chitin-triggered reactive oxygen species production, resistance to B. hordei, and small RNA accumulation in barley, while their Arabidopsis homologs AtRH11/37/52 perform conserved functions in small RNA accumulation. Mechanistically, HvRH37 and HvRH52 associate with HvAGO1, a core component of the RNA-induced silencing complex, and function as biochemically active RNA helicases capable of binding and unwinding double-stranded RNA. CSEP0004 disrupts the HvRH37/52–AGO1 association and inhibits HvRH37/52 helicase activity in a dose-dependent manner. Together, our findings uncover a previously unrecognized mechanism by which a fungal effector suppresses host RNA silencing through targeting conserved DDX3-like DEAD-box RNA helicases, establishing these helicases as key regulators of RNAi-mediated immunity and identifying RNA helicase-dependent RNA remodeling as a critical regulatory node exploited by fungal pathogens.
items.authors: Pei H, Chen Z, Li J, Gui X, Li X, Feng L, Du T, Liu Y, Yang H, Huang W, Zhang J, Wang D, Yin L, Li Y, Qi T, Jin H, Zhang X, Guo H, Fan R, Shen QH, Qiao Y

items.title: The energy sensor SnRK1 promotes starvation-induced autophagosome formation by modulating ATG13a phosphorylation in Arabidopsis
items.abstract: Abstract In eukaryotes, autophagy is an evolutionarily conserved cellular degradation and recycling process that is tightly associated with cellular nutrient status. The energy sensor SNF1-RELATED KINASE 1 (SnRK1) is thought to sense nutrient starvation and induce autophagy, but how it regulates autophagosome formation in plant cells remains largely unknown. Here, we show that the SnRK1 α-catalytic subunit KIN10 regulates autophagosome formation in Arabidopsis (Arabidopsis thaliana) by interacting with and phosphorylating AUTOPHAGY-RELATED PROTEIN 13a (ATG13a), a key component of the ATG1a–ATG13a protein kinase complex involved in autophagy initiation. KIN10 directly phosphorylates ATG13a in vitro and in vivo, inhibiting its ubiquitination and increasing its abundance. Moreover, we identified ten serine residues in ATG13a that are important for KIN10-mediated phosphorylation. Transgenic plants accumulating a nonphosphorylatable ATG13a variant with mutations of these ten residues were less tolerant of starvation than ATG13a-overexpressing plants and displayed accelerated leaf senescence and lower autophagic flux. The KIN10-mediated phosphorylation of ATG13a did not affect ATG1a–ATG13a complex formation; instead, it facilitated ATG1a phosphorylation, thereby promoting autophagosome formation. Therefore, our findings suggest that the KIN10–ATG13a module modulates SnRK1-mediated autophagosome formation, likely representing a key step in integrating energy sensing and autophagy initiation in plant cells.
items.authors: Wang LN, Wang W, Zhang HM, Lu XY, Yan ZR, Zhang TY, Wang Y, Zhong QL, Liao K, Yu S, Jiang L, Xie D, Xiao S

items.title: Whole-genome duplication reshapes gene–miRNA regulatory networks underlying improved salt stress tolerance in Medicago sativa
items.abstract: Abstract Whole-genome duplication (WGD) is a recurrent feature of plant evolution and crop improvement, yet its direct contribution to abiotic stress tolerance remains difficult to disentangle from hybridization effects. Using full-sibling diploid (2x) and neotetraploid (4x) Medicago sativa genotypes generated through bilateral sexual polyploidization, we investigated how WGD alone reshapes physiological performance and gene–miRNA regulatory networks under salt stress. Neotetraploid plants displayed enhanced tolerance to salinity, maintaining higher chlorophyll content, stomatal conductance, and shoot integrity, alongside reduced visual damage compared with diploid siblings. Transcriptome profiling revealed that ploidy level, rather than salt treatment per se, was the dominant driver of gene expression variation. Indeed, WGD resulted in extensive and largely constitutive transcriptional reprogramming, with more than 2,000 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) distinguishing 4x from 2x plants under both control and saline conditions. By contrast, under salt stress, 705 DEGs specifically differentiated tetraploids from diploids and were enriched in receptor-like kinases, phosphorylation pathways, ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis, flavonoid biosynthesis, and WRKY- and MYB-centered regulatory modules. Co-expression network analysis identified salt-associated modules linking signaling and antioxidant pathways with stress-related physiological traits. Small RNA sequencing further showed that WGD reshapes post-transcriptional regulation, with limited salt-induced miRNA changes but the emergence of ploidy-dependent miRNA hubs, including miR2593e and a novel miRNA, targeting signaling and defense-related genes. We hypothesize that WGD establishes a stress-ready regulatory architecture in which coordinated transcriptional and post-transcriptional network rebalancing acts as a buffering system that improves alfalfa physiological performance under salinity, without strong induction of canonical salt-responsive genes.
items.authors: Santoro DF, Del Regno C, Anderson AW, Cappetta E, Conte M, Carputo D, Ambrosone A, Rosellini D

items.title: Distinct root apoplastic barrier distribution and conserved peroxidase function in desert trees
items.abstract: Abstract The formation of extracellular barriers in roots plays a critical role in maintaining water balance and nutrient homeostasis; however, their molecular composition and physiological roles in desert-adapted plants remain largely unexplored. Here, we examine apoplastic barrier formation in the roots of two arid-adapted, ecologically and economically important tree species: date palm (Phoenix dactylifera) and grey mangrove (Avicennia marina). In date palm, lignin and suberin showed complementary distribution patterns within the outer root layers. In mangrove roots, lignin accumulated in the epidermis and exodermis, whereas suberin was concentrated in the exodermis. Label-free Raman spectroscopy imaging confirmed these spatial patterns. Noninvasive Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed that water distribution mirrored barrier localization: date palms retained water in the vasculature and outer tissues, whereas mangroves concentrated water in the xylem. Transcriptome analysis identified a type III PEROXIDASE (PER) highly expressed in the exodermis of both species. The PER protein localized to Golgi-derived vesicles and the plasma membrane and interacted with a component of the Golgi apparatus. Expression of date palm and mangrove PER in Arabidopsis thaliana leads to ectopic lignin deposition in the root epidermis. Together, our findings suggest that type III PEROXIDASES are transported to the plasma membrane through the Golgi vesicles and promote lignin deposition. Overall, this study reveals distinct root barrier distribution and identifies a conserved molecular component underlying structural adaptations that enable plants to thrive in challenging environments.
items.authors: Kise JG, Xiao TT, Xu X, Laptenok S, Genchi L, Guo X, Canlas CG, Liberale C, Blilou I

items.title: Transcription factor ANAC087 coordinates symplastic Cd exclusion and apoplastic Cd sequestration to enhance cadmium resistance in Arabidopsis thaliana
items.abstract: Abstract Cadmium (Cd) exclusion and sequestration are vital mechanisms for plant survival under heavy metal stress, yet the upstream regulatory networks governing these coordinated processes remain poorly understood. In this study, we identified the NAC transcription factor ANAC087 as a key positive regulator of Cd resistance in Arabidopsis thaliana. Loss-of-function anac087 mutants exhibited hypersensitivity to Cd stress and significantly higher Cd accumulation in both roots and shoots compared to the wild type (WT) Col-0. Mechanistically, we demonstrate that ANAC087 coordinates two complementary pathways involving symplastic Cd influx control and apoplastic sequestration. First, ANAC087 contributes to ABA homeostasis and directly binds to the promoter of ABSCISIC ACID-INSENSITIVE5 (ABI5) to activate its expression, which subsequently antagonizes the MYB49-bHLH38/101 regulatory module to suppress IRT1, thereby limiting Cd uptake. Exogenous ABA application partially alleviated the Cd-sensitive phenotype of anac087. Second, ANAC087 directly transactivates ANAC017 to promote XTH31-mediated xyloglucan accumulation, substantially enhancing the Cd binding capacity of the root cell wall. Genetic analyses confirmed that ectopic expression of ABI5 or ANAC017 partially rescued the Cd sensitive and high-Cd accumulation phenotypes of anac087, whereas XTH31 overexpression complemented the anac017 anac087 double mutant. Furthermore, Cd stress increases both ANAC087 transcript abundance and protein stability. Collectively, our findings support a regulatory framework in which ANAC087 coordinates processes that limit symplastic Cd accumulation and promote apoplastic Cd sequestration.
items.authors: Li S, Tao Y, Zheng L, Yu FW, Zhang Q, Chen CZ, Huang J, Wang SY, Zhang YD, Liu MQ, Shen RF, Zhu XF

items.title: OsGSK2-OsBSK3 feedback loop controls rice BR signaling
items.abstract: Abstract Brassinosteroids (BRs) are essential plant hormones that regulate growth and development, including leaf angle regulation and grain size determination. Maintaining appropriate BR signaling requires precise coordination between pathway activation and attenuation. BR signaling is initiated by OsBRI1 activation, which triggers a phosphorylation cascade that ultimately inhibits OsGSK2 kinase activity, releasing OsBZR1 from repression and activating downstream responses. However, whether additional regulatory mechanisms fine-tune BR signaling remains unclear. Here, we identify OsBSK3 as a direct substrate of OsGSK2 and uncover a phosphorylation-dependent feedback mechanism within the BR signaling pathway. OsGSK2-mediated phosphorylation enhances the interactions of OsBSK3 with OsBRI1, OsGSK2, and OsPPKL1 while attenuating the regulatory activity of OsBSK3. Genetic analyses revealed that overexpression of wild-type OsBSK3 or the phosphorylation-deficient variant OsBSK3SA enhances BR responses and fully rescues the leaf angle and grain size defects of the osbsk3 mutant, whereas the phosphomimetic variant OsBSK3SD fails to restore these phenotypes. Together, our findings establish a phosphorylation-dependent OsGSK2-OsBSK3 negative feedback mechanism that fine-tunes BR signaling homeostasis in rice.
items.authors: Tian X, Zhang W, Fu L, Wang X, Chen C, Jin X, Bu Q

items.title: Convergent evolution of an oxidative damage tolerance mechanism preserves replication fidelity in plant organellar DNA polymerases
items.abstract: Abstract Plant mitochondria and chloroplasts are sources of reactive oxygen species (ROS) that trigger oxidative DNA lesions. Among these, 8-oxo-7,8-dihydroguanine (8-oxodG) is particularly mutagenic because it exhibits ambiguous base pairing, as DNA polymerases efficiently incorporate adenine opposite 8-oxodG, leading to G·C→T·A transversions. Despite exposure to oxidative stress, plant organellar genomes exhibit some of the lowest nucleotide substitution rates in nature, implying that their DNA replication machinery may have evolved mechanisms to cope with oxidative lesions such as 8-oxodG. In family-A DNA polymerases, including yeast and animal mitochondrial DNA polymerases, the balance between faithful dCMP incorporation and mutagenic dAMP incorporation opposite 8-oxodG is governed by a bulky or positively charged residue. Surprisingly, although the equivalent position in the Arabidopsis thaliana organellar DNA polymerases AtPolIA and AtPolIB is occupied by glycine—a residue predicted to promote mutagenic dAMP incorporation—both enzymes nevertheless preferentially incorporate accurate dCMP opposite 8-oxodG. Our structure–function analyses demonstrate that AtPolI´s fidelity opposite 8-oxodG is conferred by a lysine located near the templating base, which generates steric and electrostatic constraints that favor the 8-oxodG(anti):dCTP pairing while disfavoring the mutagenic 8-oxodG(syn):dATP pair. This mechanism represents an example of convergent evolution, as the fidelity-determining lysine in plant organellar polymerases is in a different position than the analogous residues in yeast-animal mitochondrial polymerases but achieves the same function. Together, these findings suggest that plant organellar DNA polymerases have evolved specialized properties that promote accurate bypass of oxidative DNA lesions, which may contribute to the maintenance of the exceptionally low mutation rates observed in plant organellar genomes.
items.authors: Molina-Jiménez M, Baruch-Torres N, Díaz-Quezada C, Brieba LG

items.title: The homologous GRAS transcription factors RAM1 and RAD1 coordinate shared and separate gene networks to regulate arbuscular mycorrhiza symbiosis
items.abstract: Summary Arbuscular mycorrhiza (AM), a symbiosis between plants and Glomeromycotan fungi is based on the exchange of nutrients, which majorly occurs between fungal tree‐shaped arbuscules and root cortex cells. Two homologous plant GRAS transcription factors, RAM1 and RAD1, were previously reported to interact, and both were implicated in regulating arbuscule branching in Lotus japonicus . We revisited the role of L. japonicus RAM1 and RAD1 and asked whether they act together in mediating arbuscule development and gene expression, or whether they act additively. We performed comprehensive genetic, phenotypic, and transcriptome analyses of two allelic Lotus ram1 , rad1 , and ram1 rad1 mutants; and of roots ectopically expressing RAM1 and/or RAD1. We found that RAD1 is required for full root colonization in a RAM1 ‐dependent manner, but in our growth conditions, RAD1 is not required for arbuscule branching. In addition, RAM1 and RAD1 are required for activation of partially common and partially distinct sets of downstream genes. Thus, in contrast to RAM1 , Lotus RAD1 is not essential for arbuscule branching. Furthermore, RAM1 and RAD1 seem to act partially synergistically but seem to participate in additional alternative transcription factor complexes to regulate AM‐induced gene expression and AM development.
items.authors: Zeng T, Alpers J, Boniolo F, Huettl R, Berger F, Hernandez Cortes C, Gutjahr C

items.title: Engineering root development with high precision
items.abstract: Summary Root development is controlled by dynamic interactions between gene regulation, hormonal signalling, developmental history and environmental inputs, creating multiple layers of control that can be harnessed for engineering. Recent advances in single‐cell technologies, spatial transcriptomics and synthetic biology are beginning to resolve root development at the cellular level and enable increasingly precise manipulation of developmental programmes. Here, we discuss how lineage tracing, genetic recording of developmental history, cell‐type‐specific engineering and programmable genetic circuits can be integrated to understand and control root architecture. We highlight emerging strategies for engineering adaptive and context‐dependent developmental behaviours, including history‐dependent and reversible response programmes and rewired root‐environment interactions. Together, these approaches establish a foundation for programmable and adaptive root system engineering in plants.
items.authors: Bilas RD, Guiziou S

items.title: Mapping the epigenetic regulatory network of cotton single‐cell fiber elongation mediated by H3K4me3
items.abstract: Summary Histone modifications are central to plant development, yet how they coordinate cellular morphogenesis remains poorly understood. Cotton fibers, as single‐celled trichomes derived from seed epidermal cells, provide an ideal model to address this question. Multi‐omics approaches were used, including cleavage under targets and tagmentation for genome‐wide H3K4me3 profiling and transcriptome sequencing. These were integrated with molecular and genetic validation experiments such as virus‐induced gene silencing, overexpression, CRISPR/Cas9, yeast one/two‐hybrid, electrophoretic mobility shift assay, co‐immunoprecipitation, and split‐luciferase complementation assays. We identify GhMYBL as a core transcriptional repressor that negatively regulates fiber elongation. GhMYBL is subject to dual control: H3K4me3 governs its transcription, whereas GhHBI1 posttranslationally attenuates its DNA‐binding activity. GhMYBL directly represses the positive regulators GhXTH22 and GhALP1 , limiting elongation; GhHBI1 relieves this repression, enabling their normal expression and synergistic promotion of fiber elongation. Our results demonstrate that differential H3K4me3 modification orchestrates GhMYBL‐mediated transcriptional repression, which is fine‐tuned by GhHBI1 interaction to coordinate fiber cell elongation. This study provides mechanistic insights into the epigenetic control of cell elongation and highlights promising targets for cotton fiber improvement.
items.authors: Yu M, Liu L, Guo Y, Xu Y, Li Y, Li X, Wang Y, Fan L, Yang Z

items.title: PuWRKY46 drives root system architecture and enhances salt tolerance in poplar
items.abstract: Summary The developmental plasticity of lateral roots (LRs) is an essential adaptive strategy for optimizing root system architecture under salt stress. However, the molecular mechanisms by which salt stress modulates LR plasticity through cell wall remodeling remain largely elusive, particularly in woody species. This study investigates the abscisic acid (ABA)‐responsive transcription factor PuWRKY46 as a critical regulator of LR developmental plasticity under salt stress in Populus ussuriensis . This study integrated phenotypic characterization of transgenic overexpression and RNA interference (RNAi) poplar lines, molecular biochemical assays, protein–protein interaction analyses, transcriptomics, DNA affinity purification sequencing (DAP‐seq), phosphorylation assays, and cell wall biochemical analyses. Compared with wild‐type plants, PuWRKY46 overexpression promotes LR emergence and enhances salt tolerance, whereas PuWRKY46‐ RNAi lines exhibit pronounced salt sensitivity. Furthermore, the mitogen‐activated protein kinase PuMPK15 interacts with PuWRKY46, and the resulting phosphorylation stabilizes PuWRKY46 to enhance salt tolerance. The PuMPK15–PuWRKY46 module targets cell wall‐loosening gene EXPANSIN‐A11 ( PuEXPA11 ) to promote localized apoplastic acidification and relax hemicellulose cross‐linking, thereby driving root cell wall remodeling and facilitating LR development. The PuMPK15–PuWRKY46 signaling cascade regulates salt‐adaptive LR architectural plasticity in poplar. This study reveals a conditional‐plasticity regulatory mechanism and provides a valuable genetic resource for breeding salt‐tolerant woody plants.
items.authors: Zhao H, Zhao S, Sun T, Zhuang W, Gao J, Zhang H, Ren J, Liu Q, Yang J

items.title: Phosphorylation and epigenetic remodeling mediate BpEBP1 ‐dependent drought resistance in birch
items.abstract: Summary BpEBP1, an ethylene‐responsive factor VII transcription factor, coordinates stress resilience in birch ( Betula platyphylla ), but its molecular mechanisms underlying drought response remain unclear. Using transgenic birch lines (overexpression and knockout), chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP)‐seq, biochemical assays, and protein interaction studies, we dissected the multilayered regulatory network of BpEBP1. BpEBP1 enhances drought tolerance in birch by directly activating key lignin and anthocyanin biosynthesis genes ( BpMYC2 , BpCOMT , and BpPOD5 ), thereby promoting lignin deposition and anthocyanin accumulation, which reinforce cell wall rigidity and boost reactive oxygen species scavenging capacity. Beyond the canonical GCC‐box cis ‐element, BpEBP1 binds to novel Noyes and ZNF449 motifs and uses these cis ‐elements to drive expression of the previously described target genes. Mechanistically, BpEBP1 recruits the histone demethylase BpJMJ25 to remove repressive H3K9me2 marks, thereby increasing chromatin accessibility to facilitate transcriptional activation. Meanwhile, drought‐induced phosphorylation at Thr148 by BpEDR1 specifically increases the DNA‐binding affinity of BpEBP1, without affecting its transactivation activity or interaction with BpJMJ25. BpEBP1 functions as a central regulatory hub that unites transcriptional activation of anthocyanin and lignin‐related genes, BpJMJ25‐mediated H3K9me2 epigenetic remodeling, and BpEDR1‐dependent Thr148 phosphorylation. These two regulatory layers act independently yet synergistically, collectively activating drought‐adaptive metabolic pathways and conferring robust drought resistance in birch.
items.authors: Sun S, Wang P, Yang X, Wang J, Wang J, Li X, Niu S, Han X, Wu D, Wang C, Wang Y

items.title: MicroRNA 160 controls the auxin response factor–class III peroxidase module and couples salicylic acid and redox signaling networks in the potato hypersensitive response to potato virus Y
items.abstract: Summary Hypersensitive response (HR) is an effector‐triggered immune response leading to pathogen restriction and local cell death. Small RNAs (sRNAs), mediating RNA silencing, have a well‐established role in antiviral immunity; however, their role in HR has not been addressed to date. We applied a spatially resolved sRNA‐omics approach to uncover changes at the sRNA level and the dynamics of sRNA–gene regulatory networks in potato ( Solanum tuberosum L.) HR to potato virus Y (PVY). We show that miR160 is repressed in cells adjacent to HR lesions in the resistant cultivar, but not in PVY‐sensitive, salicylic acid (SA)‐depleted plants. Beyond its canonical regulation of StARF10 and StARF17 , miR160 controls a broader regulatory network spanning auxin signaling, cell‐wall remodeling, redox homeostasis, and tuberization. Elevated miR160 levels promote susceptibility‐associated traits, reduce thermotolerance, and suppress genes strongly activated in HR. Mechanistically, we identify a novel miR160– StARF10/StARF17 – StPRX28 module that links miR160 repression to the induction of a Class III apoplastic peroxidase in HR, with SA acting upstream. Together, these findings establish miR160 as an important regulatory node that connects SA–auxin–redox signaling pathways and tunes development, defense, and heat resilience, and highlight miR160 as a promising target for fine‐tuning tolerance to multiple stresses with minimal yield loss.
items.authors: Križnik M, Lukan T, Zagorščak M, Coll Rius A, Pogačar K, Marondini N, Stare K, Levak V, Široká J, Novák O, Kladnik A, Gruden K

items.title: Arabidopsis cyclin‐dependent kinases and MAP65 phosphorylation link microtubule dynamics with salt stress adaptation
items.abstract: Summary Plants possess sophisticated regulatory mechanisms to balance growth and stress responses. Cyclin‐dependent kinases (CDKs) are established regulators of cell division and endoreduplication, yet their roles in abiotic stress responses remain poorly understood. Here, using reverse genetics, biochemical, and cell biological approaches, we show that Arabidopsis ( Arabidopsis thaliana ) CDKB1s contribute to salt stress adaptation through a mechanism involving the phosphorylation of MAP65‐1 and MAP65‐2, two microtubule‐associated proteins essential for cytoskeleton dynamics under salt stress. Loss of CDKB1 function enhances salt tolerance, accompanied by attenuated plasma membrane depolarization and reactive oxygen species accumulation. In vitro phosphorylation assays demonstrate that CDKB1;1 directly phosphorylates MAP65‐1 at Ser‐503. Genetic analyses indicate that phospho‐dead MAP65 variants confer enhanced salt tolerance, whereas phosphomimetic variants compromise tolerance even in the cdkb1;1 1;2 background, supporting a critical role for MAP65 phosphorylation status at these sites in salt stress adaptation. We further found that CDKA;1 can similarly interact with and phosphorylate MAP65‐1, suggesting a potential parallel role for CDKA;1 in this process. Collectively, our findings identify a regulatory module involving CDKs, MAP65, and microtubules that links cell cycle kinases and cytoskeleton dynamics with plant salt stress adaptation.
items.authors: Qu X, Zou J, Zhang C, Yue J, Yang K, Le J

items.title: Cell‐type‐specific PIN‐FORMED 3‐mediated polar auxin transport regulates cambial activity and tension wood formation in Populus tomentosa
items.abstract: Summary Auxin is a central regulator of tree secondary growth and forms maxima in the vascular cambium, yet how these maxima are established remains elusive. Here, we functionally characterized two redundant PIN‐FORMED 3 ( PIN3 ) paralogs from Populus tomentosa to define their roles in secondary growth and gravity‐induced tension wood (TW) formation. We employed fluorescent reporter lines, clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats‐generated knockout mutants, phloem‐specific RNA interference transgenic plants and isotopic auxin transport assays to dissect PIN3 functions during secondary growth of poplar stems. Loss of function of PIN3 paralogs severely compromises cambial proliferation, secondary xylem differentiation and TW development. PIN3 proteins display cell‐type‐specific polar localization with basal polarity in phloem cells and outer lateral polarity in endodermal cells. Phloem‐expressed PIN3 facilitates basipetal auxin transport and is required for cambial auxin response. Upon gravistimulation, endodermal PIN3 repolarizes along the gravity vector, correlating with TW formation. Our findings identify a cell‐type‐specific, PIN3‐mediated auxin transport mechanism that contributes to auxin‐driven secondary growth of tree stems.
items.authors: Xiang D, Ran L, Li Y, Zong L, Li B, Chu Q, Zhang M, Fu X, Sun L, Tan S, Geisler M, Wang B, Gu X, Luo K, Xu C

items.title: Pepper RING ‐type E3 ligase, CaANKR1 , negatively regulates drought tolerance by modulating CaMAPK1 stability
items.abstract: SUMMARY Drought stress severely restricts plant growth and productivity, and abscisic acid (ABA)–mediated signaling plays a central role in coordinating adaptive responses to water deficit. Mitogen‐activated protein kinase (MAPK) cascades are widely involved in plant stress signaling; however, the ubiquitin‐mediated regulation of MAPK stability during drought responses remains poorly understood. In this study, we conducted a yeast two‐hybrid screening and identified CaMAPK1, a pepper ( Capsicum annuum ) MAPK, as an interacting partner of the RING‐type E3 ubiquitin ligase CaANKR1, which was further confirmed via in vitro and in vivo assays. CaMAPK1 expression was induced by dehydration, osmotic stress, salinity stress, and ABA treatment. Furthermore, CaMAPK1 exhibited kinase activity and was predominantly localized to the nucleus. Ubiquitination assays revealed that CaANKR1 promoted K48‐linked polyubiquitination of CaMAPK1 in a RING domain–dependent manner. Consistently, cell‐free degradation assays showed that CaMAPK1 protein stability negatively correlated with CaANKR1 expression levels, indicating that CaANKR1 promotes the proteasome‐dependent degradation of CaMAPK1. Phenotypic assays revealed that CaMAPK1 silencing in pepper reduced drought tolerance by altering ABA‐mediated stomatal responses and water retention, whereas CaMAPK1 overexpression in Arabidopsis produced the opposite phenotype. Collectively, these findings suggest that CaANKR1 negatively modulates ABA‐mediated drought tolerance through ubiquitin‐dependent destabilization of CaMAPK1. Together, they reveal a mechanism underlying ABA‐driven drought responses and highlight a promising target for enhancing crop drought resilience.
items.authors: Cho J, Lim CW, Yun B, Kim DS, Lee SC

items.title: The class VIII myosin ATM2 stabilizes actin–plasma membrane contacts in tobacco pollen tubes by locally promoting PtdIns(4,5)P2 formation
items.abstract: Abstract The intersection of actin filaments with the plasma membrane (PM) in plant cells involves lipid–protein interactions by the Arabidopsis class VIII myosin ATM2 that are currently not understood. Using pollen tube cells as a model, we describe how ATM2 enables actin–PM contacts by modulating membrane lipid nano-organization. ATM2 bound anionic PM lipids, including phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PtdIns(4,5)P 2 ), with no apparent preference for any particular lipid species. Overexpression of ATM2 unexpectedly stabilized actin dynamics and altered pollen tube morphology. Actin dynamics remained unaltered upon overexpression of a lipid-binding-defective ATM2 variant. ATM2 effects on actin dynamics required PtdIns(4,5)P 2 , as artificial PtdIns(4,5)P 2 depletion in pollen tubes abolished the effects of full-length ATM2 on actin dynamics despite its retained PM association. ATM2 colocalized and interacted with the PI4P 5-kinase PIP5K2, which resides at actin–PM contacts and forms PtdIns(4,5)P 2 nanodomains facilitating rho-of-plants-dependent actin stabilization. Upon ATM2 overexpression, a fluorescent PtdIns(4,5)P 2 biosensor decorated an extended PM region in vivo, indicating a promoting effect of ATM2 on PtdIns(4,5)P 2 abundance. The catalytic activity of purified recombinant PIP5K2 protein was enhanced upon coincubation with a purified carboxy-terminal ATM2 fragment in vitro, suggesting that ATM2 contributes to the intrinsic regulation of PtdIns(4,5)P 2 formation. Actin dynamics are thus stabilized at the actin–PM interface by ATM2 locally promoting the formation of PtdIns(4,5)P 2 nanodomains, thereby self-reinforcing ATM2 recruitment while also facilitating rho of plants activation to stabilize membrane-proximal actin filaments.
items.authors: Wagner VC, Fratini M, Uhlenberg J, Schutkowski A, Hamm G, Kastner C, Bacia K, Schwarzerová K, Heilmann I

items.title: Decoding Drought: The CBL9–CIPK11 Phosphoswitch in Guard Cells
items.abstract: Summary statement The study identifies a phosphorylation‐dependent calcium signalling module, PuCBL9–PuCIPK11, that remodels the guard‐cell actin cytoskeleton in Populus ussuriensis to accelerate stomatal closure. This work bridges a long‐standing gap between calcium decoding and cytoskeletal dynamics in trees, and opens a new translational avenue for forest improvement.
items.authors: Hasan MM, Alabdallah NM

items.title: Ethylene as a Stomatal Signalling Hub: Integrating Hormonal and Stress Signals to Optimize Stomatal Responses
items.abstract: ABSTRACT The gaseous plant hormone ethylene (ET) regulates diverse growth responses and adaptive processes to environmental stimuli. Although the role of ET in stress signalling is well established, its effects on stomatal responses remain paradoxical. ET induces stomatal closure in some contexts yet antagonizes abscisic acid‐mediated closure in others. While diverse studies have reported that ET regulates stomatal responses, the differential role of ET in stomatal signalling has not been reconciled into a unified framework. Here, we synthesize current evidence into a bidirectional model of ET‐dependent stomatal regulation, in which ET signalling produces two antagonistic outputs: a closure pathway driven by Gα‐dependent, RBOHD/F‐mediated H 2 O 2 production and downstream NO and H 2 S signals acting via SLAC1‐type anion channels; and an opposing pathway in which EIN2‐dependent flavonol accumulation scavenges guard‐cell ROS, thereby antagonizing stomatal closure. Additionally, the differential role of ET across species, dosages and stress conditions, as well as the compensatory role of ET in stomatal closure when ABA signalling is compromised is also discussed. This review offers novel insights into the function of ET in stomatal regulation and provides a mechanistic foundation for harnessing ET signalling to optimize the trade‐off between plant growth and stress resilience.
items.authors: Khan TA, Yi J, Shi Y, Ziyi L, Chen Q

items.title: Pepper RING‐Type E3 Ligase, CaAIAR1, Negatively Modulates ABA Signaling and Drought Stress Response by Controlling CaADBZ1 Stability
items.abstract: ABSTRACT The ubiquitin–proteasome pathway plays a crucial role in plant abiotic stress responses by regulating protein stability. Our previous work demonstrated that the pepper bZIP transcription factor CaADBZ1 regulates abscisic acid (ABA) signaling and drought stress responses. However, the regulatory factors controlling CaADBZ1 protein stability remain unknown. Here, we performed a yeast two‐hybrid assay to identify the E3 ubiquitin ligase involved in regulating CaADBZ1 stability. The pepper RING‐type E3 ligase CaAIAR1 ( Capsicum annuum ABA‐Induced Ankyrin repeat RING‐type E3 ligase 1) interacts with CaADBZ1 both in vitro and in vivo. CaAIAR1 ubiquitinates CaADBZ1 and exhibits E3 ligase activity that depends on its RING domain. A cell‐free degradation assay revealed that CaADBZ1 was unstable under non‐stress conditions, and CaAIAR1 accelerated its degradation via the 26S proteasome pathway. CaAIAR1 expression was significantly induced by various abiotic stresses and was associated with altered phenotypic responses to drought stress and exogenous ABA treatment. Moreover, CaAIAR1 ‐silenced pepper plants exhibited enhanced drought tolerance compared to control plants, as evidenced by reduced transpiration rates and increased ABA sensitivity in leaves. Conversely, CaAIAR1 ‐overexpressing Arabidopsis plants showed decreased drought tolerance compared to control plants and exhibited reduced ABA sensitivity at the seedling stage. In addition, co‐silencing CaAIAR1 and CaADBZ1 increased drought sensitivity, producing a phenotype opposite to that of CaAIAR1 silencing alone, indicating that CaAIAR1 functions upstream of CaADBZ1 in drought stress. Collectively, our findings suggest that CaAIAR1 negatively regulates the drought response and ABA signaling by modulating CaADBZ1 protein stability.
items.authors: Choi J, Baek W, Lim CW, Kim M, Kim DS, Lee SC

items.title: The cation/H+ exchanger ChCAX3 fine-tunes fruit ripening by modulating cytosolic Ca2+ homeostasis in Cerasus humilis
items.abstract: Abstract Cerasus humilis is a calcium-rich fruit crop with high nutritional value, but its synchronized ripening causes concentrated harvest and short shelf life. In this study, ChCAX3, a vacuolar cation/H+ exchanger, was identified as a key regulator of fruit ripening. ChCAX3 showed high expression in fruit and stem tissues and was upregulated by CaCl2 and ethephon treatments. however, repressed during fruit ripening by ChMYB16. Yeast complementation and Arabidopsis thaliana assays validated its Ca2+ transport activity. Overexpression of ChCAX3 in tomato increased fruit Ca2+ content, delayed coloration, reduced softening, and extended the ripening period by approximately 14 days. ChCAX3-mediated vacuolar Ca2+ sequestration may maintain low cytosolic Ca2+ levels, thereby potentially attenuate the expression and activity of a presumptive Ca2+ sensor ChCBL10 and its interacting kinase ChCIPK3 at the vacuolar membrane. This attenuation of the ChCBL10-ChCIPK3 module was accompanied by reduced expression of ethylene biosynthesis genes (ChACS1, ChACO1) and cell wall degradation-related genes (ChPG1, ChPG2), which may collectively delay the ethylene burst and preserving fruit firmness. Conversely, repression of ChCAX3 by ChMYB16 during late ripening may elevate cytosolic Ca2+, potentially activate the ChCBL10-ChCIPK3 signaling cascade, and accelerated senescence. Overall, these findings demonstrated that ChCAX3 positively regulates Ca2+ accumulation and delays fruit ripening via Ca2+ signaling-mediated modulation of ethylene pathways, providing new insights into Ca2+-hormone crosstalk in fruit physiology and identifying a potential target for extending shelf life and enhancing nutritional quality.
items.authors: Shan Q, Miao C, Zhang B, Lang S, Liu N, Wu Z, Zheng D, Song X

items.title: The chloroplast-localised metalloprotease EGY1 and Mg-dechelatase SGR1 control chloroplast development and senescence by modulating photosynthetic functions
items.abstract: Abstract The chloroplast plays an essential role in the production of biochemical energy and metabolism, as well as in plant development, including senescence. We describe a mutant with unusual progression of senescence and identify it as a new allele of ethylene-dependent gravitropism-deficient and yellow-green 1 (egy1-5). EGY1 encodes a chloroplast-localized metalloprotease that regulates chlorophyll metabolism. The single egy1-5 mutant exhibits various defects in chloroplast function, including abnormal accumulation of photosynthetic complexes and defects in photosynthetic parameters, as well as altered responses to the chemicals lincomycin and methyl viologen. Furthermore, chlorophyll fluorescence could not be detected in egy1 guard cells. We performed a suppressor mutant screen in the egy1 background to identify novel regulators of senescence and chloroplast development. We found two suppressors that restored green leaves, and both suppressors had mutations in STAY-GREEN 1 (SGR1). SGR1 encodes the Mg2+ dechelatase that catalyses the initial step in chlorophyll breakdown. The defects of the egy1 mutant were either fully or partially suppressed in egy1 sgr1. This allowed us to isolate the function of EGY1, independent of the pleiotropic effects of chlorophyll degradation. Our findings suggest that chlorophyll homeostasis regulates the overall development and function of the chloroplast as well as plant senescence.

items.title: Tracing the Evolutionary Origins of Jasmonate Signaling: Co-Evolution of Oxylipin Metabolism and Hormone Perception in the Green Lineage
items.abstract: Abstract Jasmonates constitute a central class of lipid-derived signaling molecules that regulate plant defense, development, and environmental adaptation. Although jasmonic acid (JA) and its bioactive conjugate jasmonoyl-L-isoleucine (JA-Ile) are well characterized in angiosperms, recent evolutionary, biochemical, and structural studies have revealed that jasmonate signaling predates the origin of land plants. Jasmonates occur in streptophyte algae but are absent from chlorophytes, indicating that jasmonate biosynthesis evolved in the last common ancestor of streptophytes. However, the molecular nature, perception mechanisms, and biological functions of jasmonates have undergone profound changes during plant evolution. During terrestrialization, the recruitment of a pre-existing transcriptional regulatory network by a newly evolved COI1 receptor module established the canonical COI1/JAZ signaling system. Early diverging land plants employed dn-OPDA, a JA precursor, as the ancestral ligand, which was progressively replaced by JA amino acid conjugates such as JA-Ile in vascular plants. Here, we synthesize current evidence supporting a stepwise evolutionary model progressively shaping the COI1/JAZ-dependent hormone pathway. We discuss how (bio)chemical diversification of oxylipins, co-evolution of receptors and ligands, and the emergence of JA-Ile in vascular plants enabled the expansion, specificity, and systemic integration of jasmonate signaling as a requirement for plant terrestrialization.
items.authors: Chini A, Jimenez-Aleman GH, Solano R

items.title: Rhizobial type III effectors as regulators of root-nodule symbiosis in legumes
items.abstract: Abstract The rhizobia-legume nitrogen-fixing symbiosis begins when plants perceive rhizobial Nod factors (NF), activating the Common Symbiosis Signalling Pathway (CSSP) that drives nodule organogenesis. Rhizobia also inject Type III effectors (T3E) into host cells through a Type III Secretion System (T3SS) related to those of pathogenic bacteria. These effectors were long viewed only as suppressors of plant immunity and determinants of host compatibility, but this picture has changed. Recent studies revealed that rhizobial effectors (known as Nodulation Outer Proteins, Nops) such as NopT, NopM, NopL, NopP and NopZ directly target NF receptors or associated kinases, thereby regulating CSSP activation. The effector-triggering nodulation proteins (ET-Nods), a separate class of T3Es found in various Bradyrhizobium species, can activate nodule organogenesis independently of NF perception by rewiring host transcriptional and SUMOylation-based signalling. We trace the evolutionary origins of these activities, which may derive either from redirection of ancestral immune-targeting effectors toward symbiotic functions or from rhizobium-specific innovations. We ask whether the T3SS contributed to nodulation. We then consider what this interference means for the host, ranging from reinforced partner choice to partial loss of host control, and argue that rhizobial effectors have evolved as specialised modulators that converge on the signalling hubs governing symbiosis.
items.authors: Camuel A, Teulet A, del Cerro P

items.title: The interplay between photoperiod and the circadian clock during vegetative growth
items.abstract: Abstract Photoperiod, the duration of the daily light phase, is a key seasonal signal that shapes vegetative growth in plants. While its role in controlling the transition to flowering has been extensively characterised, the mechanisms through which photoperiod modulates processes such as hypocotyl elongation, leaf expansion, root growth, and carbon allocation during the vegetative phase are only now coming into focus. Understanding these mechanisms is critical, as the vegetative phase establishes the architecture and resources needed for reproduction. Recent work has revealed that plants possess distinct daylength-measurement mechanisms for flowering and vegetative growth, with twilight-length sensing as a complementary mechanism. The circadian clock translates these signals into daily growth rhythms by restricting growth-promoting factors to defined time windows that widen or narrow depending on daylength, contributing to different growth outcomes between short and long photoperiods. Photoperiod further shapes the daily carbon budget, with opposing energy-sensing pathways dynamically adjusting growth to match carbon availability across the day-night cycle. In this review, we examine how photoperiod regulates vegetative growth in Arabidopsis thaliana, from daylength-measurement systems through clock-controlled transcriptional cascades that drive organ elongation and competitive shade avoidance responses, to carbon economy and stress tolerance. We consider how photoperiod modulates responses to temperature extremes, drought, and salinity, and survey emerging evidence from crops and trees. Finally, we discuss chronoculture, propose experimental recommendations, and highlight outstanding questions for the field.

items.title: A pair of chitosan receptors confer broad-spectrum fungal resistance
items.abstract: Chitosan, a major fungal cell wall component, activates plant immunity, yet the underlying perception mechanism remains unknown. In this study, we identified OsFID1, an apoplast-localized DUF26 domain protein, as a chitosan-binding receptor essential for chitosan-triggered immunity. OsFID1 forms a receptor complex with OsFID2, a plasma membrane–localized DUF26 receptor-like kinase, to mediate chitosan sensing and immune activation, requiring OsFID2 phosphorylation for function. The OsFID1-OsFID2 complex confers broad-spectrum resistance to fungal pathogens. OsFID1 homologs are conserved in land plants, which show chitosan-binding activity in both monocots and dicots. Ectopic expression of OsFID1 in wheat and maize enhanced fungal resistance without growth penalty. These findings uncover a conserved receptor complex for direct chitosan sensing, advancing our understanding of plant-fungus interactions and providing a potential strategy for engineering durable fungal resistance crops.

items.title: Structural basis for size-selective perception of chitin in plants
items.abstract: Plants detect microbes through pattern recognition receptors that perceive conserved microbial surface motifs known as microbe-associated molecular patterns (MAMPs). Lysin motif (LysM) receptors recognize and mediate downstream responses to chitinous MAMPs. In this study, we elucidated the mechanism for the specific recognition of long-chain chitin oligomers and identified a hallmark bridge domain characteristic of the CHITIN PERCEPTION (CHIP) receptor class. Structural analysis of receptor-ligand complexes, biochemistry, and in planta functional studies of inhibitory nanobodies revealed the mechanism of size-selective, high-affinity chitin perception in Lotus japonicus and Medicago truncatula . Additionally, we identified the CHITIN ELICITOR RECEPTOR KINASE (CERK) class as low-affinity, yet essential, co-receptors and propose a mechanistic model for a ligand-induced core signaling heterocomplex. Our findings establish the structural and mechanistic basis of differential chitin perception and receptor complex assembly in chitin-elicited plant immune signaling.

items.title: A CRC–MYB chromatin loop controls auxin-mediated nectary growth in Arabidopsis
items.abstract: Abstract Floral nectaries, typically located at stamen bases, secrete sugar-rich nectar containing diverse secondary metabolites. Despite their defined position and specialized function, the mechanisms governing nectary formation remain unclear. Using publicly available single-nucleus RNA-seq data and newly generated spatial transcriptomic data, we identify a putative ordering of transcriptional states associated with nectary development and a spatial regulatory network controlling nectary growth in Arabidopsis thaliana . We further show that CRABS CLAW (CRC) is central to this network, integrating transcriptional regulation with spatial auxin transport and pathways controlling phytohormone signaling, sugar transport and terpene biosynthesis. CRC interacts with MYB21, MYB24 and MYB57 to form a complex that binds the 5′ and 3′ regulatory regions of MACCHI-BOU 4 ( MAB4 ), promoting a chromatin loop that enhances MAB4 expression and supports proper nectary size. MAB4 reinforces PIN-FORMED 1-mediated auxin transport to establish auxin maxima at the nectary tip and regulates PIN6 localization to maintain auxin gradients. These findings link transcriptional regulation and auxin transport with nectary organogenesis and metabolic function.

items.title: A broad-host-range Rhizobium rhizogenes strain enables transient expression across diverse crop species
items.abstract: Agrobacterium -mediated transient expression has revolutionised plant research, enabling numerous landmark discoveries across diverse areas of plant biology. Yet this powerful approach remains largely confined to solanaceous species, leaving most economically important crop families without a comparable rapid assay platform. Here, we show that an engineered Rhizobium rhizogenes strain, AS109, mediates efficient transient expression across diverse dicot species spanning multiple taxonomic families, consistently outperforming commonly used laboratory agrobacterial strains. Leveraging the broad host range of AS109, we establish a suite of functional assays in faba bean ( Vicia faba ), including protein localisation, RNA interference-mediated gene silencing, cell-surface elicitor recognition screens, nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat receptor (NLR) activation, and infection cell biology at the host-pathogen interface. We further demonstrate that both singleton NLRs and sensor-helper NLR pairs from Solanaceae retain effector recognition and cell death activity when transferred into faba bean, establishing a rapid platform for evaluating cross-family transferability of disease-resistance genes. AS109 thus provides an accessible and versatile chassis for functional genomics in non-model crops, bridging the widening gap between hypothesis generation and experimental validation across diverse plant species.

items.title: CRISPR/Cas9 knockout of PtaAGL16 improves post-drought recovery and shoot vitality in hybrid poplar
items.abstract: Drought stress severely limits tree growth and survival, a problem intensifying under climate change due to the rising frequency of extreme weather events. Identifying genetic variants that modulate drought stress responses and enhance resilience is therefore of great interest for developing climate-adapted trees. While the MADS-box transcription factor AGL16 has been implicated in drought responses and stomatal regulation in herbaceous species, the function of its homolog in woody perennials remains largely unexplored. Here, we investigate the role of PtaAGL16 in the poplar hybrid Populus tremula × P. alba . We generated CRISPR/Cas9 knockout lines of PtaAGL16 in the poplar clone INRA 717-1B4. Plants were subjected to a severe drought stress regime followed by a re-watering recovery phase. Morphological and physiological traits, including growth, stomatal conductance, shoot vitality, and stomatal density, together with stress-associated metabolites and drought-responsive gene expression, were analyzed. All agl16 knockout lines exhibited significantly reduced drought-induced damage compared to the wild-type. While the wild-type suffered extensive defoliation and persistent stem necrosis, the knockout lines retained higher shoot vitality and resumed growth after re-watering, including the formation of new leaves. Consequently, vitality in the knockout lines reached up to 86%, compared to only 34% in the wild-type. This improved resilience was accompanied by reduced persistent oxidative membrane damage, as indicated by lower MDA levels after recovery. These findings indicate that the disruption of PtaAGL16 is associated with enhanced drought resilience in a woody perennial species and highlight its potential as a genetic target for improving climate adaptation in fast-growing forest trees.

items.title: The genome sequence of grey willow, Salix cinerea L. (Malpighiales: Salicaceae)
items.abstract: We present a genome assembly of the tetraploid Salix cinerea (2 n = 4 x = 76; grey willow; Streptophyta; Magnoliopsida; Malpighiales; Salicaceae). The submitted sequence comprises two assemblies designated haplotype 1 and haplotype 2, with total lengths of 386.72 megabases and 1,004.23 megabases, respectively. Haplotype 1 represents a single monoploid chromosome complement; 87.7% was scaffolded into 19 chromosomal pseudomolecules, including the Z sex chromosome. Haplotype 2 was assembled to scaffold level. The mitochondrial genome assembly has a length of 686.79 kilobases and the plastid genome assembly has a length of 155.63 kilobases. Gene annotation of the haplotype 1 assembly by Ensembl identified 34,898 protein-coding genes. This assembly was generated as part of the Darwin Tree of Life project, which produces reference genomes for eukaryotic species found in Britain and Ireland.
