items.title: PLANT WATER-CARBON RELATIONS IN HUANGLONGBING-AFFECTED CITRUS TREES AND THE IMPACT OF HLB EXPOSURE DURATION, FRUIT DEVELOPMENTAL STAGE, AND SOURCE-SINK MANIPULATION ON THESE RELATIONS
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Bulk phloem flow is driven by pressure gradients generated by water drawn from the xylem, coupling source-sink transport with water status. Huanglongbing (HLB), a phloem-affecting bacterial disease of citrus, disrupts phloem transport, and causes canopy water deficit. Although improved water management can enhance HLB-affected tree health, the effects of HLB on water-driven source-sink relations are unknown. Fruits function as both carbon sink and water reservoir, but the role of fruit in regulating whole-tree water status remain poorly understood. We examined leaf-fruit water relations in HLB-affected citrus and evaluated how HLB exposure duration, fruit developmental stage, and source-sink manipulation shape these dynamics. Source- sink relations were manipulated in branches of symptomatic trees with long-term (four years) and recent (six months) HLB exposure. We girdled branches with a single fruit as the sink and defoliated at (0%, 50%, or 75%), and an ungirdled, non-defoliated branch served as control. We measured stomatal conductance, leaf hydraulic traits, leaf and fruit soluble sugars, diurnal fruit shrinkage (to estimate xylem backflow) and fruit water loss. Source-sink manipulation did not affect shoot total soluble sugar. HLB-exposure resulted in less negative osmotic potential, more negative turgor potential and reduced modulus of elasticity and relative water content at turgor loss point. HLB exposure also increased diurnal fruit shrinkage, with shrinkage responses to source-sink manipulation varying across fruit development stages. Collectively, these findings suggest that long-term HLB exposure promotes leaf acclimation to water deficits, however, high sink demand may diminish the leaf water status regulation at Stage II, when fruit sink carbon demand is highest.
items.authors: Alade, D. O., Vashisth, T., Vincent, C.

items.title: From rhizome diffusion to programmable architecture: a systems framework for controllable spatial expansion in bamboo and other clonal plants.
items.abstract: IntroductionRhizome-driven spatial expansion in bamboo and other clonal plants is governed jointly by architectural patterning, belowground bud bank demography, hormonal crosstalk, carbon allocation, environmental plasticity and genomic regulation. This integrative review synthesises those strands and then asks a question the field has not yet answered explicitly: how much of the mechanistic framework now invoked for programmable rhizome control has actually been demonstrated in a woody bamboo?MethodsLiterature was retrieved from Web of Science, Scopus, PubMed and CNKI and appraised along two axes - the biological provenance of each observation (woody bamboo; other rhizomatous or stoloniferous perennial; annual, herbaceous or model system) and its causal strength (perturbation-based, correlative, or conceptual).ResultsThe appraisal shows that architectural description, running-versus-clumping contrasts and clonal integration are supported by causal or quantitative evidence in bamboo itself, whereas the auxin -cytokinin -strigolactone module, BRANCHED1/TB1 repression, KNOX-mediated architectural control and the Tre6P -SnRK1 -TOR growth switch are supported in bamboo correlatively or not at all, having been imported from Arabidopsis, rice, potato, poplar and Nicotiana.DiscussionOn that basis we propose a three-tier genome-editing framework ordered by intervention depth, and argue that in bamboo the binding constraint is delivery rather than target choice: because gregarious monocarpic flowering precludes segregation-based transgene removal, ribonucleoprotein editing of cis-regulatory elements in a transformable Dendrocalamus or Bambusa background is presently the only route to a transgene-free edited plant, and vegetative containment necessarily dominates reproductive containment. We identify five quantities that the current corpus does not report, including lateral extension rate with variance, barrier breach probability as a function of embedment and inspection interval, and the minimum regenerative rhizome fragment size, and convert them into a staged, falsifiable research agenda with explicit go/no-go criteria.
items.authors: Huang W, Hu C, Zheng S, Lu J, Chen B, Chen X, Hu J, Ouyang Z, Shu D.

items.title: Regional species turnover and local host and forest stand characteristics jointly structure early foliar mycobiomes of Scots pine seedlings.
items.abstract: The foliar mycobiome plays an important role in tree health and stress resilience, yet factors shaping foliar fungal communities in boreal conifer seedlings remain poorly understood. We investigated how geographic region, seedling origin (planted vs. naturally regenerated), needle nitrogen status, and local stand structure influence needle-associated fungal communities of Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris) seedlings. Needle samples were collected from seedlings without visible disease symptoms across 23 forest stands in southern Finland. Fungal communities were characterized using Illumina ITS2 amplicon sequencing and clustered into operational taxonomical units (OTUs). Alpha diversity was analyzed via linear mixed models (LMMs), and community composition via PERMANOVA and NMDS using Bray-Curtis dissimilarity. Geographic region was the strongest driver of fungal community composition among stands, whereas within stands, community composition was primarily associated with seedling height and birch abundance. Alpha diversity was higher in the Southeastern region compared to the Southwest, and tended to be lower in planted than naturally regenerated seedlings. Moreover, diversity decreased with higher proportions of birch and spruce but increased with higher needle C: N ratios. These findings suggest that early foliar mycobiomes reflect regional conditions and local forest structure, highlighting potential forest management impacts on fungal communities.
items.authors: Wahlman W, Velmala S, Sutela S, Terhonen E.

items.title: Stemflow as a Storm-Driven Pathway for Fungal eDNA Transport
items.abstract: Stemflow transports water and biological material from forest canopies to the stem base, yet fungal studies of this flux have largely relied on microscopy of conidia. We used ITS2 metabarcoding to characterize fungal environmental DNA (eDNA) in stemflow from 15 trees – five each of American beech (Fagus grandifolia), sugar maple (Acer saccharum), and tulip poplar (Liriodendron tulipifera) in a closed-canopy forest in northeastern Ohio, USA. Stemflow was sampled during eight rain events in the leafless season (November 2024–May 2025), along with simulated bark and gutter washes to assess near-collar and collector signals. Natural stemflow communities were compositionally distinct from both controls and occupied greater ordination space. Ascomycota dominated across all samples, with Parafenestella, Cytospora, Microcera, Nectria, and Aureobasidium among the most abundant resolved genera and 13 of the 25 most abundant taxa differed significantly among host species. Woody-plant-associated endophytes, canker fungi, and saprobes dominated ecological guild composition. Storm event explained 28.6% of taxonomic variation, host tree species 24.1%, and their interaction 10.0%. Guild composition was more strongly structured by host species (35.4%) than storm event (20.4%). Lichenized fungi and lichen-associated fungi were detected. Thus, leafless-season stemflow integrates broad bark-associated fungal eDNA, including recurrent lichen-derived material, beyond the morphologically distinctive conidia captured by traditional methods. Stemflow eDNA therefore offers a minimally invasive means of monitoring canopy fungal diversity and the strong host and temporal filtering of DNA exported from woody surfaces.
items.authors: Valdman, B. W., Jusko, B. M., Burke, D., Carrino-Kyker, S., Krebs, R. A., Van Stan, J. T.

items.title: The role of environmental gradients in the ontogenetic shift of wood traits from seedlings to adults in two temperate tree species
items.abstract: Tree development, or ontogeny, involves concurrent changes in plant size and environmental conditions, both of which can influence wood structure and function. Disentangling the factors underlying ontogenetic variation in wood traits remains a major challenge. This is important because wood underpins hydraulic efficiency, hydraulic safety, and mechanical support - functions critical for tree performance. In this study, we sampled twigs from a fixed distance from the apex from sugar maple (Acer saccharum) and yellow birch (Betula alleghaniensis) to quantify how wood traits, light availability, and water availability change across seedling, sapling, and adult developmental stages. Across both species, wood structure shifted toward greater hydraulic safety with ontogeny, demonstrated through decreased vessel diameter (Dh), increased vessel number (VN) and increased vessel reinforcement ((t/b)2) in adult trees. Despite this shift, hydraulic efficiency (Ks) was maintained across developmental stages, indicating that increases in VN and lumen fraction (F) compensated for reductions in efficiency associated with smaller Dh. Wood trait covariation was structured by a hydraulic efficiency–safety trade-off, however traits such as F varied more independently, enabling compensations such that this trade-off did not constrain tissue-level hydraulic function. Contrary to expectations, we did not detect differences in water availability across developmental stages. Although light availability increased from seedlings to adults, it explained little variation in wood traits, while height was associated with only a subset of traits in sugar maple and none in yellow birch. The shift toward smaller Dh and maintained Ks in adult apices contrasts with expectations of increasing transport efficiency in taller trees but is consistent with selection for resistance to freeze–thaw embolism in temperate environments.
items.authors: Hickey H, Prendin A, Messier J.

items.title: Rhizobia bacteroid transcription helps to coordinate the soybean nodule drought response.
items.abstract: Soybean (Glycine max L. [Merr.]) nitrogen fixation is sensitive to soil drying and is an important target for improving soybean drought resilience. Transcriptional regulation of the nodule drought response and the influence of symbiotic rhizobia are not well understood. We measured whole-plant responses to mild and moderate soil moisture deficit (41% and 20% of field capacity) alongside the nodule transcriptome, including soybean and Bradyrhizobium diazoefficiens transcripts, in two soybean genotypes ('Benning' and PI 471938) that were previously found to have diverging nitrogen fixation drought responses. The transcriptomes of the two genotypes responded very similarly to soil moisture deficit, with only eight genes responding to soil moisture deficit differently between genotypes. Mild soil moisture deficit reduced stomatal conductance and increased stem and petiole ureide while altering transcript abundance of genes involved in nitrogen assimilation-related pathways in both plant genotypes and in the bacteroid. Gene regulatory network inference identified two B. diazoefficiens loci, BAC49768 and BAC47090, as major regulators in the whole-nodule transcriptome during soil moisture deficit. Several soybean network nodes were located within quantitative trait loci previously associated with relevant drought responses. This work revealed new soybean and rhizobia candidate genes with important roles in the soybean nodule drought response.
items.authors: Locke AM, Ortiz AC, Sikes TR, Gold NL, Ramirez ME.

items.title: A Novel In Vitro Regeneration System Reveals Tissue-Specific Dynamics of Wound Repair in Poplar Stems
items.abstract: Plants are prone to injury in nature, yet how woody stems repair damaged protective and vascular tissues remains poorly understood. We established an in vitro bridge-culture system in hybrid poplar to track regeneration after longitudinal stem cutting. Lignin deposition began in diverse cells beneath the wound by 2 days after cutting (DAC), marking an early wound response. Repair then followed distinct tissue-specific trajectories. In the cortex and secondary phloem, cell division generated callus-like tissue that covered the wound by 2–4 DAC. New phellogen subsequently formed beneath the callus and produced phelloderm and ligno-suberized phellem, forming a wound periderm resembling native periderm by 12 DAC. In vascular cambium and young phloem, cells expanded and proliferated to reconnect the wound by 4 DAC, while restoration of cambium- and phloem-associated gene expression by 8–12 DAC indicated vascular recovery. Auxin responses also differed between tissues. PtaDR5::GUS activity was transiently induced during periderm regeneration but persisted in vascular regions until vascular development resumed. Exogenous auxin promoted periderm regeneration but had little effect on vascular cell divisions, whereas inhibiting polar auxin transport impaired vascular wound closure. Thus, periderm and vascular tissues undergo coordinated yet distinct repair processes regulated by tissue-specific auxin responses and transport.
items.authors: Wang X, Hu J, Zhu M, Zhang J.

items.title: A multi-tissue transcriptome strategy for genomic resource development in Pinus edulis
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Premise Conifers comprise one-sixth of global forests and landscape genomic studies are urgently needed to understand their biology, yet relatively few conifer species have reference genomes. Targeted exon-capture is a practical alternative to whole-genome sequencing, but selecting loci without a reference genome remains a barrier. We developed a multi-tissue reference transcriptome for piñon pine ( Pinus edulis ) to ask how multi-tissue sampling improves probe design, and what is lost under a conventional single-tissue approach. Methods We assembled a reference transcriptome from four diploid tissues (needle, phloem, root, vegetative bud) and one haploid tissue (megagametophyte), using the latter as a pseudo-guide. We designed a target-capture probe-set by prioritizing highly expressed P. edulis transcripts and transcripts matching a conifer exon database. Results We recovered 76% of conserved plant genes with few duplicated transcripts. Filtering yielded 15,664 transcripts totaling 31.4 Mb, ∼0.1% of the genome. Tissue-specific expression was substantial: 27.4% of transcripts occurred exclusively in non-needle tissues. Functional annotation confirmed complementary contributions, including seed-desiccation and germination genes from megagametophytes, and defense- and stress-associated genes from roots and phloem. Discussion We built a transcriptome and efficient probe set using a roadmap suitable for other non-model plants with large genomes; keys to success were prioritizing complementary tissues and using expression-based filtering.
items.authors: Macias, D. S., Gyllenhaal, E. F., Kleinkopf, J. A., Pockman, W. T., Marx, H. E.

items.title: Studying the role of climate and sex in flowering dynamics of black poplar across time and space
items.abstract: Global change has a major impact on rivers and their associated terrestrial compartment, the riparian forest. The black poplar ( Populus nigra L.), the dominant species of the European riparian forest, is considered an indicator of the biodiversity dynamics of these ecosystems, but is threatened with extinction in several parts of its range. The species is dioecious and shows wide variability in many traits, enabling it to adapt to a broad range of environmental conditions. A detailed characterization of this natural variability is therefore a key issue both for the conservation of natural populations and for biological engineering aimed at restoring riverbanks. Phenology is both an indicator of climate change and an adaptation lever for populations, particularly in perennial species such as trees. In this study, we characterized the spatial and temporal variability in flowering phenology by studying 13 natural black poplar populations along the Loire River, France. Flowering date and duration showed substantial variability both within and between populations, and males generally flowered earlier than females. Despite this variability, the ranking of individual trees’ flowering dates was highly consistent across years. Most male-female pairs shared several days of overlapping flowering each year, and this overlap was moderately stable across years. Flowering dates advanced by about five to six days per degree Celsius during early spring, with no detectable difference in sensitivity between sexes. This work contributes to the characterization of flowering variability in an economically important tree species and may inform both the conservation of genetic resources and breeding. Highlights Flowering phenology varied substantially within and among black poplar populations. Male black poplars generally flowered earlier than females. Flowering advanced by 5–6 days per °C increase in early spring temperature. Phenological diversity informs black poplar conservation and breeding.
items.authors: Cazenave, X., Marc, V., Julien, D., Veronique, J., Durufle, H.

items.title: Amorphous Silica and Drought Stress Mitigation: Unraveling Phenological Dynamics, Carbon-Water Balance, and Crop Resilience
items.abstract: Abstract Amorphous silica (ASi) is increasingly recognized for its potential to improve plant resilience to abiotic stress, especially drought. However, because drought affects crop physiology as well as its carbon and water cycling differently depending on when drought occurs during plant development, the effects of ASi across key phenological stages remain poorly understood. In a greenhouse experiment, we investigated whether ASi as a soil amendment mitigates drought stress in spring barley (Hordeum vulgare L., variety: Planet) during three key phenological stages: stem elongation, flowering, and grain filling. A factorial design was used, combining two levels of ASi (0 as control and 1 g per 100 g of dry soil) with four water regimes: a well-watered reference and drought imposed during stem elongation, flowering, or grain filling. Carbon and water flux dynamics were monitored throughout the experiment by measuring CO 2 exchange and evapotranspiration using an automated soil-plant-atmosphere enclosure system, while soil water dynamics were tracked continuously with TOMST sensors. Plant responses to drought were assessed by daily measurements of stomatal conductance, leaf water potential, abscisic acid, and soil matric potential during drought. At the end of the growing period, biomass and grain yield were determined. ASi increased soil water retention over time and reduced drought-induced stress across growth stages. Drought effects were strongest during flowering and grain filling, whereas plants exposed to drought at stem elongation recovered fully and showed no yield reduction, irrespective of their ASi treatment. In contrast, drought during reproductive stages caused early senescence, poor recovery, and strong yield loss in control plants. These effects were substantially reduced by ASi, which maintained higher leaf water potential, stomatal conductance, evapotranspiration, and CO 2 uptake, while reducing abscisic acid accumulation. ASi also improved post-drought recovery and largely preserved yield under reproductive-stage drought. These results show that ASi can mitigate drought effects, especially during drought-sensitive reproductive stages, by helping sustain plant function during water shortages and delaying the onset of physiological stress.
items.authors: Hamwi WA, Hoffmann M, Schaller J, Remus R, Dahlmann A, Dubbert M.

items.title: Thioredoxin h1-targeted proteins in European beech (Fagus sylvatica L.): Insights into metabolic control, stress response, and seed longevity.
items.abstract: Seed viability and longevity underpin forest regeneration under changing environmental conditions. European beech (Fagus sylvatica L.) produces intermediate seeds that gradually lose viability during storage, largely through oxidative stress, which makes redox homeostasis central to their longevity. Here we investigated the role of thioredoxin h1 (TRX h1), a cytosolic thiol-disulfide oxidoreductase, in the embryonic axes of beech seeds. Using a His-tagged monocysteinic (Cys to Ser) trapping mutant of TRX h1 combined with data-dependent acquisition (DDA) proteomics, we identified 161 putative TRX h1 target proteins, which fall into functional categories related to genetic information processing, metabolism, environmental and cellular signaling, and protein homeostasis. Western blotting confirmed that target capture proceeded through DTT-reducible mixed-disulfide complexes, supporting a redox-based interaction. The targets include heat shock proteins (HSP70 and HSP90) and other chaperones, calcium-binding proteins (calmodulin and calreticulin), a methyl-CpG-binding protein, glycolytic and tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle enzymes, and antioxidant enzymes such as superoxide dismutase, glutathione peroxidase and glutaredoxin. To link these targets to seed physiology, we quantified the thiol redox status of fresh and long-term stored seeds: total thiols were approximately 2.2-fold lower in stored than in fresh axes (21.0 ± 0.5 vs 45.9 ± 1.3 nmol GSH equivalents per axis), indicating that the reduced thiol pool, the substrate of the TRX h1 system, becomes depleted and more oxidized during storage. Together, these results suggest that TRX h1-dependent redox maintenance may contribute to redox homeostasis, energy metabolism and protein stability in beech embryonic axes, and provide a basis for improving seed storage and conservation strategies.
items.authors: Ratajczak E, Staszak AM, Vargas P, Sahrawy M, Serrato AJ, Fuchs H.

items.title: Distinct NIR Reflectance Spectra Associated with Foliar Symptoms of Beech Leaf Disease.
items.abstract: Beech leaf disease (BLD) is an epidemic spreading among American beech (Fagus grandifolia) populations, with characteristic symptoms including dark green, yellow, or brown bands of thickened leaf tissue between secondary veins. Because near infrared (NIR) light is reflected by leaf tissue structure, we used multispectral NIR imaging reflectance to distinguish symptomatic from asymptomatic leaves amongst affected trees, as well as to distinguish between different expressions of symptoms (dark green, yellow, and brown bands) within symptomatic leaves and symptom severity (low, moderate high) at the whole leaf scale. Key findings include significantly higher NIR reflectance in dark green bands of symptomatic tissue compared to asymptomatic tissue amongst affected trees (λ = 840, 860, 900, 940, and 980 nm; ∼26.2%, 25.9%, 35.0%, 35.3%, and 32.5% increase respectively). A partial least squares regression model predicted 97% of variation in symptomatic vs. asymptomatic NIR reflectance was attributed primarily to the increase in spongy mesophyll thickness and overall leaf thickness in symptomatic tissue. Whole leaf symptom severity (asymptomatic, moderate, severe) was most clearly diagnosed at λ = 860 nm. Water infiltration of the intercellular airspaces in symptomatic dark green bands and asymptomatic leaves removed differences in NIR reflectance, supporting a mechanistic link between increased NIR reflectance and the foliar symptoms of BLD. Our results highlight the interaction of leaf internal architecture with NIR wavelengths and inform the development of targeted remote sensing tools.
items.authors: Moore E, Dabydeen LC, Salha R, Bichler J, Moore K, Borsuk AM.

items.title: Frequent recovery of Sydowia polyspora from brown spot needle blight-associated loblolly pine (Pinus taeda) needles in Alabama
items.abstract: Sydowia polyspora is a widespread conifer-associated fungus that can function as an endophyte, saprophyte, or opportunistic pathogen, but its occurrence in southeastern pine systems remains poorly characterized. During surveys of symptomatic loblolly pine (Pinus taeda) in Washington and Cullman counties, Alabama, fungal isolates morphologically consistent with Sydowia spp. were recovered from needles exhibiting foliar disease symptoms. Isolates were characterized using colony morphology, microscopy, ITS sequencing, translation elongation factor 1-alpha (EF1-α) sequencing, species-specific EF1-α primers, and maximum-likelihood phylogenetic analyses. Colonies exhibited morphological features consistent with Sydowia spp., including melanized septate hyphae, chlamydospore-like structures, and catenate conidia. ITS and EF1-α sequence analyses supported assignment of the isolates to S. polyspora, with phylogenetic analyses placing Alabama isolates within the broader S. polyspora lineage alongside reference sequences from North America, Europe, and Asia. Species-specific amplification using the EF1-α primers SpolEF4F and SpolEF3R provided additional support for species identification. In a broader 2019–2021 survey across nine counties in Alabama, S. polyspora was recovered from 60% of surveyed stands. To our knowledge, this study represents the first peer-reviewed documentation of S. polyspora in Alabama. These findings identify S. polyspora as a widespread and common component of fungal communities associated with symptomatic loblolly pine needles in Alabama.
items.authors: Folorunso T, Silva G, Olatinwo R, Eckhardt L, Chen H, Willoughby J.

items.title: Decomposition trajectories in mixed-species leaf litter in cool-temperate deciduous forest with understory dwarf bamboo
items.abstract: Litter decomposition plays a central role in nutrient cycling in forest ecosystems, but the effects of species mixing on decomposition of individual litter species remain poorly understood. We conducted a two-year litterbag experiment in a cool-temperate deciduous forest in northern Japan using litter from two dominant canopy tree species (oak and birch) and the dominant understory bamboo (Sasa). Single-species and mixed-species litterbags were used to examine litter mass loss, litter chemistry (carbon, nitrogen, and lignin), and microbial communities assessed by phospholipid fatty acid (PLFA) analysis. Oak and birch litter decomposed significantly faster than Sasa litter, whereas decomposition rate constants did not differ between the two deciduous tree species. Changes in litter chemistry relative to mass loss were similar between oak and birch but differed markedly in Sasa, indicating a distinct decomposition trajectory of Sasa. Total microbial biomass increased rapidly during the early stage of decomposition in all litter types owing to fungal colonization, whereas the fungal-to-bacterial PLFA ratio was substantially lower in Sasa litter than in deciduous tree litter. Species mixing had no significant overall non-additive effect on decomposition, although mixtures of oak and birch tended to accelerate decomposition, whereas mixtures including Sasa tended to suppress it. These changes in decomposition rate were accompanied by corresponding changes in microbial biomass, while decomposition trajectories remained largely unchanged within each litter species. Our results suggest that Sasa contributes a distinct decomposition process in cool-temperate forests and that species mixing primarily modifies decomposition rates rather than the sequence of chemical transformations during decomposition.
items.authors: Yoshitake, S., Asai, C., Ohtsuka, T.

items.title: Coarse Woody Debris of Mixed Tree Species Overrides Soil Matrix Constraints on Microbial Richness and Abundance in an Ancient Broad-Leaved Forest
items.abstract: Annotation The mechanisms by which coarse woody debris (CWD) affects soil microbial diversity across different spatial scales and forest disturbance regimes remain poorly understood. This study investigated the impact of CWD from multiple tree species on forest floor bacterial and fungal communities under varying landscape-scale conditions, specifically comparing old-growth forests situated on Phaozems and Retisols with mass-windthrow areas located on loamy Retisols and sandy Podzols. We analyzed both chemical compound and metagenomic profiles of 63 CWD-associated soil samples collected from the Kaluzhskie Zaseki Nature Reserve (European part of Russia). High-throughput Illumina sequencing of the 16S rRNA gene and the ITS region was used to profile both bacterial and fungal communities, respectively. Scale-dependent diversity patterns and taxonomic accumulation were assessed using GLM, NMDS, dbRDA, and iNEXT frameworks. Our findings revealed a profound spatial decoupling in forest floor microbial communities, where a localized reduction in alpha-diversity under CWD drove a sharp increase in landscape-scale gamma-diversity. While standard soil physicochemical properties rigidly dictated baseline matrix richness, CWD operated as a powerful micro-environmental hotspot overriding these constraints. Deadwood inputs filtered out dominant matrix-associated taxa, creating highly specialized micro-refugia characterized by high compositional dispersion. This niche selection was particularly pronounced beneath Quercus logs on Phaozems and Retisols. Furthermore, post-windthrow microbial responses were heavily filtered by wood traits and baseline soil textures. On loamy Retisols within the windthrow mosaic, this breakaway dynamic was highly taxon-specific: while Acer and Fraxinus CWD triggered partitioned, site-specific hotspot dynamics yielding an exceptionally large pool of unique ASVs for bacteria, the distinct enrichment for fungal communities was primarily driven by Ulmus CWD and log-free windthrow areas. Ultimately, iNEXT accumulation profiles confirmed that deadwood does not merely multiply common soil taxa, but enriches the forest landscape by injecting critical beta-level heterogeneity into the soil matrix. These insights emphasize the role of diverse CWD retention in buffering forest microbiomes against large-scale environmental disturbances across heterogeneous soil landscapes. Highlights Sandy soils suppress bacterial abundance but trigger massive fungal proliferation. Bacterial richness is determined by soil pH; fungal diversity responds to nitrogen. Soil pH and nitrogen shift fungal composition along decoupled orthogonal axes. Coarse woody debris acts as hotspots of micro-environmental diversity. Post-windthrow microbial hotspots are strongly shaped by tree species.

items.title: The miPEP408-miR408 module regulates plant susceptibility to Rhizoctonia solani through LAC3-mediated lignin deposition in Arabidopsis.
items.abstract: Plant microRNAs (miRNAs) function as critical regulators of various developmental and physiological processes by downregulating the expression of their target genes. miRNA-encoded peptides (miPEPs) represent an additional regulatory layer by enhancing the transcription of their cognate miRNAs. . Although miPEP408 has been implicated in heavy-metal tolerance through regulation of sulfur assimilation, its role in plant immunity remains unknown. Here, we investigate the role of the miPEP408-miR408-Laccase3 (LAC3) regulatory cascade in defense against the necrotrophic fungus Rhizoctonia solani AG-1A using Arabidopsis thaliana. Providing mechanistic insight, we demonstrate through DNA-protein interaction assays that miPEP408 directly binds the MIR408 promoter, promoting miR408 accumulation and regulating its downstream target, Laccase3 (LAC3). We further show that LAC3 is a key determinant of defense by promoting lignin deposition in the cell wall to restrict pathogen invasion. In-planta bioassays further demonstrate that infection with the necrotrophic fungal pathogen R. solani AG-1A suppresses miPEP408 accumulation, thereby reducing miR408 expression and enhancing LAC3-mediated defense in Arabidopsis thaliana. Consistently, genetic manipulation of miR408 or LAC3 inversely modulates lignin deposition and disease susceptibility. Together, our findings establish the miPEP408-miR408-LAC3 module as a regulator of lignification-mediated cell wall immunity and identify miPEP408 as a promising target for engineering crops with enhanced resistance to biotic stress.
items.authors: Datta T, Shromona A, Kumar RS, Sinha H, Dwivedi A, Rai T, Gupta S, Ch R, Srivastava S, Singh A, Trivedi PK.

items.title: Bacterial-dominated niche partitioning and metabolic plasticity are associated with phosphorus acquisition in pure and mixed Cotinus coggygria forests
items.abstract: Abstract Aims Cotinus coggygria , a pioneer tree species in the Three Gorges Reservoir Area, is increasingly constrained by progressive phosphorus (P) limitation under long-term monoculture. Mixed-species plantations may alleviate this stress by reshaping the root–soil microbiota, but the underlying microecological mechanisms remain unclear. Methods Here, we examined soil properties, extracellular enzyme stoichiometry, and microbial community assembly across bulk soil, rhizosphere, and endosphere niches in pure C. coggygria stands (C) and two mixed stands ( C. coggygria + Quercus acrodonta , CQ; C. coggygria + Pinus massoniana , CPM). Results Mixed stands had lower total P but 99.64% (CQ) and 82.72% (CPM) higher specific phosphatase activity (SPA) than pure stands, driven mainly by downregulation of C- and N-acquiring enzymes and enhanced acid phosphatase (ACP) investment. Enzyme stoichiometry indicated stronger P limitation in CQ than in C and CPM. Along the root–soil interface, bacteria in mixed stands re-established a clear bulk soil–rhizosphere–endosphere filtration gradient, whereas fungi showed strong host conservatism, with dark septate endophytes (e.g., Cladophialophora ) dominating the endosphere. The two mixing patterns differed: CQ featured lower bulk soil pH and elevated ACP activity, whereas CPM developed a more complex and connected bacterial co-occurrence network with high average degree and low competitive antagonism. Conclusions These results suggest that mixed planting, especially conifer-broadleaf mixtures, may enhance microbial investment in phosphorus acquisition through bacterial niche differentiation and increased network connectivity. However, direct measurements are needed to determine whether these responses increase phosphorus mobilization and plant phosphorus uptake.
items.authors: Chang W, Wei L, Zhou X, Luo T, liu B, Guo R, Feng D, Wang Y.

items.title: Belowground Fungal Volatile Exposure Induces Systemic Metabolic Reprogramming in Poplar.
items.abstract: Although trees encounter diverse soil-associated fungi, it is unclear how they adjust their physiology in response to volatile organic compounds (VOCs) from fungi with contrasting ecological strategies before physical contact. Here, we tested whether VOCs emitted by fungi are sufficient to induce systemic, fungus-dependent metabolic responses in poplar. Populus × canescens roots were exposed to VOCs from a pathogen (Heterobasidion annosum), a saprotroph (Postia placenta), or an ectomycorrhizal mutualist (Laccaria bicolor) for 6 weeks in a contact-free pot-in-pot system. Untargeted LC-MS metabolomics was used to characterize VOC-induced metabolic reprogramming in roots and leaves. Fungal VOC exposure alone reconfigured root and leaf metabolomes, with both shared and fungus-dependent responses despite VOC exposure being restricted to the belowground compartment. Treatment-associated differences varied between tissues. H. annosum was associated with pronounced suppression of high-confidence features in leaves but a more balanced response in roots. P. placenta showed several uniquely upregulated root features together with selected lipid-associated changes, and L. bicolor produced comparatively few unique high-confidence changes. These results show that poplar can respond systemically and differentially to VOCs from contrasting fungal species before physical contact, while the extent to which these responses can be generalised across fungal lifestyles remains to be established.
items.authors: Zhu P, Zimmer I, Padmanaban PBS, Rosenkranz M, Ghirardo A, Schnitzler JP.

items.title: Zinc homeostasis in plants: the role of ZIP, MTP and HMA transporters and chelating agents
items.abstract: Zinc (Zn) is an essential micronutrient involved in numerous physiological processes in plants, serving catalytic, structural, and regulatory functions. Maintaining its appropriate concentration requires precise control of uptake, transport, distribution, and storage, as both Zn deficiency and excess lead to disruptions in plant growth and development. This paper presents the mechanisms regulating zinc homeostasis in plants, with a particular focus on the role of membrane transporters and chelating compounds. The ZIP, MTP, and HMA protein families play a key role, being responsible for cellular Zn uptake, its sequestration within organelles, and inter-tissue transport, respectively. Low-molecular-weight chelating ligands maintain safe zinc levels in the cytosol, and some of them facilitate its storage in vacuoles. Furthermore, they enhance its symplastic mobility and enable zinc transport in the xylem and phloem, thereby facilitating its distribution to shoots and seeds. Overall, this demonstrates the complex and multilevel nature of zinc homeostasis regulation in plants
items.authors: Borzęcka E, Barabasz A.

items.title: Bark Functional Traits and Phytochemical Diversity in Forest Trees: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Ecological Functions and Sustainable Utilization
items.abstract: Abstract Tree bark is a structurally complex and chemically diverse component of woody plants that performs essential protective, physiological, and defensive functions while serving as an important reservoir of bioactive compounds with considerable medicinal and industrial value. Despite growing interest in bark as a renewable forest resource, information on its anatomical characteristics, chemical composition, extractive diversity, and utilization remains fragmented across forestry, wood science, plant anatomy, phytochemistry, pharmacology, and industrial processing literature. Consequently, a comprehensive synthesis of the available evidence is required to improve understanding of bark diversity and support sustainable resource utilization. This study systematically reviewed and quantitatively synthesized published literature on bark anatomy, chemical composition, extractive variation, medicinal properties, industrial applications, and implications for sustainable forest management among forest tree species. The review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA 2020) guidelines. Literature published between January 1980 and June 2026 was retrieved from major bibliographic databases, institutional repositories, and selected grey literature sources. Following systematic screening and eligibility assessment, 574 studies were included in the qualitative synthesis, while 311 studies provided sufficient quantitative data for random-effects meta-analysis. Standardized mean differences (Hedges' g) were calculated, and heterogeneity among studies was evaluated using Cochran's Q statistic and the I² statistic. The findings revealed substantial interspecific variation in bark anatomical characteristics, including bark thickness, periderm development, secondary phloem organization, secretory structures, and rhytidome formation. items.title: Variation among populations of Quercus macrocarpa in a reciprocal transplant experiment across a latitudinal gradient.
items.abstract: Ongoing climate change will negatively impact tree populations unless they are able to acclimate to the changes in their local environment. Effective planning for climate adaptation management requires an understanding of the current state of local adaptation and physiological performance to assess whether populations are at risk of local extinction, to determine if seed movement is appropriate, and to select appropriate seed sources if intervention is needed. We established a new reciprocal transplant experiment (Adaptation to Climate and Environment [ACE]) across a latitudinal gradient in North America spanning a range of climate and soil conditions to examine the impacts of warming on three bur oak (Quercus macrocarpa) populations across much of the species' range. We established common gardens in Minnesota, Illinois, and Oklahoma in 2021 grown from seeds collected in 2018-2019 within 50 km of each of those locations from a total of 60 maternal families. In 2023, we measured physiology and 3-year growth and survival to understand local adaptation in bur oak populations. We aimed to (1) assess local adaptation in each of the populations using survival and size as fitness metrics and (2) evaluate physiological responses to different environments along the latitudinal gradient. We found evidence for local adaptation of the southern population in the southernmost garden, but that the northern populations were maladapted to high levels of warming, as evidenced by their low survival, growth, and photosynthetic rates in the warmest common garden. However, mild climate and relatively high nutrient conditions in the middle garden resulted in the highest fitness and best physiological performance for all populations. Growth and survival were correlated in the middle garden but were decoupled in the northern and southern gardens, likely due to stress associated with more extreme climates at the ends of the gradient. Our results suggest that southern seed sources may perform well in warmer conditions in the north brought on by climate change, which has important implications for managers assisting broadly ranged tree species in adapting to climate change.
items.authors: Rea LMS, Ostrowsky L, Mohn R, Garner M, Worcester L, Lapadat C, McCarthy HR, Hipp AL, Cavender-Bares J.

items.title: Enemy escape to enemy accumulation: fungal pathogens are associated with mortality in the invasive conifer Pinus contorta
items.abstract: Invasive species are predicted to escape their natural enemies, yet whether this release is overcome by co-invasion of specialist enemies and/or gain of diverse assemblages of generalist antagonists remains unresolved. Here we describe a natural experiment where invasive Pinus contorta conifers experienced a die-off in the Mackenzie Basin on the South Island of New Zealand. Using a combination of visual surveys, culturing, and next-generation sequencing, we show that fungal pathogens likely contributed to this mortality event this mortality event. The fungal communities of living pines were significantly more diverse than dead pines, characterized by many low abundance fungal OTUs alongside a few dominant species. Indicator OTUs of living tree communities were most closely related to a diverse suite of putative plant pathogens, some of which are known to infect pines; dead pines were associated with saprotrophic white and brown rot fungi. Critically, no single pathogen explained the mortality; living vs. dead status accounted for less than 3% of fungal community variation. We argue that these invasive conifers have accumulated a disparate assemblage of both co-invasive and novel latent pathogens that act opportunistically in concert with harsh abiotic conditions, suggesting enemy accumulation may predispose invasive species to population-level mortality.
items.authors: Marion Z, Cox G, Dickie IA.

items.title: Extremely low light promotes adventitious shoot regeneration via RpPHYA/RpHYH-antagonized auxin biosynthesis and transport through dual regulation of RpPIN1 in Robinia pseudoacacia.
items.abstract: Extremely low light (ELL) is widely applied as a strategy to enhance adventitious shoot (AS) regeneration in woody plants. However, how ELL acts as an environmental signal to reprogram regenerative competence remains unclear. Here, we show that ELL for 14 days (ELL14) markedly promotes AS regeneration across multiple genotypes of Robinia pseudoacacia. Transcriptomic and functional enrichment analyses revealed that auxin biosynthesis, transport, and signaling constitute the core pathways activated under ELL14. Consistently, auxin levels increased, and the inhibition of biosynthesis or transport largely abolished the regeneration-promoting effect. Integrative weighted gene co-expression network analysis and regulatory analyses identified RpPHYA as a key integrator of ELL-responsive networks. Under ELL14, the RpPHYA-associated module promotes auxin biosynthesis by upregulating RpAMI1 and coordinates auxin transport through RpPIN1 via transcriptional regulation and RpROS1-mediated CHG demethylation, forming a dual regulatory mechanism. In contrast, under normal light, RpHYH antagonizes this regulatory program, thereby restricting regenerative capacity. Overexpression of RpPHYA, RpAMI1, RpPIN1, and RpROS1 significantly enhanced AS regeneration, functionally validating this ELL14-induced module. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that ELL functions as an environmental signal that promotes AS regeneration in R. pseudoacacia through coordinated transcriptional and DNA demethylation of auxin transport, providing mechanistic insights for improving regeneration in woody plants.
items.authors: Han J, Tian Y, Liu J, Deng H, Han K, Si H, Ling S, Zhang S, Yu L, El-Kassaby YA, Sun Y, Peng Z, Li Y, Zhao Y.

items.title: A Robust Machine-Learning Classification Framework for Early Detection of Charcoal and Bleeding Canker in Cork Oak Bark
items.abstract: The cork oak (Quercus suber) is an ecologically and economically significant species, supporting forest biodiversity, carbon sequestration, and the global cork industry. Climate-driven pathogens, specifically Biscogniauxia mediterranea and Phytophthora cinnamomi, increasingly threaten cork oak forests with charcoal and bleeding cankers, respectively, leading to rapid forest decline. Early, reliable identification of these pathogens in the field is critical for effective management, but distinguishing visually similar diseases remains challenging for non-specialist personnel. This study investigates whether a small set of representative bark images can provide an interpretable, field-oriented approach to cork oak disease classification. Using a dataset of 1,198 bark images including healthy, B. mediterranea-infected, and P. cinnamomi-infected samples, we extracted features with MobileNet-v3 Small and applied K-Means clustering to identify pseudo-centroids, or real, representative images closest to each cluster’s center. These pseudo-centroids serve as interpretable reference points that field workers can visually compare with new samples, rather than relying solely on "black box" model outputs. A k-Nearest Neighbor (KNN) classifier evaluated against these pseudo-centroids achieved 74.90% accuracy across the three classes. To assess resilience to human labeling errors, a common source of error in field-collected datasets, we simulated noise by randomly swapping pseudo-centroid labels, which resulted in only a 5.44% decline in accuracy, demonstrating that the framework degrades gracefully rather than catastrophically under noisy conditions. This robustness, combined with the interpretability of the pseudo-centroid approach, makes the framework practical for forest rangers and conservation workers to prune or treat infected limbs based on direct visual similarity ranking, without requiring deep machine learning or biological expertise. Given the environmental and economic importance of cork production, this approach offers a scalable, field-ready tool for monitoring the health of cork oak forests. Future work will expand the framework to larger, more diverse datasets and additional pathogens, broadening its applicability across cork-producing regions.
items.authors: Yang J, Salotra G, Pinsky E.

items.title: Ecophysiology of soursop seedlings fertilized with calcium silicate under different irrigation frequencies
items.abstract: Abstract Propose: The soursop tree ( Annona muricata L.) is a tropical fruit tree cultivated in the semi-arid region of Brazil; however, it is sensitive to water deficit. The application of calcium silicate can promote plant growth and development under water stress. Therefore, the objective was to evaluate the ecophysiological and biochemical changes in soursop seedlings fertilized with calcium silicate under different irrigation frequencies. Methods: The experiment was conducted in a greenhouse using a randomized block design with a 4 × 2 factorial scheme and four replications. The treatments consisted of four irrigation frequencies: TR1 – daily irrigation; TR2 – irrigation every two days; TR3 – irrigation every four days; TR4 – irrigation every six days, combined with the presence or absence of calcium silicate (CaSiO₃), applied via soil, at a dose of 3.5 g plant⁻¹. Results: Soursop seedlings subjected to TR3 associated with CaSiO₃ showed improved gas exchange, including transpiration, stomatal conductance, and photosynthetic rate. Fertilization with CaSiO₃ regulated proline synthesis, increased leaf biomass and silicon and calcium content in leaf tissues, conferring greater tolerance to water deficit. Treatments TR2 and TR3 were similar to TR1 in plant height, number of leaves, leaf area, biomass accumulation, chlorophyll a fluorescence, chlorophyll content, and total soluble sugars, whereas TR4 significantly reduced these variables, regardless of CaSiO₃ fertilization. Conclusions: The application of CaSiO₃ under moderate stress (TR3) increases soursop seedlings' tolerance to deficit irrigation regimes.
items.authors: Amorim PEC, Mendonça V, Reis Td, Ferreira FN, Silva DEGd, Lima JL, Silva RRd, Silva MA, Ferreira AdS, Ribeiro JEdS, de Oliveira AMF, Silva GCd, Vieira ECM, Costa LPd, Souto AGdL, Sá FVdS.

items.title: Radial growth resilience assessment and management implications for major planted forests in the west loess plateau based on improved parameters.
items.abstract: Under the background of global climate change, frequent and severe drought have led to forest decline and tree mortality, ultimately threatening the structure, function, and stability of forest ecosystems. However, forest ecosystems and individual trees exhibit a certain degree of growth resilience to the impacts of drought. A profound understanding of the growth resilience of forest ecosystems and individual trees to drought is of great significance for maintaining the stability of forest ecosystems, particularly for plantation ecosystems. Based on an improved resilience assessment framework (maximum averaged growth reduction and recovery rate with the flexible time window), this study compared the radial growth resilience of major tree and shrub species between planted forests across different sub-climatic zones of the west Loess Plateau and corresponding natural forest species in adjacent area. The results indicate that: 1) Compared to plantations, natural forest tree species exhibit higher growth resilience. 2) Platycladus orientalis, Hippophae rhamnoides, and Caragana korshinskii possess high growth resilience, rendering them highly suitable for afforestation across the arid regions of the Loess Plateau. In contrast, Picea crassifolia and Pinus tabulaeformis showed lower resilience and should be confined to high altitude, semi-arid zones with higher precipitation. 3) In terms of plantation management in areas with insufficient precipitation, appropriate silvicultural interventions, such as rainwater harvesting, soil moisture conservation, and stand tending, must be supplemented to maintain the healthy and sustainable development of planted forests. These findings provide a scientific basis for species selection and adaptive plantation management on the Loess Plateau.
items.authors: Xiao Y, Peng X, Tian Q, Che C, Su J.

items.title: Crown-based growth strategies explain the distribution and co-occurrence of tree functional groups along environmental gradients
items.abstract: Elucidating interspecific variation in growth strategies across environments is critical for understanding tree diversity and distribution. However, a systematic analysis across diverse forests remains scarce due to limited large-tree crown measurements. We analysed 3,814 trees from 107 canopy species in 23 natural forests using forest census data and unmanned aerial vehicle. Relative growth rate (growth rate/biomass) was decomposed into growing space efficiency (growth rate/crown area) and crown area ratio (crown area/biomass). Relative growth rates were similar among functional groups (deciduous broadleaf, evergreen broadleaf, evergreen conifer), but their underlying components differed. Deciduous trees exhibited 34-43% higher crown area ratio but 24-27% lower growing space efficiency than evergreen broadleaf and conifer trees. Across environments, growing space efficiency correlated positively with mean annual temperature, likely from extended growing seasons while crown area ratio correlated negatively, particularly in deciduous species. Snow loading limited crown area ratio in evergreen species, while deciduous achieved higher values through avoiding snow loads. Correlation between crown area ratio and specific leaf area indicated a coordinated strategy between crowns and leaves. Different functional groups achieve comparable growth efficiency either through crown expansion or biomass production, explaining their distinct distribution as well as co-occurrence across broad environments.
items.authors: Htoo, K. K., Onishi, M., Rahman, M. F., Takeshige, R., Kitajima, K., Onoda, Y.

items.title: Modeled Leaf Assimilation Increases Under Rising CO₂ in Anatolian Forest Trees Despite Warming and Drying, While Thermal Threshold Exceedance Increases
items.abstract: Rising atmospheric CO₂ suppresses photorespiration, whereas warming and drying can limits leaf carbon gain. We coupled a Farquhar-von Caemmerer-Berry photosynthesis model with an ATP/NADPH budget, soil-plant hydraulics, and leaf energy balance, assigning photosystem II thermal thresholds based on leaf habit. Using ISIMIP3b forcing from five CMIP6 models, we simulated eight tree species across 27 species-site combinations at six locations in Türkiye, comparing the periods 2020–2030 and 2070–2080 under the SSP5-8.5 scenario. With soil moisture reset each season, the mean seasonal net assimilation increased by 130.3 gC m⁻² of leaf area (95% CI: 76–187 gC m⁻²). The forcing-channel contributions were +219.5 gC m⁻² from CO₂, −66.7 gC m⁻² from temperature/VPD, −38.8 gC m⁻² from precipitation, and −2.8 gC m⁻² from radiation (residual: +19.1). Species and sites accounted for 81% of the fitted variance, compared to 3.1% for GCMs. Under year-round soil water tracking, the mean increase was 106.5 gC m⁻² (95% CI: +43 to +167), with declines in 11 of 135 cells. Days with peak leaf temperature exceeding assigned thermal thresholds increased from 1.5 to 12.2 per season, primarily in broad-leaved species. These counts were sensitive to thermal parameters and stomatal assumptions and do not directly quantify tissue damage. Within the tested configurations, higher modeled leaf assimilation coexisted with more frequent threshold exceedance. Neither outcome alone establishes stand productivity or forest resilience.
items.authors: Yazar E, Akgün B, Babur E.

items.title: Intraspecific leaf morphometric diversity in the endangered and narrow endemic Quercus trojana subsp. euboica (Fagaceae): a quantitative dataset from three natural populations in Euboea, Greece.
items.abstract: This study provides the first quantitative dataset on leaf morphometric diversity for Quercus trojana subsp. euboica (Papaioannou) K.I.Chr., a narrow endemic oak of Greece. This subspecies is of high conservation priority, listed in the Red Data Book of Rare and Threatened Plants of Greece and its restricted range in Northern Euboea was heavily impacted by a catastrophic wildfire in 2021. We sampled 301 leaves from three natural populations (Kerasia1, Kerasia2 and Prokopi) and processed them using a custom Python pipeline to extract 14 size and shape variables. Statistical analyses (PCA and LDA) showed that, while leaf shape remains relatively stable across populations, there is significant variation in leaf size. Specifically, the Prokopi population, where only understorey individuals were found, had much larger leaves (mean leaf area 1,015 mm2) than those in Kerasia1 (648 mm2) and Kerasia2 (715 mm2). These data establish a baseline for monitoring the species' recovery and will be used alongside future genomic data to better understand the role of phenotypic plasticity in its conservation.
items.authors: Lyrou F, Tourvas N, Aravanopoulos F.

items.title: Root Age Structure Governs Long-Term Architecture and Hydraulic Function in Perennial Plants: a Modelling Framework
items.abstract: Summary Background and aims Perennial root systems develop over decades and exhibit continuous turnover of structural and absorptive components, yet most root architecture models treat woody roots as permanent and neglect root age structure. We developed an empirically constrained modelling framework that explicitly represents age-structured demography, growth regulation and dormancy in perennial root systems. Methods We extended the functional–structural plant model CPlantBox to simulate perennial root development over decades by integrating age-dependent survival, secondary radial growth and climate-driven dormancy. The model was parameterised using unique three-dimensional root system data from young and mature grapevines, together with dendrochronological root age measurements, and coupled to root hydraulic properties. Key results Empirical analyses revealed multi-cohort age distributions and substantial turnover of lignified structural roots, contradicting the assumption of a static woody scaffold. The model reproduced age distributions, order-specific survival probabilities and fine-to-structural root length ratios, and generated realistic, genotype-specific three-dimensional architectures. Simulated uptake profiles and hydraulic scenarios showed strong age- and architecture-driven effects. Conclusions Explicitly representing woody root age distributions and age-dependent processes may fundamentally change predictions of perennial root system architecture and function. The framework advances root modelling beyond annual paradigms and provides a transferable tool for analysing long-term architectural and hydraulic consequences of genotype × climate interactions in perennial crops.
items.authors: Giraud, M., Fichtl, L., Leitner, D., Schnepf, A., Steng, K., Friedel, M.

items.title: Biome-scale heterogeneity in Scots pine drought resilience across Eurasia
items.abstract: Abstract The stability of global forest ecosystems is challenged by the accelerated pace of climate change, raising questions about their role as future carbon reservoirs. Intensifying drought events affect forest productivity and dieback at regional scales, yet how drought sensitivity and resilience components vary across the full distribution of widespread tree species remains insufficiently quantified. Here, we compile a pan-Eurasian network of 534 Pinus sylvestris tree-ring chronologies spanning the species’ full ecological range and quantify growth departures and resilience components during the most extreme summer droughts of the past century. Drought impacts diverge systematically along major climatic gradients. Growth reductions exceed 70% in cold-dry and warm semi-humid regions, while cool–humid forests show muted and even positive departures. Resistance is lowest under prolonged droughts in continental cold–dry interiors and under short summer droughts in semi-humid lowlands, while recovery capacity is highest where growth losses are most severe, reflecting local adaptations in drier regions. Despite coherent biome-scale patterns, substantial site-level variability indicates that growth legacies often persist beyond the event year. Nonlinear models show that resilience-climate relationships are shaped not only by mean climate conditions, but also by atmospheric water demand, site-level water balance, and thermal stability across climatic domains. Together, these results provide a range-wide assessment of drought impacts, demonstrating how prevailing climate conditions modulates forest stability and carbon sequestration capacity under intensifying climate extremes.
