items.title: The core taxa connectivity in leaf microbiomes in ash trees stands is modulated by host-related and environmental factors.
items.abstract: BackgroundForests cover large areas of the terrestrial land surface and play a key role in climate regulation and biodiversity conservation. Tree-associated microbial communities are integral components of forest ecosystems and contribute to plant functioning, stress tolerance, and interactions with the environment. However, the factors shaping the phyllosphere microbiome of forest trees across large environmental gradients remain less explored. Here, we investigated the bacterial leaf microbiome of Fraxinus excelsior across different climatic regions in Germany to identify its core microbiome and determine the relative importance of environmental and host-related factors shaping the phyllosphere microbiome of forest trees across large environmental gradients assembly. Therefore, 30 ash trees were sampled at each of the 12 sites across Germany, at which we assessed their leaf microbiome, leaf physio-chemical properties and a set of site parameters.ResultsIn total, 755 genera were detected. Only three genera Hymenobacter, Massilia and Sphingomonas were predominant across all sites. Geographical position, precipitation, tree age and the leaf and soil chemistry parameters were significant factors that explained 22.1% of variance between microbiome structures between the different sites. Seven genera were identified as the core leave microbiome of F. excelsior. The core microbiome assessed for each sampling site was mostly more diverse and differed between sites. Complex co-occurrence networks separated by sites with the identified six hub bacterial taxa proved that they were essential for the local core microbiomes. However, the network complexity differed significantly between the sampling sites.ConclusionOur findings clearly indicate the existence of an ash core microbiome on leaves that occurred at all sites but was locally differently interconnected to further microbiome members. The network analyses revealed that less frequent genera play important roles as hub taxa. Furthermore, we were also able to prove the modulating role of biotic and abiotic factors on the ash phyllosphere microbiome. An optimized core microbiome may be considered crucial for improving tolerance against plant diseases, such as ash dieback, in future.
items.authors: Burghard V, Wende S, Kahlenberg G, Häuser H, Kätzel R, Kolb S, Ulrich A.

items.title: Flooding with brackish water disrupts Liriodendron tulipifera sap flux in an ecosystem-scale experiment.
items.abstract: Coastal forests are retreating due to sea‑level rise and extreme precipitation events, yet the physiological mechanisms that precede woody plant decline remain poorly constrained. We used the ecosystem‑scale TEMPEST (Terrestrial Ecosystem Manipulation to Probe the Effects of Storm Treatments) experiment; annual, plot‑level freshwater and saltwater flooding of a mid‑Atlantic deciduous forest, to quantify short‑ and long‑term responses of sap flux in three tree species: Acer rubrum, Fagus grandifolia, and Liriodendron tulipifera. We analyzed five years of sap flux density measurements (2021-2025) using a Before-After Control-Impact (BACI) framework and linear mixed‑effects models to assess short and long-term changes in tree hydraulic function. Across the study period, species differed markedly in their responses to repeated flooding. A. rubrum showed no significant change in sap flux density under any treatment, while F. grandifolia exhibited plot‑specific increases or decreases consistent with relief from drought in the freshwater treatment plot. L. tulipifera sap flux density increased over time in all plots, but increases were dampened in the freshwater plot and strongly suppressed under saltwater flooding. Soil electrical conductivity rose progressively in the saltwater plot and emerged as a key predictor of both immediate and cumulative reductions in L. tulipifera sap flux density. As L. tulipifera constitutes a large share of canopy basal area in this coastal forest, continued saltwater intrusion is poised to accelerate mortality and drive ecosystem state-change. Our findings illustrate how ecosystem‑scale manipulations can uncover physiological thresholds relevant to coastal forest vulnerability under future sea‑level rise.
items.authors: Srinivasan RV, McDowell N, Pennington SC, Stearns AE, Bond-Lamberty B, Megonigal JP, Morris KA.

items.title: Silvicultural Management, Tree-Ring Analysis and Timber Quality Improvement in Zambian Forest Plantations: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: Abstract Forest plantations play a critical role in meeting demand for timber, poles, pulpwood, fuelwood and other forest products while reducing pressure on natural forests. In Zambia, plantation forestry is dominated by exotic species, particularly Pinus and Eucalyptus, but timber quality is influenced by silvicultural practices, site conditions, climate variability, pests, diseases and management interventions. This systematic review synthesizes evidence on silvicultural management, timber quality improvement and dendrochronological applications in Zambian forest plantations. Following the PRISMA 2020 framework, literature published between 1980 and 2026 was identified from Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, Wiley Online Library, CAB Abstracts, Google Scholar and additional forestry and institutional sources. The review evaluates species–site matching, spacing, thinning, pruning, weed control, fertilization, fire management, pest and disease control, and the use of tree-ring analysis to understand growth dynamics, climate responses, wood formation and rotation-age decisions. A total of 1,624 records were identified, 1,310 were screened after duplicate removal, 382 full texts were assessed, and 142 studies met the inclusion criteria. Because of substantial heterogeneity among studies, thematic synthesis was used rather than quantitative meta-analysis. The evidence indicates that management interventions can influence stem form, diameter growth, knot development, wood density and timber value, while dendrochronology provides long-term information on growth patterns, climatic responses, disturbances and management effects. Integrating silvicultural management with tree-ring monitoring offers a practical framework for improving timber quality, growth modelling and climate-adaptive plantation management in Zambia.
items.authors: Nsofu BM, Hatimbula K.

items.title: Regeneration After Severe Wildfire: Hotter Microclimates Exceed Hydraulic and Thermal Tolerances in Sierra Nevada Conifer Seedlings.
items.abstract: Tree seedling regeneration after wildfire will determine the long-term trajectory of forests under climate change, yet increasing drought and heat extremes can suppress regeneration and result in forest type conversion. We combined field observations and a controlled drought-heat growth chamber experiment to investigate how these stressors independently and jointly affect drought- and heat-tolerance physiology in seedlings of montane conifer species from drought- and wildfire-prone regions in the southern Sierra Nevada. In both the field and growth chamber experiment, we found that exposure to elevated leaf temperatures in post fire-like environments dwarfed the effect of physiological adjustments in heat tolerance (temperatures causing initial impairment (Tcrit) or 50% loss (T50) of photosystem II capacity) and drought tolerance (turgor loss point). In the field, this resulted in narrower thermal safety margins across five conifer species in burn scars with no remaining canopy, while in the growth chamber experiment three species showed narrower or even negative thermal and hydraulic safety margins. In the growth chamber experiment, leaf temperatures were also frequently decoupled from air temperature, highlighting that biophysical feedbacks between leaf temperature and transpiration may amplify seedling water loss even under stomatal closure. For both the field and growth chamber experiment, we found no evidence of a trade-off between drought and heat tolerance within or among species. Among species, seedlings of the range-restricted Sequioadendron giganteum (giant sequoia) were observed to be the most vulnerable to combined drought and heat stress in the growth chamber experiment. Our results highlight that direct thermal stress may strongly constrain post-fire conifer regeneration and underscore the need to integrate seedling energy balance and microclimate into predictions of post-fire recovery and management strategies, especially for vulnerable species such as giant sequoia.
items.authors: Kerr KL, Trugman AT, Anderegg LDL.

items.title: Pine wilt disease as a holobiont disorder: microbiome assembly as a potential management target
items.abstract: Pine wilt disease (PWD), caused by the pinewood nematode (PWN) Bursaphelenchus xylophilus, continues to expand globally despite decades of pathogen-focused management. Here, we propose that disruption of microbiome assembly within the pine holobiont may contribute to disease progression and help explain variation in disease outcomes and responses to microbial interventions. Drawing on recent advances in microbial ecology, multi-omics, and synthetic biology, we synthesize evidence of PWD-associated changes in host-associated microbial communities and examine how altered functional redundancy and pathobiome formation may contribute to disease progression. We propose that microbiome assembly, shaped by host traits, environmental filters, and biotic interactions, is a plausible and underexplored determinant of disease outcome. Building on this framework, we outline a shift from single-agent biocontrol toward assembly-informed microbiome engineering. To support reproducible design and future validation, we outline criteria for selecting candidate consortium members and assessing synthetic microbial community (SynCom) establishment, persistence and functional stability. We further propose experimentally testable strategies to compare assembly-informed versus conventional interventions and identify measurable indicators of microbiome stability and disease suppression. By reframing PWD as a problem of microbiome assembly and stability, this work provides a testable framework for developing durable, holobiont-level management strategies. Integrating ecological theory with applied microbiome engineering offers a path forward to move beyond inconsistent control outcomes and toward resilient forest health under ongoing environmental change.
items.authors: Pires D, Espada M, Proença D, Vicente C.

items.title: Wood Anatomical Traits and Their Influence on Carbon Sequestration, Hydraulic Efficiency and Climate Resilience of Indigenous Tree Species in Southern Africa: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.abstract: Abstract Climate change is increasingly affecting forest ecosystems worldwide through rising temperatures, prolonged droughts, altered precipitation patterns, and increasing frequencies of extreme climatic events. These environmental changes influence tree growth, mortality, carbon sequestration, water relations, and ecosystem resilience. Understanding the biological traits that enable tree species to adapt to climatic stress has therefore become a major priority in forestry and ecological research. Among these traits, wood anatomical characteristics play a critical role in regulating hydraulic conductivity, carbon storage, mechanical support, and drought tolerance. Anatomical features such as vessel diameter, vessel density, vessel arrangement, fibre morphology, ray dimensions, and parenchyma abundance influence how trees transport water, store carbon, and respond to environmental disturbances. Southern Africa contains extensive woodland and forest ecosystems, including miombo, mopane, Kalahari, and dry evergreen forests, which support numerous indigenous tree species of ecological, economic, and conservation importance. However, information linking wood anatomical traits to carbon sequestration, hydraulic efficiency, and climate resilience remains fragmented across multiple disciplines and geographic regions. Consequently, there is limited synthesis of how anatomical adaptations influence forest responses to climate change and their implications for climate-smart forestry and sustainable forest management. This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesizes available evidence on the influence of wood anatomical traits on carbon sequestration, hydraulic efficiency, and climate resilience among indigenous tree species in Southern Africa. Following the PRISMA framework, published journal articles, forestry reports, dissertations, conference proceedings, and institutional publications were reviewed. Data were extracted on vessel characteristics, fibre properties, ray dimensions, parenchyma abundance, wood density, biomass accumulation, carbon storage, hydraulic conductivity, cavitation resistance, drought tolerance, and climate adaptation indicators. The review demonstrates that wood anatomical traits are strong predictors of ecosystem functioning and climate adaptation. Vessel architecture emerged as a primary determinant of hydraulic efficiency and drought resistance, while fibre characteristics and wood density were strongly associated with biomass accumulation and long-term carbon sequestration. Species possessing narrow vessels, high vessel density, thick fibre walls, abundant parenchyma, and dense wood generally exhibited greater hydraulic safety, drought tolerance, and carbon storage potential. The findings highlight the importance of integrating wood anatomical information into climate-smart forestry, forest landscape restoration, carbon accounting systems, species selection programmes, and sustainable forest management strategies. The review further identifies critical research gaps, including limited species-specific anatomical databases, inadequate long-term hydraulic monitoring, and insufficient integration of anatomical traits into climate adaptation models.
items.authors: Nsofu BM.

items.title: High temperature disrupts sporocyte development in Camellia meiocarpa.
items.abstract: High temperature has a significant impact on plant reproductive development, driving the formation of 2n gametes by interfering with the meiosis and cytokinesis of sporocytes. This study used Camellia meiocarpa as the material, integrating cytological and molecular biology approaches to reveal the cytological effects and regulatory mechanisms of high temperature on sporocyte development. The results showed that meiosis in microsporocyte and megasporocyte of C. meiocarpa exhibits pronounced spatiotemporal heterogeneity. High temperature markedly disrupted sporocyte development and induced abnormal phenomena, inducing disordered cytokinesis, leading to the formation of dyads, triads in microsporocyte, as well as multinucleate cells occurring during the development of megaspores into mature embryo sacs. RNA-seq sequencing analysis indicates that the CoNPK1 gene may regulate meiotic and cytokinetic behavior in response to high temperature. Meanwhile, heterologous transformation in tobacco verified that the CoNPK1 gene induces the formation of dyads and triads through upregulated expression, which further leads to the production of 2n gametes. We speculate that the CoNPK1 gene regulates cell plate synthesis via the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling pathway, thereby affecting cytokinesis and generating 2n gametes. This lays a theoretical foundation for ploidy breeding of woody oil crops.
items.authors: Zhang T, Xiao W, Liu X, Song J, Zhang C, Cheng Y, Xia Y, Han Z.

items.title: Impact of drainage on soil CH4 and N2O fluxes in nutrient-rich hemiboreal peatland forests of Europe.
items.abstract: Background and aimsPeatland forests play a significant, yet highly variable, role in atmospheric methane (CH4) and nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions. Drainage reduces CH4 but increases N2O fluxes from nutrient-rich soils, creating complex climate trade-offs. To refine regional climate strategies, a clearer understanding of soil fluxes and influencing factors across forest types in the hemiboreal zone is needed.MethodsThis study presents two years of soil flux and environmental data collected from 2020 to 2023 using manual chambers at 18 drained (DF) and 7 undrained (UF) sites, with different tree species, in Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania.ResultsSoil water‑table depth was the primary control on annual CH4 exchange; DF sites acted as CH4 sinks (-4.6 kg ha-1 y-1), whereas UF sites were net sources (38.2 kg ha-1 y-1). In contrast, N2O emissions occurred at all sites, averaging 5.9 kg ha-1 y-1 in DF and 1.4 kg ha-1 y-1 in UF soils. Within DF sites, Myrtillus‑type pine stands exhibited the lowest N2O fluxes, while alder stands showed the highest, followed by birch- and spruce-dominated stands, reflecting differences in hydrology, pH, and C/N ratios of the soil.ConclusionsOur findings reveal significantly lower CH4 and moderately higher N2O emissions from DF soils than the IPCC Tier 1 temperate zone emission factor (EF), which has thus far been used for the hemiboreal zone. This study can improve national GHG inventories using specific information. We recommend applying Baltic region-specific EFs, as the mean annual CH4 and N2O emissions showed no significant difference across the three countries.Graphical abstractSupplementary informationThe online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s11104-026-08920-x.
items.authors: Kamil-Sardar M, Laiho R, Jauhiainen J, Butlers A, Schindler T, Vahter H, Čiuldienė D, Vigricas E, Teemusk A, Kull A, Lazdiņš A, Haberl A, Bārdule A, Līcīte I, Samariks V, Mander Ü, Armolaitis K, Soosaar K.

items.title: Sulfoquinovosyldiacylglycerol (SQDG) in Chloroplast-Poor Tissues: What Can Lipidomics Tell Us?
items.abstract: Sulfoquinovosyldiacylglycerol (SQDG) is an anionic sulfolipid of plastid membranes, classically associated with chloroplasts and thylakoids. Its detection by lipidomics in chloroplast-poor tissues raises a central problem: how can a reported SQDG signal be validated, and what evidence is required to determine its plastid context and biological meaning? Here, we critically reassess evidence beyond chloroplast-dominated tissues and evaluate both the strength of evidence for SQDG occurrence or function and the steps required to test lipidomics-derived hypotheses. The literature supports context-dependent rather than universal interpretations. Direct organelle-level lipid evidence from isolated non-green plastids remains limited; etioplast genetics supports an SQDG-related role in non-photosynthetic plastid membrane development; phosphate-deprived roots support phosphorus-economy remodeling; and sulfur-starvation studies establish regulated SQDG turnover and sulfur remobilization. By contrast, chromoplast and woody-tissue interpretations remain unresolved. These findings show that SQDG abundance alone is hypothesis-generating rather than diagnostic of function. We therefore propose a decision-tree framework that moves from chemical confirmation of the lipid signal to spatial localization, SQD1/SQD2-associated biosynthetic capacity, nutrient context, tissue-specific perturbation, and phenotype testing. This framework provides criteria for moving from lipidomic detection to supported biological interpretation in chloroplast-poor tissues.
items.authors: Potijun S, Sirikantaramas S, Schaller H.

items.title: A high spatial resolution transcriptomics of tension wood reveals the genetic program of contractile G-layer formation.
items.abstract: Tension wood (TW) formation in Populus involves the differentiation of G-fibers that deposit a cellulose-rich, contractile gelatinous layer (G-layer). Despite extensive study, the biosynthetic programs underlying G-layer formation have remained incompletely resolved, in part due to imprecise sampling of developmental stages. Here, we generate a high spatial-resolution transcriptome atlas of developing Populus tremula wood by tangential cryo-sectioning of TW and normal wood (NW) forming tissue. We overlaid microscopically determined cell wall thickening profiles with whole-transcriptome data, resulting in seven distinguishable TW and three NW stages and a clear separation of early and late G-layer-specific transcriptional programs during TW formation. Across 22,363 expressed genes, 90 co-expression clusters captured major programs defining cell wall biosynthesis, signaling, cytoskeleton dynamics, and stress responses. Differential expression analysis identified 2,898 genes specifically regulated during early or late G-layer formation-indicating a massive transcriptional reorganization unique to TW. Genes involved in cellulose, rhamnogalacturonan I, arabinogalactan II, and callose metabolism showed distinct induction patterns, including CAZymes not previously implicated in G-layer formation. We also identified G-layer-specific genes, including XTH26 (PtXTH5), SCL18, AGL29, and genes encoding FLA12-like AGPs and LIM protein. Thirty transcription factors different than the secondary wall-inducing NACs and MYBs, and several genes involved in hormonal regulation specifically induced at the onset of G-layer formation represent novel putative regulators of the tertiary G-layer differentiation. Together, this spatially resolved transcriptome provides the most detailed map to date of the molecular program underlying TW formation, offering new insights into G-layer biosynthesis, signaling networks, and cell wall specialization in woody plants.
items.authors: Kumar M, Grones C, Allen H, Lundberg-Felten J, Delhomme N, Sundberg B, Mellerowicz EJ.

items.title: Benchmarking ensemble and deep learning models for drought-responsive gene prioritisation in rice using multi-omics data.
items.abstract: Identifying drought-responsive genes is critical for climate-resilient crop breeding, yet computational gene-trait association often relies on single-omics or generalized genomic datasets. Optimal algorithm selection for high-dimensional, small multi-omics datasets also remains a persistent challenge. We present a machine learning framework that extends the QTG-Finder feature set by integrating transcriptomic and proteomic features to classify drought-responsive genes in rice. Using MBKBase annotations, we evaluated the ability of these models to prioritise 336 drought-responsive genes among 2,416 abiotic stress-associated genes, of which the remaining 2,080 constituted an operational background set. We tested four algorithms: Random Forest, XGBoost, one-dimensional convolutional neural network, and multilayer perceptron, while addressing severe class imbalance and assessing model stability. Tree-based ensemble methods achieved higher performance than the deep learning models in this dataset, which showed early overfitting. The fine-tuned Random Forest achieved a recall of 0.67 and an AUC-ROC of 0.87 under nested cross-validation, conditional on a feature matrix assembled before gene-level data splitting. Across repeated evaluations of a small internal holdout of 10 genes, mean accuracy and recall were 0.90 and 0.63; this set is too small to support a generalizability claim and is reported only as a consistency check. The newly added transcriptomic and proteomic features improved recall from 0.47 to 0.67 compared with genomics alone. Feature importance and ablation analyses indicated that transcriptomics-derived features, particularly measures of expression distribution, magnitude, and direction, contributed most to predictive performance. Functional enrichment analysis supported the biological relevance of the prioritised genes. These results demonstrate the value of multi-omics integration for gene prioritisation in small tabular datasets while highlighting current limitations of deep learning in this setting.
items.authors: Govaichelvan KN, Pathmanathan D, Zainal-Abidin RA, Abu A.

items.title: Machine Learning Identification of Functional Trait Syndromes Associated with Responsiveness to Arbuscular Mycorrhizal Fungi
items.abstract: Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) are widespread plant symbionts that enhance nutrient acquisition, growth, and stress tolerance, yet plant responsiveness to AMF varies substantially and remains difficult to predict. We developed Trait2Myco, a Random Forest based machine-learning framework that integrates plant functional traits and environmental variables to predict mycorrhizal growth response (MGR). The framework was trained using 80 observations spanning four grass species grown under four precipitation regimes. Predictor variables included leaf and root economic traits together with precipitation, while total MGR served as the response variable. A full model incorporating ten functional traits and precipitation was trained using 80% of observations and evaluated on an independent testing dataset (20%, n = 16). The full model explained 41% of variation in MGR (R² = 0.41), whereas a reduced ecological model containing only specific leaf area, specific root area, root carbon concentration, and precipitation improved predictive performance and explained 51.7% of variation (R² = 0.517). Ten-fold cross-validation of the full model yielded an R² of 0.983, RMSE of 0.046, and MAE of 0.036. Variable importance analysis identified specific leaf area, precipitation, root carbon concentration, and specific root area as the strongest predictors of responsiveness. Partial dependence analysis revealed nonlinear relationships between these predictors and MGR, while principal component analysis showed that highly responsive plants occupied distinct regions of functional trait space characterized by resource-acquisitive trait syndromes. Leaf and root traits contributed nearly equally to model performance, accounting for 41.9% and 41.3% of cumulative importance, respectively, while environmental factors contributed 16.8%. An exploratory analysis using an independent AMF colonization dataset produced similarly strong predictive relationships, suggesting that trait-based machine-learning approaches may generalize across multiple AMF-associated responses. Trait2Myco provides a reproducible framework for identifying plant trait syndromes associated with responsiveness to AMF and offers a practical tool for predicting mycorrhizal benefits across environmental gradients. items.authors: Shah, T., Errahmouni, M. A., Hijri, M.

items.title: Nanoscale magnesium oxide reduces the accumulation and toxicity of micro/nanoplastics by accelerating root lignification and alleviating endoplasmic reticulum stress.
items.abstract: The risk to agricultural production and human health from micro/nanoplastics (MNPs) exposure cannot be ignored, making it imperative to find effective mitigation strategies. Nanoscale magnesium oxide (MgO·NP) has been widely demonstrated to enhance plant stress resistance by activating defense pathways. However, its ability to mitigate MNPs stress remains unexplored. A greenhouse soil culture experiment was conducted by co-adding five predominant soil MNPs (polyethylene terephthalate (PET), polyethylene (PE), polystyrene (PS), polypropylene (PP), and polyvinyl chloride (PVC)) at 1 g·kg⁻¹ each. After 30 days, pyrolysis gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (Py-GC/MS) analysis of tomato leaves revealed a distinct absorption profile for MNPs: PET > PE > PS > PP > PVC. Soil amendment with 40 mg·kg⁻¹ MgO·NP significantly inhibited MNPs accumulation in tomatoes, reducing PET, PS, and PVC by 57.44%, 76.14%, and 31.82%, respectively. Multi-omics analyses revealed that MgO·NP upregulates phenylpropanoid biosynthesis genes (PAL, 4CL, CCR). This upregulation elevated lignin content by 26.7% and stimulated root lignification, a response that may be linked to the observed reduction in apoplastic uptake and transport of MNPs. Furthermore, MgO·NP was associated with changes in ERAD‑related gene expression and may have contributed to mitigating protein misfolding and organelle stress under MNPs exposure. In conclusion, this study demonstrates that exogenous application of 40 mg·kg⁻¹ MgO·NP significantly inhibits the accumulation and mitigates the toxicity of MNPs in tomato plants. These findings may offer a feasible strategy for alleviating the adverse impacts of MNPs contamination on agricultural production.
items.authors: Liu Z, Pan J, Li W, Jia T, Sun X, Qin M, Li R, Liu P, White JC, Shi Q.

items.title: Chromosome-level genome assembly of Tilia mandshurica reveals divergence of duplicated TPP genes associated with fructose-rich nectar formation.
items.abstract: Tilia mandshurica is an important woody nectar plant, but the genomic and transcriptional basis of its nectar sugar accumulation remains poorly understood. Here, we generated a chromosome-level reference genome for T. mandshurica and integrated comparative genomics, gene duplication analysis, RNA-seq across seven floral developmental stages, qRT-PCR validation, carbohydrate measurements and metabolite profiling. Gene family analysis revealed lineage-specific expansion of families involved in carbohydrate metabolism, ion transport and specialized metabolism. Ks and synteny analyses identified an ancient Eocene whole-genome duplication likely shared with Craigia yunnanensis, whereas duplication-mode analysis indicated that subsequent small-scale duplications contributed to lineage-specific duplicate retention. Among the enriched carbohydrate-related categories, trehalose-phosphatase activity provided a link between genome evolution and floral sugar accumulation. Sixteen trehalose-phosphate phosphatase (TPP) genes separated into fructose-positive C1 and fructose-negative C2 classes, with strong divergence at both the gene level (Δ = 1.060) and module level (Δ = 1.294). C1 TPP genes tracked fructose accumulation, whereas C2 genes followed starch-related developmental programs. Coexpression analysis further revealed contrasting network architectures: C1 TPP genes formed a convergent network with enriched vacuolar/tonoplast-related targets, whereas C2 genes showed a dispersed architecture with no consensus targets. C1-co-expressed candidates included genes related to vacuolar ion homeostasis, cell-wall/glycan remodeling, and isoprenoid/carotenoid metabolism. Together, these results support a model in which duplicated TPP genes are associated with distinct carbohydrate-associated transcriptional programs for starch remobilization and fructose-rich nectar formation. This study provides a genomic resource for Tilia and identifies candidate TPP-centered networks for nectar sugar accumulation in woody honey plants.
items.authors: Lin L, Du J, Li Q, Yu C, Chen L, Li W, Xia F, Mu H.

items.title: Explainable growth stage classification of cacao (Theobroma cacao L.) leaves and key feature visualization using vision transformer and transfer learning.
items.abstract: Accurate and objective plant phenotyping is crucial for optimizing agricultural practices, understanding plant development, and enabling rapid responses to environmental changes. Traditional methods, often relying on visual observation, can be subjective, time-consuming, and may overlook subtle but important differences. This study demonstrates the power of combining digital imaging with deep learning to classify plant material with high accuracy, even when visual differences are minimal. We focused on differentiating between stage D (light green) and stage E (dark green) leaves of cacao (Theobroma cacao L.), which are visually very similar in size and overall structure. Using cleared and stained leaves of the SCA 6 genotype to highlight the venation network, we trained a Vision Transformer (ViT) model, a deep learning architecture, on image patches. At the patch level, the model achieved an overall accuracy of 97.03% on an independent test set, with a recall of 96.0% for stage D and 98.3% for stage E. At the whole-leaf level, majority voting correctly classified 14 of 15 independent test leaves (93.3%). Attention maps indicated that image regions containing the midrib and primary lateral veins contributed strongly to classification. These attention maps identify discriminative image regions, but they do not by themselves determine the biological mechanism underlying the signal. The major-vein signal may reflect developmental differences in vein-associated structure, stage-associated differences in Safranin O uptake or optical density, tissue thickness, or a combination of these factors. Because vascular anatomy, lignification, hydraulic conductance, phloem loading, and source-sink status were not directly measured, these mechanisms are treated as hypotheses requiring future anatomical, histochemical, and physiological validation. Thus, this study provides a proof-of-concept for interpretable image-based classification of stage D and stage E leaves within greenhouse-grown SCA 6 cacao. Extension to other cacao genotypes, field-grown plants, independent seasons, staining batches, stress detection, species identification, genotype discrimination, or precision-agriculture deployment will require external validation.
items.authors: Ahn E, Park ES, Kim MS, Kim H, Kandpal LM, Park S, Lim S, Meinhardt LW, Cho BK, Baek I.

items.title: Soil Contamination by Salinity and Heavy Metals as a Stress Factor in Fraxinus excelsior Saplings Under Natural and Laboratory Conditions
items.abstract: One of the main causes of common ash decline is the impact of heavy metals and salts accumulated in the soil. Furthermore, harmful chemical compounds contribute to the development of abnormalities in the morphogenesis of plant cells. Studies in natural conditions (in vivo) were conducted to select common ash populations with the highest resistance to salts (NaCl) at varying concentrations and heavy metals such as zinc (Zn), cadmium (Cd), and chromium (Cr). The studies were conducted to facilitate the precise and rapid assessment of the harmful substances impact on the plants health from a given population. Saplings from three populations originating from different geographical and climatic regions in southern and southeastern Poland. To ensure the full multidimensionality of the studies, experiments were also conducted under controlled laboratory conditions (in vitro). The in vitro seedlings grown under sterile conditions, served as a reference pattern with the best physiological. The in vitro plants were used for comparison with saplings grown in vivo. To determine the effect of selected abiotic factors on the saplings, measurements were taken of chlorophyll fluorescence parameters, the maximum quantum yield of photosystem II (Fv/Fm), the maximum efficiency of the water-splitting complex on the donor side of PSII (Fv/Fo), and the time to reach maximum chlorophyll fluorescence (Tfm) for both in vivo and in vitro plants. The studies showed that the values of the parameters studied varied depending on the geographical origin of the studied populations. The analyses of the Fv/Fm and Fv/Fo parameters of individual ash populations showed that the in vivo saplings population from southeastern Poland had the lowest resistance to Zn and Cd. In turn, Zn was the compound that caused the greatest disruptions in Fv/Fm and Fv/Fo functioning in in vivo saplings across all the studied populations. The analysis of the Tfm parameter showed that all toxic substances significantly affected the development of disturbances in the photosynthetic system of all saplings populations examined. The obtained results will help foresters in breeding healthy and resistant saplings and increasing the species population using both in vivo and in vitro methods, taking into account the influence of climate on resistance and the development of adaptive capacity of common ash saplings to the effects of soil contamination.
items.authors: Nawrot-Chorabik K, Osmenda M, Jankowiak R, Latowski D.

items.title: Decoupling Community Complexity From Efficacy: A Meta-Analysis of Synthetic Microbial Communities for Plant Stress Resilience.
items.abstract: Drought, salinity, pollution and nutrient deficiency substantially impair plant growth by disrupting water balance, ion homoeostasis, redox regulation and metabolism. Synthetic microbial communities (SynComs) represent a frontier in microbiome engineering, theoretically offering superior stability over single-strain inoculants through functional redundancy. However, the design rules governing their efficacy - specifically the trade-off between community complexity and phenotypic output - remain empirically unresolved. This meta-analysis evaluated how synthetic microbial communities (SynComs) affect plant growth and stress-related physiological responses under different stress conditions and examined whether their efficacy was associated with community complexity or specific microbial functional traits. Data from 34 studies (433 independent comparisons) were collected. Then, the natural log response ratios (lnRR) of plant morphological and physiological traits were calculated. A random-effects model was used to estimate global effect sizes and quantify between-study heterogeneity. Plant performance was significantly enhanced following SynComs inoculation, evidenced by a 111.93% increase in total biomass (mean lnRR = 0.751). The highest efficacy was observed under biotic stress (total plant dry weight +191.57%) and pollution (underground dry weight +154.23%), with biomass accumulation being more pronounced in belowground traits than in aboveground components. Physiologically, this growth promotion was associated with the alleviation of oxidative stress in plants, as manifested by the significant upregulation of antioxidant enzymes (CAT + 47.09%, POD + 41.55%, and SOD + 44.71%) and a concurrent reduction in lipid peroxidation. Furthermore, the weighted meta-analysis revealed that single-genus communities significantly outperformed multi-genus communities in the present dataset (p = 0.004). However, efficacy was entirely decoupled from community richness, measured as strain number (R2 = 0.000, p = 0.490). These findings suggest that greater taxonomic breadth or higher strain richness was not necessarily associated with improved SynCom performance. Rather, efficacy appeared to be driven by specific microbial functional traits (such as IAA production and phosphorus solubilisation). We propose that the rational design of SynComs should prioritise strain function over community size to maximise agricultural sustainability and reduce metabolic burden.
items.authors: Luo W, Wang B, Ma H, Li H.

items.title: Significant effects of host hydraulic traits and host nitrogen-fixing ability on functional traits in the mistletoe Taxillus chinensis
items.abstract: Mistletoes are hemiparasitic plants that rely on hosts for water and nutrients. How host functional traits influence mistletoe’s physiology, especially the interplay between hydraulic architecture and nitrogen acquisition, remains unclear. This study examined the effects of host hydraulic traits and host nitrogen-fixing ability on the mistletoe Taxillus chinensis across seven hosts. We quantified key hydraulic traits in both hosts and parasites, including predawn water potential (ΨPD), minimum water potential (Ψmin), vessel diameter (D), vascular fraction (VF), parenchyma fraction (PF) and fiber fraction (FF). Wood density (WD) and saturated water content (SWC) were measured only in the hosts. Measurements specific to the mistletoe included chlorophyll content (SPAD), sapwood-specific hydraulic conductivity (Ks), and photosynthetic rate (A). The mistletoe maintained lower water potentials than hosts, ensuring unidirectional resource flow, and its ΨPD was only weakly correlated with that of the host, indicating some hydraulic autonomy. Correspondingly, the mistletoe had a smaller D, consistent with a developmental response to the lower water potential at the distal end of the water-transport pathway. Host xylem anatomy further shaped mistletoe water status. Hosts with higher VF provided better water supply. Consequently, the mistletoe's ΨPD was less negative. Meanwhile, a lower host WD was associated with a higher saturated water content in the host stem, which buffered drought stress and mitigated declines in the parasite's Ψmin. This improved water status consequently supported the development of larger leaves. Mistletoes on the leguminous hosts Bauhinia purpurea and Erythrina variegata had higher chlorophyll content than those on non-fixing hosts. Mistletoes on Acacia confusa had an intermediate chlorophyll content. Photosynthetic rate was significantly higher in mistletoes on the three nitrogen-fixing hosts than in those on non-fixing hosts. These results are consistent with the host-quality hypothesis and the nitrogen-parasitism hypothesis.
items.authors: Ma R, Ma X, Wang X, Huang C, Li W, Huang Z, Zhang Q.

items.title: Drought Legacies Can Extend to Nutrient Stoichiometry: Relative Potassium Enrichment in Sugar Maple Foliage Outlasts Hydrological Recovery
items.abstract: Abstract Background and Aims : Drought legacies are well documented for growth, carbon allocation and carbohydrate reserves, but whether they extend to mineral nutrition is largely untested. We asked whether a stoichiometric imprint persists in sugar maple foliage once soil moisture has recovered, and whether it can be traced to soil nutrient supply or to wood composition. Methods : In a sugar maple (Acer saccharum Marsh.) forest in Quebec, Canada, throughfall was reduced by about 75% over four growing seasons in three paired plots. The following growing season, when moisture no longer differed from controls, we sampled foliage and fine-branch wood of mature trees and saplings, along with soil pH and ion supply. Six nutrients (N, P, K, Ca, Mg, Mn) were expressed as five isometric log-ratio (ilr) balances, [NPK|CaMgMn], [NP|K], [N|P], [CaMg|Mn] and [Ca|Mg], analysed with linear mixed and structural equation models. Results : Of the five balances, only [NP|K] retained a treatment signal, at both stages: the geometric mean of N and P relative to K was 17.2% lower in exclusion plots, while [N|P] was unchanged, indicating a relative shift toward potassium. No indirect route to the foliage was supported, through either soil supply or wood composition. Conclusion : A nutrient imbalance persisted after hydrological recovery, without a supported source in either soil or wood, pointing to tree regulation as a plausible explanation. Transfer between wood and foliage did not follow the conventional division between mobile and immobile elements. Nutritional constraints may outlast the hydrological signature of drought.
items.authors: Simoneau M, Maheu A, Rivest D, Desrochers A, Nolet P.

items.title: Reading Climate in Wood: A Systematic Review of Dendro-Anatomical Proxies for Climate Reconstruction, Forest Health, and Sustainable Forest Management
items.abstract: Abstract Dendrochronology is increasingly moving from measurements of ring width and density toward cellular-scale records of xylem formation. Wood anatomical elements—including tracheid dimensions, cell-wall characteristics, rays, resin canals, earlywood–latewood structure, and density profiles—can retain environmental information at annual and intra-annual scales. This systematic review synthesizes evidence on how dendro-anatomical proxies contribute to climate reconstruction, forest-health assessment, disturbance history, and sustainable forest management. Following the review protocol described in the supplied manuscript, literature published primarily between 1950 and 2026 was searched across Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, Wiley Online Library, CAB Abstracts, JSTOR, and Google Scholar, supplemented by authoritative forestry sources and citation tracking. The selection process identified 3,274 records, removed 728 duplicates, screened 2,546 records, assessed 812 full texts, and retained 287 publications. The synthesis shows that ring width provides a broad annual growth signal, whereas anatomical traits can add information on water availability, temperature, hydraulic adjustment, defence investment, and disturbance timing. Quantitative wood anatomy (QWA) is particularly valuable because it links dated rings to cellular traits such as lumen area and cell-wall thickness, while densitometry and maximum latewood density provide established high-resolution temperature information in appropriate settings. Resin canals can preserve records of defence investment and disturbance but require careful attribution because multiple stressors can produce similar anatomical responses. The review identifies a central research opportunity: integrating anatomical, density, isotopic, remote-sensing, and computational evidence into standardized multi-proxy chronologies, with greater representation of tropical and African forests.
items.authors: Nsofu BM.

items.title: Comparative Analysis of Classical Machine Learning and Deep Learning Regression Models for Codon-Level k-mer Composition Analysis of the Nipah Virus Genome
items.abstract: Abstract The Nipah virus (NiV) is highly virulent zoonotic paramyxovirus, where a complete genome sequence resource is relatively limited compared to other emerging pathogens. In this study, the codon level (3-mer) k-mer composition analysis of 93 complete Nipah virus genome sequences retrieved from the NCBI Nucleotide database was presented. The genomes were encoded into a vector of 64 elements representing the number of appearances of each of the 64 three-nucleotide combinations. The feature set was subjected to descriptive statistics, covariance and Pearson correlation between each feature, which showed very high degrees of pairwise collinearity in the set of codon-count features. Using a correlation-based feature-selection procedure (|r| > 0.99), the feature space was reduced from 64 to 5 almost independent codon counts (AAA, TAG, TCG, CGC and CCG). We considered seven regression algorithms across three learning paradigms (classical models: Linear Regression, K-Nearest Neighbors, Support Vector Machine/SVR, an ensemble model: Random Forest, deep sequential models: Long Short-Term Memory network and Simple Recurrent Neural Network, and a Decision Tree baseline) and compared their performance using the number of codons CCG as a regression target and the remaining four codon counts as predictors. The 70/20/10 train/validation/test split was used to train all models, and they were compared using the coefficient of determination (R²), root mean squared error (RMSE), and mean absolute error (MAE). Decision Tree Regression achieved the best performance (R² = 0.9945), followed by Linear Regression (R² = 0.9908), Random Forest (R² = 0.9892), LSTM (R² = 0.9731), and SimpleRNN (R² = 0.9718), while KNN (R² = 0.8038) and SVM/SVR (R² = 0.1038 with feature scaling) underperformed. The results are evaluated with the knowledge of the large compositional constraints on codon usage over a set of Nipah virus genomes, the known sensitivity of instance- and margin-based regressors to unscaled, collinear small-sample data, and the limited benefit of deep sequential architectures on a pseudo-sequence of a very small tabular sample (no temporal dimension). This paper presents in a transparent manner the pipeline results, statistical results and comparative modeling results, along with the limitations of the dataset, as a baseline for future codon-composition based computational studies of Nipah virus.
items.authors: Abid¹ A, Bilal¹ M, Khan SUR.

items.title: Effects of winter waterlogging on apple root and soil summer microbiome
items.abstract: Abstract Background Winter waterlogging is an increasingly common abiotic stress factor in temperate horticulture. While the physiological responses of apple ( Malus × domestica ) to waterlogging during the active growing season have been investigated, the impact of waterlogging on the soil and root microbiome, especially during the winter dormant period, remains unknown. This study investigated the legacy effects of winter waterlogging on apple root and soil microbiota 6–9 months after treatment. Potted MM106 rootstocks were subjected to four weeks of continuous waterlogging in December across two independent experimental replicates, with one cohort subjected to two waterlogging treatments over two consecutive winters. Fungal (ITS) and bacterial (16S rRNA gene) communities were assessed using amplicon sequencing to determine community size, diversity, structure, and taxonomic responses to waterlogging. Results Results indicated that community assembly was primarily driven by experimental replicate and temporal succession rather than the waterlogging treatment. However, a specific anaerobic legacy was identified. The anaerobic bacterial genera Geomonas , Geobacter , and Desulfuromonas were consistently enriched across experiments, with an increase in the abundance of Geomonas associated with single and repeated waterlogging events. Conversely, aerobic saprotrophs were depleted, and potential fungal pathogens, Gibellulopsis and Plectosphaerella , were also depleted. Conclusions These findings suggest that winter waterlogging induces a stable shift in the microbiota characterised by a persistent anaerobic bacterial signature and a simplified fungal community. This legacy effect may influence nutrient cycling and stress resilience when trees resume active growth in the spring.
items.authors: McLean H, Mikaberidze A, Deakin G, Xu X, Papp-Rupar M.

items.title: Interfacial Electron-Proton Dual Modulation of Fe Single-Atom Catalyst by α-MoC for O2 Activation and Lignin Depolymerization.
items.abstract: Efficient O2 activation under mild conditions is central to oxidative biomass valorization, yet single-atom catalysts often suffer from sluggish proton-coupled oxygen intermediate conversion, particularly because of overly strong *OH adsorption. Inspired by the cooperative electron and proton management in cytochrome c oxidase, we report an α-MoC/Fe-N4 catalyst in which α-MoC nanoparticles are interfaced with Fe-N4 single-atom sites on a nitrogen-doped carbon scaffold. The α-MoC component plays a dual role: it withdraws electron density from Fe sites to weaken oxygen-intermediate adsorption and promotes water dissociation to provide local protons for *OH-to-H2O conversion. As a result, α-MoC/Fe-N4 exhibits a 2.8-fold higher Vmax for O2 activation than Fe-N4 and proceeds through a nearly four-electron oxygen reduction pathway with negligible reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation. This interfacial strategy is generalizable to various M-N-C single-atom catalysts, including Mn, Co, Ni, Cu, Sn, Ir, and Pt. Enabled by efficient O2 activation, α-MoC/Fe-N4 depolymerizes native birch lignin under mild alkaline conditions, substantially decreasing its molecular weight and cleaving β-O-4, β-β, and β-5 linkages. This work establishes an electron-proton dual-modulation strategy for constructing high-performance single-atom catalysts for biomass conversion.
items.authors: Shi R, Wu J, Song B, Liu Q, Liu L, Li F, Li X, Wang X, Chen Y, Zheng X, Li Y, Mao Y, Chen K, Wu Y.

items.title: Chicken manure and cow manure regulate phytoremediation of cadmium-contaminated alkaline soils through distinct mechanisms.
items.abstract: Phytoremediation can completely remove harmful heavy metals from soil; however, it is limited by low efficiency and long cycling times. In this study, to further improve the efficiency of phytoremediation of alkaline cadmium (Cd)-contaminated soils, we investigated the enhanced Cd uptake capacity of Tagetes patula L. through manure application and explored its underlying mechanisms. The results indicate that chicken manure significantly increased soil available Cd through pH reduction, thereby enhancing Cd enrichment in T. patula. In contrast, cow manure did not alter soil pH or available Cd. However, it substantially promoted plant biomass, leading to increased total Cd uptake primarily via a biomass-amplification mechanism. Both manures improved plant physiological status and altered root metabolomic profiles, upregulating Cd-related defense pathways. They also enriched beneficial soil microbial taxa (e.g. Bacteroidota and Patescibacteria) and enhanced soil enzyme activity. Overall, livestock manures can enhance phytoremediation of Cd-contaminated alkaline soils but via distinct mechanisms: chicken manure acts through Cd mobilization and direct uptake, whereas cow manure relies on growth promotion and improved plant tolerance. These findings provide a theoretical basis and application value for optimizing manure-assisted phytoremediation strategies: chicken manure is suitable for short-term Cd removal scenarios, while cow manure is better suited for long-term soil remediation combined with sustainable agricultural practices.
items.authors: Mi L, Qin X, Huang Q, Zhao L, Sun Y.

items.title: Distribution, Development, and Function of Resin Canals in Conifers: Insights from Cellular and Genomic Perspectives.
items.abstract: Resin canals are tunnel-like tissue structures primarily responsible for synthesizing and secreting resin. They consist of specialized secondary metabolite-synthesizing epithelial cells and supportive subsidiary cells, which are arranged to form distinctive intercellular spaces. In conifers, resin canals can develop during normal development or be induced by environmental stimuli, which often form an interconnected network and play a crucial role in defense against pathogens and insects. Despite their importance in resin secretion and defense, the mechanisms underlying their formation and function remain poorly understood. In this review, we summarize recent advances in the study of resin canals in conifers from the perspectives of cellular development, defense mechanisms, and molecular regulation. We analyze the distribution patterns, subcellular characteristics and formation and developmental processes of resin canals across different conifer species. Based on studies of traumatic resin canals, we propose a developmental model that depicts the initiation from cambial activity to cell differentiation and canal formation. Furthermore, we focus on resin canal-specific genes and analyze the functions and expression patterns of identified related genes. With the advancement of conifer genome sequencing and single-cell technologies, future research on resin canal regulatory mechanisms and functions is facing unprecedented opportunities. We propose a strategic framework aimed at enhancing conifer breeding, particularly for traits such as stress resilience, disease resistance and wood quality.
items.authors: Feng Y, Diao S, Lin X, Wang C, Wang X, Wang Y, Yin H.

items.title: Multiple evolutionary routes to cytoskeletal arborization revealed by the rhizarian amoeba Filoreta ramosa.
items.abstract: The eukaryotic cytoskeleton generates remarkable diversity in cellular architecture despite being built from conserved actin and tubulin polymers. Diversification of cytoskeletal regulators, motors, and filament-organizing proteins produces varied morphologies, yet certain architectures repeatedly emerge in distantly related lineages. One notable example is cytoskeletal arborization, occurring in metazoan neurons and amoeboid lineages throughout the eukaryotic tree. Whether these similar branched architectures arise through conserved cytoskeletal organization, shared molecular reuse, or convergence driven by common physical constraints remains unresolved. Here, we investigate the rhizarian amoeba Filoreta ramosa, which forms a multinucleate reticulated network through branching and anastomosis. Using live imaging, immunofluorescence, morphometric analyses, and cytoskeletal drugs, we define how actin and microtubule systems organize branch formation, intracellular transport, and large-scale network architecture. Actin-rich protrusions initiate exploratory branchlets that become selectively stabilized through microtubule incorporation. Longitudinal microtubule arrays reinforce mature branches and support rapid bidirectional organelle transport, while branch nodes function as distributed sites of microtubule nucleation. These cytoskeletal features parallel key mechanisms underlying neuronal arborization, yet unlike neurons, Filoreta develops a decentralized reticulated network through repeated anastomosis and distributed microtubule organization, thereby scaling transport capacity and structural support with network growth. Our findings suggest that shared cytoskeletal mechanisms repeatedly support branching architectures, while distinct topologies and modes of organization allow evolution to reach arborization through different routes as increasing cellular scale imposes common demands on transport and structural integrity. Filoreta therefore provides a tractable model for investigating how conserved cytoskeletal systems generate arborized architectures that scale with cellular size.
items.authors: Guest SL, Dawson SC.

items.title: Rapid evolutionary responses to climate change in maritime pine (Pinus pinaster Ait.) despite widespread adaptive lag
items.abstract: Climate change is profoundly affecting species worldwide and poses a major threat to their long-term persistence. Although trees may have the potential for rapid adaptation to changing climates, empirical evidence remains limited, and whether these long-lived organisms can adapt quickly enough to keep pace with ongoing climate change is still an open question. To investigate real-time responses to contemporary climate change, we combined genomic data from 82 range-wide populations of the widespread tree Pinus pinaster Ait. with intensive sampling of two successive cohorts from two natural populations. Using an original genotype-environment association (GEA) approach to quantify climate (mal)adaptation, we found that most individuals from both target populations showed evidence of an adaptive lag to current climatic conditions, and are predicted to face substantial risk of maladaptation under future climates. Importantly, changes in genomic composition at climate-associated loci between cohorts were consistent with rapid evolutionary responses to ongoing climate change and could not be explained by neutral demographic processes alone, as supported by forward-time genetic simulations. We also observed a lower realised genetic load in the younger cohort, suggesting that the dynamics of deleterious mutations may change with climatic pressure. Our work provides evidence suggesting genetic responses to contemporary climate change within a single generation, including signals of rapid evolutionary changes in genomic composition at climate-associated loci and signatures of purifying selection, despite widespread adaptive lag to current climates. These findings challenge the view that trees only respond slowly to environmental change and highlight the need to integrate evolutionary dynamics into predictive models of species persistence under future climates.
items.authors: Francisco, T., Lesur-Kupin, I., Scotti, I., Avanzi, C., Bagnoli, F., Vendramin, G. G., Grivet, D., Westergren, M., Vajana, E., Archambeau, J., Piotti, A., Gonzalez-Martinez, S. C.

items.title: Invasive Chinese tallow is associated with distinct rhizosphere microbial communities, core microbiomes, and functional potential relative to native Loblolly pine
items.abstract: Plant invasions frequently reshape belowground microbial communities, yet their effects on rhizosphere microbiome structure and function remain poorly understood. We compared the rhizosphere bacterial and fungal microbiomes of invasive Chinese tallow (Triadica sebifera) and native Loblolly pine (Pinus taeda) using 16S rRNA gene and ITS amplicon sequencing, together with microbial, functional, and soil analyses. Chinese tallow exhibited significantly greater bacterial and fungal richness and distinct microbial community composition than Loblolly pine. The invasive rhizosphere was enriched in plant-beneficial bacterial taxa, including Streptomyces, Bradyrhizobium, and Rhizobium, and ectomycorrhizal-associated fungi such as Russula and Cenococcum. This enrichment is consistent with enhanced nutrient acquisition, plant growth promotion, and stress tolerance, potentially favoring Chinese tallow establishment and persistence. Further, core microbiome and co-occurrence network analyses revealed extensive reorganization of persistent (Streptomyces, Russula) and highly connected microbial taxa that may be associated with Chinese tallow invasion. Functional predictions indicated greater representation of carbohydrate degradation, nitrogen fixation, plant growth promotion, nutrient mineralization, and ectomycorrhizal guilds in the Chinese tallow rhizosphere, whereas lignin degradation and saprotrophic or pathogen-associated fungal guilds were relatively more abundant under Loblolly pine. Soil physicochemical properties were also strongly correlated with dominant bacterial and fungal taxa, indicating that host-mediated microbial recruitment and environmental filtering jointly shaped rhizosphere community assembly. Overall, our findings identify rhizosphere microbiome reassembly as an important belowground feature associated with Chinese tallow invasion.
items.authors: Khan, M., Pant, B., Kabir, A. H.

items.title: Gene expression dynamics through time reveal low pleiotropy genes underlying local adaptation in silver birch (Betula pendula)
items.abstract: Understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying local adaptation in boreal trees is important for assessing their adaptive potential under climate change. The role of pleiotropy in polygenic local adaptation remains poorly understood. Here we studied growth and temporal transcriptomic responses to photoperiod in three photoperiod treatments in three populations of Betula pendula within a two-week time period to identify genes and co-expression networks underlying local adaptation and to estimate the level of pleiotropy in population specific gene expression. We used RNA sequencing to characterize the temporal transcriptomic responses which were analyzed with variance partitioning, differential gene expression and weighted co-expression network analyses. Photoperiod treatment and sampling time were the main drivers of gene expression variation both at the co-expression module and single gene level. The majority of circadian clock and flowering time genes exhibited striking similarity across populations. Nevertheless, we detected small but significant population effects in the temporal gene expression patterns which were concentrated on the periphery of the co-expression networks consistent with low pleiotropy effects. Our findings suggest that local adaptation to growing season length among populations exhibiting very low genetic differentiation along a latitudinal cline in B. pendula is likely polygenic and potentially governed through low pleiotropy genes.
items.authors: Siren, J., Vuosku, J., Kujala, S. T., Kärkkäinen, K., Perraud, Y., Punttila, J., Verta, J.-P., Pyhäjärvi, T.

items.title: Integrated multi-omics analysis of root transcriptomic, metabolomic, and bacterial-community responses associated with rhizobial inoculation and cadmium exposure in Robinia pseudoacacia
items.abstract: Abstract Cadmium (Cd) contamination threatens soil ecosystems and food security. Robinia pseudoacacia is a potential candidate for phytoremediation, but the molecular responses and root-associated microbial responses accompanying rhizobial symbiosis under Cd exposure remain incompletely understood. We integrated root transcriptomic, internal-root metabolomic, and 16S rRNA gene sequencing data to characterize responses to Cd exposure and rhizobial inoculation in SX, the high shoot-Cd accumulator, and HB, the low shoot-Cd accumulator. SX and HB exhibited distinct transcriptional patterns and exploratory candidate-metabolite profiles. In SX, the transcriptional responses were associated with the greater shoot Cd translocation reported previously for this genotype. In HB, rhizobial inoculation under Cd exposure was associated with broader changes in candidate metal-transport and compartmentalization genes, consistent with its previously reported greater root Cd retention. Rhizobial inoculation was also associated with higher candidate abundances of leucine, trehalose, palmitic acid, thymine, and pantothenates in HB, whereas inoculated SX showed higher candidate abundances of leucine and isoleucine but lower internal L-malic acid. Cd exposure, rhizobial inoculation, and root compartment were associated with variation in bacterial community composition, including abundance patterns involving Pseudomonas, Devosia, and Rhizobium. Exploratory Spearman correlation analyses revealed compartment-specific patterns of covariation between candidate metabolites and bacterial genera; however, no metabolite-genus association remained statistically significant after Benjamini-Hochberg correction in the rhizoplane, endosphere, or rhizosphere. None of the compartment-specific Procrustes tests indicated significant overall concordance between bacterial community composition and root-metabolite profiles. Collectively, these findings identify candidate genes, metabolites, and bacterial taxa and provide testable hypotheses that could inform future genotype selection and microbiome-assisted phytoremediation strategies.
items.authors: Gao L, Sun X, Wang X, Wang S, Du H, Ma M

items.title: Species-specific budburst responses to diurnal temperature cycles during chilling and forcing in temperate deciduous trees
items.abstract: Abstract Cold temperatures (‘chilling’) perceived by tree buds progressively release winter dormancy and initiate sensitivity to warmer temperatures (‘forcing’) required for budburst. Phenology of temperate trees may also respond to daylength, but it remains unclear whether chilling and forcing accumulation is linked to the diurnal cycle. Here, we tested whether chilling accumulation is influenced by light–dark cycle frequency, and whether forcing is more effective during daylight. We harvested twig cuttings from four temperate tree species (Fagus sylvatica, Carpinus betulus, Quercus robur and Acer pseudoplatanus) with contrasting chilling and forcing requirements. In Experiment 1, twigs were harvested in November and exposed to 3°C under three light–dark cycle frequencies: 12h light/12h dark, 6h/6h, and 4h/4h (1, 2 or 3 cycles/day) for one or two months (short vs. long chilling). Twigs were then transferred to two forcing regimes with the same daily mean but different day/night temperatures (25°C/10°C and 20°C/15°C). In Experiment 2, twigs were harvested after substantial chilling and exposed to opposite day/night forcing regimes (25°C/10°C vs. 10°C/25°C). In Experiment 1, shorter light–dark cycles under long chilling delayed budburst in C. betulus, whereas effects on budburst success depended on chilling duration in C. betulus and Q. robur. Interestingly, budburst occurred significantly earlier at 25°C/10°C than at 20°C/15°C in all species, up to 12 days in F. sylvatica, suggesting more effective daytime forcing or non-linear forcing accumulation. Experiment 2 demonstrated that forcing was more effective during daylight, with 10%, 19% and 51% more degree days required for budburst under warm nights in Q. robur, C. betulus and F. sylvatica, respectively, but no difference in A. pseudoplatanus. Our study shows that light–temperature interactions and non-linear forcing responses can shape budburst timing, implying that tree phenological responses to warming may depend not only on its magnitude but also on its timing within the diurnal cycle.
items.authors: Vitasse Y, Hoch G, Pepin S, Giardina F

items.title: Xylogenesis and wood anatomical traits of Pinus pinaster under different resin tapping regimes
items.authors: Carvalho A, Campelo F, Nabais C, Garcia-Forner N

items.title: Dormancy type, seed traits, and species identity shape seed‐associated fungal community composition in tropical pioneer trees
items.abstract: Summary Seed germination is regulated in many plants by seed dormancy, while postdispersal survival is often determined by soilborne fungi that infect seeds. In tropical forests, seeds in each of three dormancy types (physical, physiologically dormant, or quiescent) often share similar physical and chemical traits. We hypothesized that variation in seed traits aligned with seed dormancy should shape seed‐associated fungal communities, linking dormancy to seed survival. Seeds of 18 pioneer tree species were buried in each of five common garden plots in a lowland tropical forest in Panama for up to 36 months. Seeds were screened for viability and fungal infection at intervals throughout the experiment. Plant species with different dormancy types harbored distinct fungal communities. Dormancy type explained 6.5% of variation in fungal community composition after accounting for the far stronger signature of plant species identity (34%). Within dormancy types, differences in seed traits among species explained 49–56% of the variation in fungal communities, suggesting that seed traits drive niche partitioning beyond what is imposed by dormancy type alone. This study shows that variation in seed traits within a dormancy type filters seed‐associated fungal communities, which likely shapes the demography of tropical forest trees by influencing seed survival and germination.

items.title: Provenance and environment jointly shape early regeneration in fir and beech: evidence from distributed participatory trials across Europe
items.abstract: Summary Forest regeneration is shaped by strong demographic filters during germination and early establishment, yet the relative contributions of seed provenance and environment remain poorly understood under natural conditions. We combined climate‐chamber trials with a continental‐scale, field‐based citizen science seed‐sowing experiment to quantify germination, early phenological development, and 3‐yr postgermination survival of fir ( Abies spp.) and beech ( Fagus spp.) provenances across Europe. We estimated germination metrics, reconstructed phenological trajectories, and quantified successive demographic filters from seed to established seedling. Germination was structured by provenance‐by‐environment interactions in both genera, but with contrasting expression. Fir showed broadly parallel environmental responses among provenances and partial concordance between climate‐chamber and field results, whereas beech exhibited strong provenance‐by‐environment responses and weak predictability from controlled conditions. Seed weight was a key axis of variation in beech (lighter seeds germinated more frequently and developed faster), but its effects in fir were confounded with geographic differentiation. Post‐establishment survival was dominated by site‐level environmental filtering and site‐by‐provenance interactions, with limited consistent provenance effects. This reveals a life‐stage shift from fine‐scale provenance‐by‐environment effects during germination and early development to broader environmental control of survival – an important consideration for regeneration‐based management and assisted migration.

items.title: Quantifying Dynamic Changes in Stem Storage‐Water Use and Rehydration in Mature Trees: A Study on Pinus sylvestris Trees Exposed to Increased Atmospheric and Soil Drought
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Forests increasingly experience hot droughts, characterized by rising vapour pressure deficits (VPD) and declining soil moisture, highlighting the need to better understand water fluxes within trees. While stomatal conductance and transpiration are well studied, upstream fluxes such as internal stem water storage use and rehydration dynamics remain poorly quantified, despite their importance for maintaining tissue hydration and growth. Here, we quantify storage‐water use and rehydration dynamics by combining high‐resolution sap flow and dendrometer measurements in mature Pinus sylvestris at the VPDrought experiment of the Pfynwald research platform, where rain‐water input and VPD are independently manipulated. Fluxes were analyzed over the 2024 growing season in relation to VPD and soil water potential ( ψ soil ). The relative contribution of internal stem water storage to daily transpiration increased with drought, rising from about 10% under well‐watered conditions to up to 55% under dry conditions, mainly caused by reduced transpiration while storage water use is sustained. Notably, under mild soil drought, high nighttime VPD substantially constrained nighttime tissue rehydration fluxes. Overall, our novel framework highlights the dynamic role of stem water storage in modulating water potentials during drought and demonstrates the importance of explicitly considering temporal stem water storage dynamics when assessing tree water‐use strategies.

items.title: Peptide Signalling as a Control Layer for Signal Prioritisation in Plant Stress Networks
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Plants in the field rarely encounter single stresses, and simultaneous stresses impose conflicting physiological demands that cannot be satisfied at once. Responses to such combinations are frequently non‐additive and cannot be predicted from single‐stress responses, a result that crosstalk models struggle to accommodate because they describe which pathways interact without specifying which prevails. This review proposes that peptide signalling functions as a control layer governing signal prioritisation. Under this hypothesis, secreted peptides act above the shared modules of cytosolic calcium, reactive oxygen species, and mitogen‐activated protein kinase cascades, and determine which competing input is permitted to dominate their behaviour. Evidence for this proposal spans several peptide families. CEP, CLE and RALF signalling illustrate systemic demand signalling, developmental stabilisation, and receptor complex reorganisation respectively, and the same logic extends to PEP, IDA and PSK signalling across immune, developmental, and drought contexts. Combined drought and nitrogen limitation, resolved through ABA and CEP, provides a worked case in which a global signal sets operating boundaries within which a local signal refines the response, supported by evidence now extending from Arabidopsis into cereals. We derive falsifiable predictions tested against hormone‐pathway negative controls and graded drought intensities rather than single treatments, which allows loss of prioritisation to be distinguished from general signalling fragility. We also identify a trade‐off constraining crop application, since enhancing peptide‐mediated nutrient foraging may reduce drought resilience. Substantial gaps remain in detecting peptide signals directly and in ranking peptide families under field conditions. Reframing plant signalling as a decision system rather than an input‐output relay offers a testable foundation for improving stress resilience and nutrient use efficiency in crop breeding.

items.title: Mapping wood formation across scales: Models, methods and experiments
items.abstract: Abstract The formation of xylem and phloem by the vascular cambium is a cellular process that is influenced by biotic and abiotic factors at sub-seasonal timescales. However, the significance of cambial activity extends across space (up to ecosystems) and time (up to centuries). This relates to the functional importance of xylem and phloem and the extremely long persistence of woody tissues, which are also a major carbon sink. Hence, studying this phenomenon involves a wide variety of approaches and methods that fundamentally vary in their temporal and spatial scales. From global vegetation dynamics to maple syrup production, the articles in the special collection ‘Advances in Xylem and Phloem Formation Research’ well reflect this diversity. Collectively, they reveal the complexity of underlying mechanisms and the potential for implementation of simpler schemes into global models.
